subject: natural-sciences-sp
description: Natural Sciences Senior Phase question bank. Keyed by atomic skill id (topic id IS skill id). Grade 7 topic skeletons in place; ~20-item pools authored per topic in the content phase.

NSSP.G7.LL.A1.title: The biosphere
NSSP.G7.LL.A1.description: The biosphere as the part of Earth where life exists; the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere as its components; and the five requirements for sustaining life (air, water, food, shelter, suitable temperature).
NSSP.G7.LL.A1.recovery_strategy: Anchor each sphere to one word: lithosphere = land/rock, hydrosphere = water, atmosphere = air. The biosphere is where all three overlap and life can live.

questions.question: What is the biosphere?
options: The part of Earth where living things can survive
The hot centre of the Earth
A layer of rock deep underground
The empty space between the planets
questions.expected: The part of Earth where living things can survive
questions.memo: The biosphere is the thin zone of land, water and air where life exists.

questions.question: Which word names the LAND or rock part of the Earth?
questions.memo: Litho- means rock or stone, so the lithosphere is the solid land.

questions.question: Which word names the WATER part of the Earth?
questions.memo: Hydro- means water, so the hydrosphere is all the oceans, rivers and lakes.

questions.question: Which word names the AIR that surrounds the Earth?
questions.memo: The atmosphere is the layer of gases (air) that surrounds the Earth.

questions.question: True or false: the biosphere is the part of Earth where living things are found.
questions.memo: True — the biosphere is exactly the zone where life exists.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The ___ is made up of the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere working together to support life.'
questions.memo: Life depends on land, water and air together — that overlap is the biosphere.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT something living organisms need to survive?
questions.memo: Living things need air, water, food, shelter and a suitable temperature — not plastic.

questions.question: A fish spends its whole life in a river. Which sphere is its main home?
questions.memo: A river is water, so the fish lives mainly in the hydrosphere.

questions.question: An astronaut steps onto the Moon, which has almost no air. Which requirement for life is missing there?
questions.memo: The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so there is no air to breathe.

questions.question: Which list gives FIVE things living organisms need to stay alive?
options: Air, water, food, shelter, suitable temperature
questions.expected: Air, water, food, shelter, suitable temperature
questions.memo: The five basic needs are air, water, food, shelter and a suitable temperature.

questions.question: Sort each place into the correct sphere of the Earth.
questions.expected: Land features → lithosphere; water → hydrosphere; air and clouds → atmosphere.
questions.memo: Solid land (mountain, soil) is the lithosphere; water (ocean, river) is the hydrosphere; air and clouds are the atmosphere.

questions.question: True or false: the atmosphere is mostly made of solid rock.
questions.memo: False — the atmosphere is made of gases (air). Solid rock is the lithosphere.

questions.question: Why is most life found where land, water and air meet?
options: Living things need all three to survive
Water keeps away from the air there
questions.expected: Living things need all three to survive
questions.memo: Most living things need land or water to live in or on, plus air — so life thrives where the spheres overlap.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Animals take in ___ from the air so their bodies can release energy from food.'
questions.memo: Animals breathe in oxygen from the air (the atmosphere).

questions.question: A cactus survives in a hot desert where it almost never rains. Which requirement for life is hardest to get there?
questions.memo: Deserts have very little water, so getting enough water is the main challenge for life there.

questions.question: An earthworm tunnels through garden soil. Which sphere is it living in?
questions.memo: Soil is part of the solid land, so the earthworm lives in the lithosphere.

questions.question: True or false: life in the biosphere is found only exactly at sea level, and nowhere higher or lower.
questions.memo: False — life is found deep in the oceans, down in the soil, and high up where birds fly. The biosphere is a whole zone, not a single line.

questions.question: There are no living things on the Moon. Which is the BEST reason why?
options: It has no air, no liquid water and no suitable temperature
It is too close to the Sun
questions.expected: It has no air, no liquid water and no suitable temperature
questions.memo: The Moon lacks air, liquid water and a stable suitable temperature, so it cannot support life.

questions.question: How does 'shelter' help an animal survive?
options: It protects the animal from harsh weather and from danger
It makes food appear from nothing
questions.expected: It protects the animal from harsh weather and from danger
questions.memo: Shelter protects living things from harsh weather and from predators.

questions.question: A sealed glass jar holds soil, a small plant, water and air, and is left in the light. Why can the plant keep living inside?
options: The jar provides air, water, light and a suitable temperature — the needs of life
questions.expected: The jar provides air, water, light and a suitable temperature — the needs of life
questions.memo: The closed jar acts like a tiny biosphere: it supplies air, water, light and warmth, so life can continue.

NSSP.G7.LL.A2.title: Biodiversity & classification
NSSP.G7.LL.A2.description: Biodiversity as the variety of life; classifying living things into groups; and the diversity of animals (vertebrates and invertebrates) and plants.
NSSP.G7.LL.A2.recovery_strategy: Sort by key features, not where it lives: vertebrates have a backbone; mammals breathe air and feed young on milk. Test each organism against the feature, not the habitat.

questions.question: What does the word 'biodiversity' mean?
options: The variety of different living things
The number of rocks in an area
The size of the biggest animal
questions.expected: The variety of different living things
questions.memo: Bio- means life and diversity means variety, so biodiversity is the variety of living things.

questions.question: An animal WITH a backbone is called a...
questions.memo: Animals with a backbone (spine) are vertebrates.

questions.question: An animal WITHOUT a backbone is called an...
questions.memo: Animals with no backbone, like insects and worms, are invertebrates.

questions.question: True or false: classifying living things means sorting them into groups by their features.
questions.memo: True — classification groups living things by shared features.

questions.question: Which features place an animal in the mammal group?
options: It has hair or fur and feeds its young on milk
It has feathers and a beak
It has dry scales and lays eggs
questions.expected: It has hair or fur and feeds its young on milk
questions.memo: Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.

questions.question: Sort each animal into the correct group.
questions.expected: Dog, snake and frog have backbones (vertebrates); spider and earthworm do not (invertebrates).
questions.memo: Check for a backbone: dogs, snakes and frogs have one; spiders and earthworms do not.

questions.question: A whale lives in the sea, but it breathes air and feeds its young on milk. Which group does it belong to?
questions.memo: Living in water does not make it a fish — breathing air and feeding young milk make the whale a mammal.

questions.question: Which of these animals is an invertebrate?
questions.memo: A butterfly has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate. The others are vertebrates.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Animals that have a backbone are called ___.'
questions.memo: Animals with a backbone are vertebrates.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a vertebrate group?
questions.memo: Insects are invertebrates. Mammals, birds and reptiles are all vertebrate groups.

questions.question: A lizard has dry, scaly skin and lays its eggs on land. Which group does it belong to?
questions.memo: Dry, scaly skin and eggs laid on land are signs of a reptile.

questions.question: A frog has smooth, moist skin and can live both in water and on land. Which group does it belong to?
questions.memo: Moist skin and a life both in water and on land are signs of an amphibian.

questions.question: True or false: insects are vertebrates.
questions.memo: False — insects have no backbone, so they are invertebrates.

questions.question: Why is biodiversity important?
options: A variety of living things keeps ecosystems healthy
It increases the number of rocks
It has no effect on nature
questions.expected: A variety of living things keeps ecosystems healthy
questions.memo: A rich variety of living things helps ecosystems stay balanced and healthy.

questions.question: Sort each living thing into the correct group.
questions.expected: Oak tree, grass and fern are plants; lion and eagle are animals.
questions.memo: Plants make their own food and stay in one place; animals move and feed on other living things.

questions.question: Which feature is found only in birds?
questions.memo: Feathers are unique to birds. Many animals have a backbone, eyes and a heart.

questions.question: A gardener finds a small creature with eight legs and no backbone. Is it a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
questions.memo: No backbone means it is an invertebrate (this one is a spider).

questions.question: Which feature do all fish share?
options: They live in water and breathe using gills
They have fur and feed young milk
questions.expected: They live in water and breathe using gills
questions.memo: Fish live in water and use gills to take oxygen from the water.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ has a backbone and fur, and feeds its young on milk.'
questions.memo: Fur and feeding young on milk are signs of a mammal.

questions.question: Two animals look very different, but both have a backbone, fur, and feed their young on milk. What is the BEST conclusion?
options: They both belong to the mammal group
They must be the same species
questions.expected: They both belong to the mammal group
questions.memo: Shared features (backbone, fur, milk) place both in the mammal group, even though they look different.

NSSP.G7.LL.A3.title: Sexual reproduction
NSSP.G7.LL.A3.description: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants (parts of a flower, pollination, fertilisation, seeds and fruit) and an introduction to human reproduction.
NSSP.G7.LL.A3.recovery_strategy: Two steps, in order: pollination = pollen moves to the stigma; fertilisation = the male cell joins the egg inside the ovule. Pollination comes first and makes fertilisation possible.

questions.question: What is pollination?
options: Pollen moving from the anther to the stigma
A seed growing into a plant
A flower opening in the morning
questions.expected: Pollen moving from the anther to the stigma
questions.memo: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther (male part) to the stigma (female part).

questions.question: Which is the MALE part of a flower that makes pollen?
questions.memo: The stamen, with its anther, is the male part that makes pollen.

questions.question: Which is the FEMALE part of a flower that receives pollen?
questions.memo: The stigma is the female part that receives pollen.

questions.question: True or false: fertilisation happens when the male cell joins the egg cell.
questions.memo: True — fertilisation is the joining of the male cell with the egg cell.

questions.question: Look at the flower. Which labelled part is the female part that receives pollen?
questions.memo: The stigma sits at the top of the female part and is sticky to catch pollen.

questions.question: Put the steps of plant reproduction in the correct order, from first to last.

items.text: A fruit develops around the seed

questions.memo: The order is pollination → fertilisation → seed develops → fruit develops.

questions.question: After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a...
questions.memo: Once fertilised, the ovule becomes a seed.

questions.question: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into a...
questions.memo: The ovary grows into a fruit that protects the seeds inside.

questions.question: A bee carries pollen from one flower to another flower. What is this process called?
questions.memo: Moving pollen between flowers is pollination.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: '___ comes first and makes fertilisation possible.'
questions.memo: Pollen must first reach the stigma (pollination) before fertilisation can happen.

questions.question: Which of these can carry pollen between flowers?
questions.memo: Pollen is commonly carried by insects (like bees) and by the wind.

questions.question: True or false: pollination and fertilisation are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: False — pollination is pollen reaching the stigma; fertilisation is the male cell joining the egg. They are two different steps.

questions.question: Why are the petals of many flowers brightly coloured and scented?
questions.memo: Bright colour and scent attract insects, which then carry pollen between flowers.

questions.question: During puberty, the human body...
options: changes and becomes able to reproduce
questions.expected: changes and becomes able to reproduce
questions.memo: Puberty is the time when the body matures and becomes able to reproduce.

questions.question: Human fertilisation joins a sperm cell and...
questions.memo: In humans, a sperm cell joins an egg cell at fertilisation.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In humans, a baby grows and develops inside the mother's ___.'
questions.memo: A baby develops in the uterus (womb), not the stomach.

questions.question: What must happen before a seed can form in a flower?
questions.memo: A seed only forms after the egg inside the ovule is fertilised.

questions.question: A flower is covered with a fine bag so that no insects or wind can reach it. What is most likely to happen?
options: It will grow twice as fast
It will turn into an animal
questions.memo: With no insects or wind to carry pollen, pollination cannot happen.

questions.question: Which part protects the flower while it is still a bud?
questions.memo: The sepals enclose and protect the flower bud before it opens.

questions.question: A plant has flowers with no scent, dull colours, and produces lots of light, dry pollen. How is it MOST likely pollinated?
questions.memo: Dull, scentless flowers with light dry pollen are usually wind-pollinated — they do not need to attract insects.

NSSP.G7.LL.A4.title: Variation
NSSP.G7.LL.A4.description: Variation as the differences between individuals of the same species, and how variation helps a species survive in a changing environment.
NSSP.G7.LL.A4.recovery_strategy: Variation is differences within one species — like tall and short people. Two different species (dog vs cat) is not variation.

questions.question: What does 'variation' mean?
options: Differences between individuals of the same kind (species)
questions.expected: Differences between individuals of the same kind (species)
questions.memo: Variation is the small differences between individuals of the same species.

questions.question: True or false: all humans are exactly identical to one another.
questions.memo: False — humans show variation in height, eye colour, fingerprints and much more.

questions.question: Which is an example of variation in humans?
questions.memo: Different heights vary from person to person. The others are shared by all humans.

questions.question: Two dogs of the same breed have different coat colours. What is this an example of?
questions.memo: Differences within the same kind of animal are variation.

questions.question: A dog and a cat are different from each other. Is this variation within a species?
options: No, they are two different species
Yes, they are the same species
No, because they are both pets
questions.expected: No, they are two different species
questions.memo: Variation is differences within ONE species. A dog and a cat are different species, so this is not variation.

questions.question: Cheetahs in a group can run at slightly different top speeds. How can this variation help the group?
options: The faster ones can catch more food and survive better
It makes them all run the same speed
It has no effect at all
questions.expected: The faster ones can catch more food and survive better
questions.memo: Variation means some individuals are better suited to survive — here, the faster cheetahs catch more food.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Differences within one ___ are called variation.'
questions.memo: Variation describes differences within a single species.

questions.question: True or false: variation happens between different species, not within one species.
questions.memo: False — variation is the differences WITHIN one species.

questions.question: Which list shows variation among people?
options: Height, eye colour and hand size
Having lungs, a heart and blood
questions.expected: Height, eye colour and hand size
questions.memo: Height, eye colour and hand size differ from person to person — that is variation.

questions.question: Why is variation useful for a species?
options: Some individuals may survive changes in the environment better
It makes every individual exactly the same
It stops the species from reproducing
questions.expected: Some individuals may survive changes in the environment better
questions.memo: When the environment changes, variation means some individuals are more likely to cope and survive.

questions.question: A disease spreads through a group of rabbits. A few rabbits are naturally resistant and survive. The reason some survived is...
questions.memo: Natural differences (variation) meant a few rabbits were resistant and survived.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT variation within a species?
options: Two cats with different fur lengths
questions.memo: A frog and a fish are different species, so that is not variation. The others are differences within one species.

questions.question: Plants of the same kind can show variation in...
questions.memo: Flower colour can differ between plants of the same kind — that is variation.

questions.question: True or false: variation gives a species a better chance of surviving when the environment changes.
questions.memo: True — with more variation, it is more likely that some individuals can cope with the change.

questions.question: Even learners who look very alike still differ in their...
questions.memo: Fingerprints are unique to each person — a clear example of variation.

questions.question: Winters become very cold. Some sheep in a flock naturally have thicker wool and survive better. They survive because of...
questions.memo: The natural difference in wool thickness (variation) helped some sheep survive the cold.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Variation is differences ___ a species, not between species.'
questions.memo: Variation describes differences within (inside) one species.

questions.question: A farmer keeps seeds only from the tallest maize plants each year. He is making use of...
questions.memo: By choosing the tallest plants, the farmer uses the variation in height that already exists.

questions.question: Which sentence BEST shows variation?
options: Lions in one pride have manes of slightly different sizes
All lions need to eat food
A lion is different from a zebra
questions.expected: Lions in one pride have manes of slightly different sizes
questions.memo: Differences among lions in the same pride is variation within a species.

questions.question: Why might a species with LOTS of variation survive a brand-new disease better than a species with very little variation?
options: Some individuals are more likely to be naturally resistant
It will have no individuals left
questions.expected: Some individuals are more likely to be naturally resistant
questions.memo: More variation raises the chance that at least some individuals are resistant and survive to reproduce.

NSSP.G7.MM.A1.title: Properties of materials
NSSP.G7.MM.A1.description: Physical properties of materials (strength, flexibility, hardness, electrical and thermal conductivity, magnetism) and how a material's properties suit it to a use — plus the environmental impact of using materials.
NSSP.G7.MM.A1.recovery_strategy: Match the job to the property it needs: a wire needs to conduct electricity (copper), a pot handle needs to NOT conduct heat (plastic/wood). Name the property the job needs first.

questions.question: A material that lets electricity pass through it easily is a good...
questions.memo: A conductor lets electricity (or heat) pass through it easily.

questions.question: A material that does NOT let electricity pass through it is an...
questions.memo: An insulator blocks the flow of electricity (or heat).

questions.question: Which property means a material can bend without breaking?
questions.memo: Flexibility is the ability to bend without breaking.

questions.question: True or false: copper is a good conductor of electricity.
questions.memo: True — copper conducts electricity very well, which is why it is used in wires.

questions.question: Why is copper used for electrical wires?
questions.memo: Copper is chosen because it is an excellent conductor of electricity.

questions.question: Why is the handle of a metal pot often made of plastic or wood?
options: Plastic and wood do not conduct heat well, so the handle stays cool
Plastic conducts heat better than metal
questions.expected: Plastic and wood do not conduct heat well, so the handle stays cool
questions.memo: Plastic and wood are poor heat conductors (insulators), so the handle does not burn your hand.

questions.question: You are choosing a material to make a raincoat. Which property matters most?
questions.memo: A raincoat must keep water out, so being waterproof is the key property.

questions.question: Sort each material by whether it conducts electricity.
questions.expected: Metals (copper, iron, aluminium) conduct; rubber and wood are insulators.
questions.memo: Metals conduct electricity; rubber and wood are insulators that block it.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A material that resists being scratched or dented is described as ___.'
questions.memo: Hardness is the ability to resist scratching or denting.

questions.question: Which material is magnetic?
questions.memo: Iron is attracted to a magnet; plastic, glass and wood are not.

questions.question: Which property makes glass a good material for a window?
options: It is transparent, so light passes through
questions.expected: It is transparent, so light passes through
questions.memo: A window must let light through, so transparency is the important property.

questions.question: True or false: all metals are poor conductors of heat.
questions.memo: False — most metals are GOOD conductors of heat.

questions.question: Which material is best for the body of a cooking pot that must heat up quickly and be strong?
questions.memo: Metal conducts heat well and is strong, so it suits a cooking pot.

questions.question: A bridge must hold up very heavy loads. Which property is most important for the material used?
questions.memo: A bridge carries heavy loads, so strength is the key property.

questions.question: Which property lets you see clearly through a material?
questions.memo: Transparency means light passes through, so you can see through the material.

questions.question: Why is recycling metal good for the environment?
options: It saves resources and reduces the need for new mining
It uses up more raw metal
It has no effect at all
questions.expected: It saves resources and reduces the need for new mining
questions.memo: Recycling reuses metal, so less needs to be mined and less waste is created.

questions.question: A spoon used to stir hot soup should be made of a material that does not burn your hand. Which is best?
options: Wood, because it is a poor conductor of heat
Copper, because it conducts heat well
questions.expected: Wood, because it is a poor conductor of heat
questions.memo: Wood does not conduct heat well, so the handle end stays cool and safe to hold.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Materials that let heat pass through them easily are good ___ of heat.'
questions.memo: Materials that let heat pass through easily are good conductors of heat.

questions.question: Why can using a lot of plastic harm the environment?
options: Plastic waste does not break down easily and pollutes the land and sea
questions.expected: Plastic waste does not break down easily and pollutes the land and sea
questions.memo: Plastic takes a very long time to break down, so it builds up as pollution.

questions.question: An engineer must choose a material for the wiring inside a wall. Which combination is safest and works best?
options: A conductor (copper) covered by an insulator (plastic)
An insulator covered by another insulator
questions.expected: A conductor (copper) covered by an insulator (plastic)
questions.memo: The metal conductor carries the current; the plastic insulator around it keeps people safe from shocks.

NSSP.G7.MM.A2.title: Separating mixtures
NSSP.G7.MM.A2.description: Mixtures and methods of physical separation (hand-sorting, sieving, filtration, evaporation, magnetism), plus sorting and recycling of materials.
NSSP.G7.MM.A2.recovery_strategy: Choose the method by the difference: different sizes → sieving; insoluble solid in liquid → filtration; dissolved solid → evaporation; magnetic bits → a magnet.

questions.question: What is a mixture?
options: Two or more substances mixed together but not chemically joined
questions.expected: Two or more substances mixed together but not chemically joined
questions.memo: In a mixture the substances are mixed but not chemically joined, so they can be separated again.

questions.question: What is the best way to separate sand from small stones, which are different sizes?
questions.memo: A sieve lets the smaller sand fall through and keeps the larger stones — it separates by size.

questions.question: How would you separate insoluble sand from water?
questions.memo: Filtration traps the solid sand in the filter while the water passes through.

questions.question: How would you get the salt back from a cup of salty water?
questions.memo: Heating the water makes it evaporate, leaving the dissolved salt behind.

questions.question: How would you separate iron filings from sand?
questions.memo: A magnet attracts the iron filings but not the sand.

questions.question: Match each mixture to the best way to separate it.
questions.expected: Different sizes → sieving; insoluble solid in water → filtration; dissolved solid → evaporation; iron → magnet.
questions.memo: Pick the method by the difference: size (sieve), insoluble solid (filter), dissolved solid (evaporate), magnetic (magnet).

questions.question: True or false: in a mixture the substances are chemically joined and can never be separated.
questions.memo: False — the substances in a mixture are not chemically joined, so they can be separated by physical methods.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Separating a dissolved solid from water by heating until the water turns to vapour is called ___.'
questions.memo: Evaporation removes the water as vapour and leaves the dissolved solid behind.

questions.question: You have muddy water and want clean water. What is the best step to remove the mud?
questions.memo: Filtration traps the solid mud and lets cleaner water pass through.

questions.question: A magnet is useful for separating which kind of material from a mixture?
questions.memo: Only magnetic materials like iron are attracted to a magnet.

questions.question: Why does filtration work to separate sand from water, but NOT salt from water?
options: Sand is insoluble and stays solid, but salt dissolves and passes through the filter
Water cannot pass through a filter
questions.expected: Sand is insoluble and stays solid, but salt dissolves and passes through the filter
questions.memo: Filters trap solids. Sand stays solid so it is trapped; dissolved salt passes straight through with the water.

questions.question: When sorting materials for recycling, which is grouped correctly?
options: All glass together, all paper together
questions.expected: All glass together, all paper together
questions.memo: Recycling works best when each material is sorted into its own group.

questions.question: You have a mixture of iron filings, salt and sand. Which set of steps separates all three?
options: Magnet for the iron, then add water and filter out the sand, then evaporate to get the salt
Boil everything and keep the steam
questions.expected: Magnet for the iron, then add water and filter out the sand, then evaporate to get the salt
questions.memo: Remove iron with a magnet, dissolve and filter out the insoluble sand, then evaporate the water to recover the salt.

questions.question: True or false: sieving separates particles by their different sizes.
questions.memo: True — a sieve lets small particles through and holds back larger ones.

questions.question: Why do we recycle materials instead of throwing them all away?
options: To save resources and reduce waste
To use up more raw materials
questions.expected: To save resources and reduce waste
questions.memo: Recycling reuses materials, saving resources and cutting down on waste.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Passing a mixture through filter paper to trap the solid bits is called ___.'
questions.memo: Filtration uses filter paper to trap solids while liquid passes through.

questions.question: After all the water has evaporated from a dish of salty water, what is left in the dish?
questions.memo: The water leaves as vapour and the dissolved salt is left behind in the dish.

questions.question: You have made tea with loose tea leaves. How do you remove the leaves before drinking?
questions.memo: A tea strainer is a filter — it traps the leaves and lets the liquid through.

questions.question: Which mixture could be separated simply by hand-sorting?
questions.memo: Large, clearly different objects like coloured beads can be picked apart by hand.

questions.question: You have a mixture of sawdust and iron nails. Which method separates them most easily, and why?
options: A magnet, because iron is magnetic and sawdust is not
Sieving, because they are the same size
questions.expected: A magnet, because iron is magnetic and sawdust is not
questions.memo: A magnet pulls out the iron nails and leaves the non-magnetic sawdust behind.

NSSP.G7.MM.A3.title: Acids, bases & neutrals
NSSP.G7.MM.A3.description: Tastes of substances as a clue to acids and bases; properties of acids, bases and neutral substances; and using acid–base indicators (litmus, universal indicator) to test them.
NSSP.G7.MM.A3.recovery_strategy: Litmus: acid turns it red, base turns it blue ('A' before 'B', red before blue). Neutral stays in between. Learn one indicator's colours solidly before adding others.

questions.question: Acids usually taste...
questions.memo: Acids such as lemon juice and vinegar taste sour. (Never taste lab chemicals to test them!)

questions.question: Lemon juice and vinegar are examples of...
questions.memo: Lemon juice and vinegar are common everyday acids.

questions.question: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acid?
questions.memo: Acid turns blue litmus red. ('A' before 'B' — red before blue.)

questions.question: What colour does red litmus paper turn in a base?
questions.memo: A base turns red litmus blue.

questions.question: True or false: pure water is a neutral substance.
questions.memo: True — pure water is neutral, neither acid nor base.

questions.question: The table shows what happens to BLUE litmus paper in three liquids. Which liquid is an acid?
questions.memo: Acid turns blue litmus red, so Liquid A is the acid.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A substance that is neither an acid nor a base is ___.'
questions.memo: A substance that is neither acid nor base is neutral.

questions.question: Soap and bicarbonate of soda (baking soda) are examples of...
questions.memo: Soap and baking soda are common bases; they often feel soapy.

questions.question: A liquid turns blue litmus paper red. What is the liquid?
questions.memo: Turning blue litmus red is the test result for an acid.

questions.question: Which of these is an indicator used to test for acids and bases?
questions.memo: Litmus is an indicator that changes colour to show acids and bases.

questions.question: Sort each substance as an acid, a base or neutral.
questions.expected: Lemon juice and vinegar are acids; soap and baking soda are bases; pure water is neutral.
questions.memo: Sour kitchen liquids (lemon, vinegar) are acids; soapy substances (soap, baking soda) are bases; pure water is neutral.

questions.question: True or false: it is safe to taste any acid to test it.
questions.memo: False — many acids are harmful. Use an indicator to test, never taste lab chemicals.

questions.question: Universal indicator turns red in a strong acid and purple in a strong base. A substance turns it green. The substance is...
questions.memo: Green is the middle colour of universal indicator, which means the substance is neutral.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'An acid turns blue litmus ___.'
questions.memo: Acid turns blue litmus red.

questions.question: Vinegar is an acid. Which of these is a base?
questions.memo: Bicarbonate of soda is a base; the others are acidic.

questions.question: A gardener's soil is too acidic for the plants. Adding a base to the soil would...
questions.memo: A base cancels out (neutralises) some of the acid, bringing the soil closer to neutral.

questions.question: Which is NOT a property of many acids?
questions.memo: Feeling soapy is a property of bases, not acids.

questions.question: The table shows the pH of three substances. Which substance is the MOST acidic?
questions.memo: The lower the pH, the more acidic. Lemon juice (pH 2) is the most acidic.

questions.question: Red litmus paper stays red when dipped in lemon juice. This tells you lemon juice is...
questions.memo: Red litmus stays red in acids (it only turns blue in a base), so lemon juice is an acid.

questions.question: Why should you never identify an unknown chemical by tasting it in the laboratory?
options: Many acids and bases are harmful — use an indicator instead
Tasting always gives the wrong answer about colour
It is against the rules but perfectly safe
questions.expected: Many acids and bases are harmful — use an indicator instead
questions.memo: Lab acids and bases can burn or poison you, so always test safely with an indicator.

NSSP.G7.MM.A4.title: Introduction to the Periodic Table
NSSP.G7.MM.A4.description: The Periodic Table as an organised list of the elements; the arrangement into rows and columns; and the properties that separate metals, semi-metals and non-metals.
NSSP.G7.MM.A4.caps_topic: Introduction to the Periodic Table of Elements
NSSP.G7.MM.A4.recovery_strategy: Metals: shiny, conduct electricity and heat, bend rather than shatter, on the left of the table. Non-metals: dull, poor conductors, brittle, on the right. Semi-metals sit on the dividing line.

questions.question: What is the Periodic Table?
options: An organised table of all the known elements
A list of all the mixtures
questions.expected: An organised table of all the known elements
questions.memo: The Periodic Table arranges all the known elements in an organised way.

questions.question: What is an element?
options: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom
questions.expected: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom
questions.memo: An element is a pure substance made of just one kind of atom, like gold or oxygen.

questions.question: On which side of the Periodic Table are most metals found?
questions.memo: Most metals are on the left and middle of the table; non-metals are on the right.

questions.question: Which is a property of most metals?
options: They are shiny and conduct electricity
questions.expected: They are shiny and conduct electricity
questions.memo: Most metals are shiny and good conductors of electricity and heat.

questions.question: Which is a property of most non-metals?
options: They are dull and poor conductors
They are shiny and bend easily
questions.expected: They are dull and poor conductors
questions.memo: Most non-metals are dull and do not conduct electricity well.

questions.question: True or false: oxygen is a non-metal.
questions.memo: True — oxygen is a non-metal.

questions.question: Sort each element into the correct group.
questions.expected: Iron, copper and gold are metals; oxygen and sulfur are non-metals.
questions.memo: Iron, copper and gold are shiny metals; oxygen and sulfur are non-metals.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Elements on the dividing line, with properties of both metals and non-metals, are called ___.'
questions.memo: Semi-metals (metalloids) sit on the line and share properties of both metals and non-metals.

questions.question: Which of these elements is a metal?
questions.memo: Iron is a metal; oxygen, sulfur and chlorine are non-metals.

questions.question: A shiny element conducts electricity and bends without breaking. It is most likely a...
questions.memo: Shiny, conducts electricity, and bends — these are classic metal properties.

questions.question: A dull element is brittle and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely a...
questions.memo: Dull, brittle and a poor conductor — these are non-metal properties.

questions.question: True or false: each element has its own chemical symbol.
questions.memo: True — every element has its own short chemical symbol, like O for oxygen.

questions.question: The chemical symbol 'O' stands for which element?
questions.memo: O is the symbol for oxygen.

questions.question: Look at the Periodic Table shown. In which region are most of the metals found?
questions.memo: Metals fill the left and middle of the table; non-metals are on the right.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Metals usually ___ electricity and heat well.'
questions.memo: Metals conduct electricity and heat well.

questions.question: Why are the elements arranged in a particular order in the Periodic Table?
options: So that elements with similar properties are grouped together
To list them in alphabetical order
questions.expected: So that elements with similar properties are grouped together
questions.memo: The arrangement groups elements with similar properties together, making patterns easy to see.

questions.question: An unknown element is shiny, can be bent, and conducts electricity. Is it a metal, non-metal or semi-metal?
questions.memo: Shiny, bendable and a good conductor are all metal properties.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a metal?
questions.memo: Sulfur is a non-metal; iron, copper and gold are metals.

questions.question: Where in the Periodic Table are the semi-metals found?
options: Along the line between metals and non-metals
questions.expected: Along the line between metals and non-metals
questions.memo: Semi-metals lie along the staircase line that divides metals from non-metals.

questions.question: An element conducts electricity only a little, and is shiny but brittle. It is best described as a...
questions.memo: Sharing some metal and some non-metal properties (shiny but brittle, conducts a little) describes a semi-metal.

NSSP.G7.EC.A1.title: Sources of energy
NSSP.G7.EC.A1.description: Renewable and non-renewable sources of energy, examples of each, and why renewable sources matter for the future.
NSSP.G7.EC.A1.recovery_strategy: Renewable = will not run out / refills (sun, wind, water, biomass). Non-renewable = a fixed amount that runs out (coal, oil, gas, uranium). Ask: does it refill in a human lifetime?

questions.question: A renewable energy source is one that...
options: will not run out and is replaced naturally
can only be used once and then is gone
questions.expected: will not run out and is replaced naturally
questions.memo: Renewable sources, like the Sun and wind, are replaced naturally and will not run out.

questions.question: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
questions.memo: Sunlight is renewable — it will not run out. Coal, oil and gas are non-renewable.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-renewable source of energy?
questions.memo: Coal is non-renewable — once burned it cannot be replaced quickly.

questions.question: True or false: wind is a renewable source of energy.
questions.memo: True — wind keeps blowing and will not run out, so it is renewable.

questions.question: Sort each energy source as renewable or non-renewable.
questions.expected: Sun, wind and moving water are renewable; coal and oil are non-renewable.
questions.memo: Ask if it refills in a human lifetime: sun, wind and water do (renewable); coal and oil do not (non-renewable).

questions.question: Why are renewable sources better for the future?
options: They are always cheaper to buy
They can only be used once
questions.memo: Renewable sources keep being replaced naturally, so they will not run out.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Coal, oil and gas are ___ sources because they will eventually run out.'
questions.memo: Coal, oil and gas are non-renewable — there is a fixed amount that runs out.

questions.question: A town puts solar panels on its roofs. Which energy source is it using?
questions.memo: Solar panels capture energy from sunlight, which is renewable.

questions.question: Which group contains ONLY non-renewable sources?
questions.memo: Coal, oil and natural gas are all fossil fuels and all non-renewable.

questions.question: Which group contains ONLY renewable sources?
questions.memo: Sun, wind and moving water are all renewable.

questions.question: True or false: non-renewable sources can be replaced quickly once they run out.
questions.memo: False — non-renewable sources take millions of years to form, so they cannot be replaced quickly.

questions.question: Why is burning a lot of coal a problem?
options: It releases pollution and the coal cannot be replaced
It produces no energy at all
questions.expected: It releases pollution and the coal cannot be replaced
questions.memo: Burning coal pollutes the air, and the coal used up is gone for good.

questions.question: A region is often cloudy and has little wind, but it has a large fast-flowing river. Which renewable source could it rely on?
questions.memo: Fast-flowing water can turn turbines to make electricity (hydropower), even when there is little sun or wind.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Energy from moving water is a ___ source.'
questions.memo: Moving water is renewable — rivers keep flowing and rain keeps refilling them.

questions.question: Uranium, which is used in nuclear power stations, is a...
questions.memo: Uranium is mined and there is a limited amount, so it is non-renewable.

questions.question: What is the best reason for a country to use more renewable energy?
options: It reduces pollution and will not run out
It always works only at night
questions.expected: It reduces pollution and will not run out
questions.memo: Renewable energy pollutes less and is not used up, which is better for the future.

questions.question: Why do solar panels not produce electricity at night?
options: There is no sunlight at night for them to use
They are switched off by law
questions.expected: There is no sunlight at night for them to use
questions.memo: Solar panels need sunlight; at night there is none, so they do not generate power.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a fossil fuel?
questions.memo: Wind is a renewable source, not a fossil fuel. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun is a renewable source of energy.
questions.memo: True — the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, so it is renewable.

questions.question: A country wants energy that will not run out AND causes little pollution. Which choice fits BOTH needs best?
options: Renewable sources like the sun, wind and water
questions.expected: Renewable sources like the sun, wind and water
questions.memo: Renewable sources meet both needs: they do not run out and they cause far less pollution.

NSSP.G7.EC.A2.title: Potential & kinetic energy
NSSP.G7.EC.A2.description: Potential energy (stored, e.g. in food, fuels and raised objects) and kinetic energy (energy of movement); how they change into each other in a system; and the law of conservation of energy.
NSSP.G7.EC.A2.recovery_strategy: Energy is never made or destroyed — only changed from one form to another. A raised ball has potential energy; falling, it becomes kinetic; at the bottom it transfers to sound and heat.

questions.question: Kinetic energy is the energy of...
questions.memo: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object.

questions.question: Potential energy is energy that is...
questions.memo: Potential energy is stored energy — for example, in a raised object or stretched spring.

questions.question: A ball is held high up in the air and is not moving. It has mostly...
questions.memo: A raised, still object stores potential energy because of its high position.

questions.question: A ball is rolling quickly across the floor. It has mostly...
questions.memo: A moving object has kinetic energy.

questions.question: True or false: energy can be changed from one form into another.
questions.memo: True — energy changes form, for example potential energy changing into kinetic energy.

questions.question: The law of conservation of energy says that energy is...
options: never made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another
made new whenever we need it
questions.expected: never made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another
questions.memo: Energy is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only changed into a different form.

questions.question: A roller-coaster car goes over a high hill. Put the energy stages in order, from the top of the hill to the bottom.

items.text: At the top: mostly potential energy
Going down: potential changes into kinetic
At the bottom: mostly kinetic energy

questions.memo: Potential energy is greatest at the top; as the car drops it turns into kinetic energy, which is greatest at the bottom.

questions.question: A rubber band is stretched but not yet released. What kind of energy does it store?
questions.memo: A stretched rubber band stores potential energy, ready to be released.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The energy of movement is called ___ energy.'
questions.memo: Movement energy is kinetic energy.

questions.question: Food and fuels store which kind of energy?
questions.memo: Food and fuels store potential (chemical) energy that can be released later.

questions.question: As a ball falls towards the ground, its potential energy changes into...
questions.memo: As it falls and speeds up, the stored potential energy turns into kinetic energy.

questions.question: True or false: when a bouncing ball finally stops, its energy has been completely destroyed.
questions.memo: False — the energy is not destroyed; it has spread to the surroundings as heat and sound.

questions.question: A swing is at its highest point and is about to swing back. At this moment it has...
options: the most potential energy and the least kinetic energy
questions.expected: the most potential energy and the least kinetic energy
questions.memo: At the highest point the swing is momentarily still, so its energy is mostly stored as potential energy.

questions.question: Which of these has kinetic energy?
options: A book resting on a shelf
questions.memo: Only the moving car is in motion, so it has kinetic energy. The others store potential energy.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Energy is never made or destroyed, only ___.'
questions.memo: Energy is only changed (transferred) from one form to another.

questions.question: A child slides down a slide and is moving fast at the bottom. Most of their energy is now...
questions.memo: At the bottom the child is moving fast, so the energy is now mostly kinetic.

questions.question: A wind-up toy is wound up tightly and then let go. What happens to its stored energy?
options: It changes into kinetic energy and the toy moves
It turns into more stored energy
questions.expected: It changes into kinetic energy and the toy moves
questions.memo: Winding stores potential energy; releasing it changes that into kinetic energy that moves the toy.

questions.question: Which of these stores potential energy?
questions.memo: A stretched spring stores potential energy; the others are moving, so they have kinetic energy.

questions.question: True or false: a raised object has potential energy because of its high position.
questions.memo: True — a raised object stores potential energy because of where it is (its height).

questions.question: A diver stands still on a high board, then dives off. Which BEST describes the energy change as she falls?
options: Potential energy changes into kinetic energy
Kinetic energy changes into potential energy
Energy is created as she falls
questions.expected: Potential energy changes into kinetic energy
questions.memo: Standing high up she has potential energy; as she falls and speeds up it becomes kinetic energy.

NSSP.G7.EC.A3.title: Heat transfer
NSSP.G7.EC.A3.description: Heating as a transfer of energy, and the three ways heat moves: conduction (through solids), convection (in liquids and gases) and radiation (through space, no medium needed).
NSSP.G7.EC.A3.recovery_strategy: Conduction needs touching solids; convection needs a moving liquid or gas; radiation needs nothing — it crosses empty space. The Sun warms Earth by radiation.

questions.question: Heat always moves from a...
options: hotter object to a cooler object
cooler object to a hotter object
heavy object to a light object
big object to a small object
questions.expected: hotter object to a cooler object
questions.memo: Heat energy always flows from where it is hotter to where it is cooler.

questions.question: Heat moving along a solid metal spoon is an example of...
questions.memo: In a solid, heat passes from particle to particle by conduction.

questions.question: Heat moving through a liquid or gas, with the warm part rising, is called...
questions.memo: In liquids and gases, warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks — this is convection.

questions.question: Heat from the Sun reaching the Earth through empty space is an example of...
questions.memo: Radiation needs no material to travel through, so the Sun's heat crosses empty space this way.

questions.question: True or false: conduction happens best in solids, especially metals.
questions.memo: True — solids, especially metals, conduct heat well.

questions.question: Sort each example by the way heat is transferred.

items.text: A metal spoon heating up in hot tea
Warm air rising above a heater
Feeling a fire's warmth from across the room
Hot water circulating in a boiling pot

questions.expected: Through solids → conduction; moving warm fluids → convection; across space without a medium → radiation.
questions.memo: Solid touching solid is conduction; warm liquid or gas moving is convection; heat crossing space is radiation.

questions.question: The Sun warms the Earth across millions of kilometres of empty space. Which type of heat transfer is this?
questions.memo: Only radiation can cross empty space, where there is no material to conduct or carry the heat.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Heat moving through a solid by passing from particle to particle is called ___.'
questions.memo: Particle-to-particle heat transfer through a solid is conduction.

questions.question: Which way of transferring heat does NOT need any material to travel through?
questions.memo: Radiation can travel through a vacuum (empty space); conduction and convection both need material.

questions.question: The metal handle of a pot on a stove becomes hot. The heat travelled to the handle mainly by...
questions.memo: Heat passed along the solid metal from the hot pot to the handle by conduction.

questions.question: True or false: convection takes place in solids.
questions.memo: False — convection happens in liquids and gases, where the warm fluid can move. Solids transfer heat by conduction.

questions.question: Why does warm air rise during convection?
options: Warm air is lighter (less dense) than cool air
Warm air is heavier than cool air
questions.expected: Warm air is lighter (less dense) than cool air
questions.memo: Warming makes air expand and become less dense, so it rises above the cooler, denser air.

questions.question: A heater stands on the floor, yet the whole room warms up. Why?
options: Warm air rises and cooler air sinks, setting up a convection current
Heat is conducted through the air instantly
The floor pushes the heat up
questions.expected: Warm air rises and cooler air sinks, setting up a convection current
questions.memo: The heater warms the air, which rises; cooler air sinks to replace it, circulating heat around the room (convection).

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The Sun warms the Earth by ___.'
questions.memo: The Sun's heat reaches us by radiation, across empty space.

questions.question: Which of these is the best conductor of heat?
questions.memo: Metals conduct heat well; wood, plastic and wool are insulators.

questions.question: Why can you feel the warmth of a fire from across the room without touching it?
options: Heat reaches you by conduction through the air
The floor carries the heat to you
You cannot feel a fire from far away
questions.memo: The fire's heat travels to you as radiation, without needing to touch you.

questions.question: Water in a pot heats up evenly when boiled on a stove. Why?
options: Convection currents carry the heat through the water
The water conducts heat like a metal
The water does not actually heat evenly
questions.expected: Convection currents carry the heat through the water
questions.memo: Hot water rises and cooler water sinks, creating convection currents that spread the heat through the pot.

questions.question: Heating an object means transferring ___ energy to it.
questions.memo: Heating transfers thermal (heat) energy to an object, raising its temperature.

questions.question: True or false: radiation can travel through empty space.
questions.memo: True — radiation needs no material, so it can cross the empty space between the Sun and Earth.

questions.question: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are both left standing in a pot of hot soup. Why does the metal spoon's handle get hot much faster?
options: Metal conducts heat much better than wood
Wood conducts heat better than metal
The wooden spoon radiates more heat
Metal traps air better than wood
questions.expected: Metal conducts heat much better than wood
questions.memo: Metal is a good conductor, so heat travels quickly up the handle; wood is an insulator and stays cooler.

NSSP.G7.EC.A4.title: Insulation & energy saving
NSSP.G7.EC.A4.description: Insulating materials that slow heat transfer, and how using them (in homes, clothing and appliances) saves energy.
NSSP.G7.EC.A4.recovery_strategy: Insulators trap heat by being poor conductors and holding still air (wool, polystyrene, fibreglass). To keep warmth in, choose an insulator, not a metal.

questions.question: An insulator is a material that...
options: slows down the transfer of heat
speeds up the transfer of heat
questions.expected: slows down the transfer of heat
questions.memo: An insulator is a poor conductor, so it slows heat transfer.

questions.question: Which of these is the best heat insulator?
questions.memo: Wool traps air and is a poor conductor, so it is a good insulator. The metals are conductors.

questions.question: A metal is usually a good ___ of heat.
questions.memo: Metals conduct heat well, so they are good conductors, not insulators.

questions.question: True or false: insulation can help keep heat in or keep heat out.
questions.memo: True — insulation slows heat transfer in both directions, keeping warmth in or heat out.

questions.question: Why do many houses have insulation in the roof?
options: To stop heat escaping, keeping the house warmer
questions.expected: To stop heat escaping, keeping the house warmer
questions.memo: Roof insulation slows heat loss, so the house stays warmer and needs less heating.

questions.question: Which container keeps a hot drink warm for longer?
options: A polystyrene cup, because it is a good insulator
A metal cup, because it conducts heat
questions.expected: A polystyrene cup, because it is a good insulator
questions.memo: Polystyrene is a good insulator, so it slows the heat escaping and keeps the drink warm.

questions.question: Sort each material by whether it is a good heat insulator or a good heat conductor.
questions.expected: Wool, polystyrene and trapped air are insulators; copper and iron are conductors.
questions.memo: Materials that trap air (wool, polystyrene) insulate; metals (copper, iron) conduct heat.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Trapped, still ___ is a good insulator.'
questions.memo: Still air is a poor conductor, so trapping it makes a good insulator.

questions.question: Why do we wear a jersey in winter?
options: It insulates and keeps our body heat in
It conducts heat away from us
It makes our body produce more heat
questions.expected: It insulates and keeps our body heat in
questions.memo: A jersey is an insulator that slows the loss of body heat, keeping us warm.

questions.question: How does using insulators save energy?
options: They reduce heat loss, so less energy is needed to keep things warm
They have no effect on energy use
questions.expected: They reduce heat loss, so less energy is needed to keep things warm
questions.memo: Less heat escapes, so a heater uses less energy to keep a space warm.

questions.question: True or false: a metal blanket would keep you warmer than a wool blanket.
questions.memo: False — metal conducts heat away from you. Wool is an insulator and keeps you warmer.

questions.question: A cooler box keeps ice frozen for hours on a hot day. Why?
options: Its insulating walls slow heat moving in from outside
It conducts heat to the ice quickly
It has no effect on the ice
questions.expected: Its insulating walls slow heat moving in from outside
questions.memo: The insulating walls slow the outside heat from reaching the ice, so it melts more slowly.

questions.question: Which clothing keeps you warmest in cold weather?
questions.memo: Thick wool traps lots of air and insulates well, keeping body heat in.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'To keep warmth in, choose an ___, not a metal.'
questions.memo: Insulators slow heat loss; metals (conductors) let heat escape quickly.

questions.question: Why do many good insulators trap air inside them?
options: Still air is a poor conductor, so trapped air slows heat transfer
questions.expected: Still air is a poor conductor, so trapped air slows heat transfer
questions.memo: Trapped, still air does not conduct heat well, which is why materials full of air (wool, polystyrene) insulate.

questions.question: Double-glazed windows have two panes of glass with a layer of air trapped between them. Why does this reduce heat loss?
options: The trapped air between the panes acts as an insulator
The extra glass conducts heat out faster
The air makes the glass magnetic
It does not reduce heat loss
questions.expected: The trapped air between the panes acts as an insulator
questions.memo: The still air between the panes is a poor conductor, so less heat escapes through the window.

questions.question: Closing the curtains at night helps keep a room warm because...
options: they add insulation and reduce heat loss through the windows
questions.expected: they add insulation and reduce heat loss through the windows
questions.memo: Curtains add a layer of insulation over the windows, slowing the heat escaping.

questions.question: True or false: wrapping a hot-water tank in an insulating jacket saves energy.
questions.memo: True — the insulation keeps the water hot for longer, so less energy is used to reheat it.

questions.question: Which action would save the most heating energy in a cold home?
questions.memo: Most heat is lost through the roof and walls, so insulating them saves the most energy.

questions.question: Two identical houses stand side by side; one is insulated and one is not. In winter the insulated house uses less heating energy. Why?
options: Insulation slows heat escaping, so less energy is needed to stay warm
The insulated house is colder inside
questions.expected: Insulation slows heat escaping, so less energy is needed to stay warm
questions.memo: Because less heat leaks out of the insulated house, the heater needs less energy to keep it warm.

NSSP.G7.EC.A5.title: Energy transfer to surroundings
NSSP.G7.EC.A5.description: Useful versus 'wasted' energy: in every transfer some energy spreads to the surroundings (often as heat), so no device is perfectly efficient.
NSSP.G7.EC.A5.recovery_strategy: 'Wasted' energy is not gone — it has spread to the surroundings, usually as heat. A bulb's useful output is light; the heat it gives off is the wasted part.

questions.question: In every energy transfer, some energy spreads out into the...
questions.memo: In any transfer, some energy always escapes to the surroundings, usually as heat.

questions.question: The energy that is NOT used for the job we want is called...
questions.memo: Energy that does not do the useful job is called wasted energy.

questions.question: What is the USEFUL energy output of a light bulb?
questions.memo: A bulb is used to give light, so light is its useful output.

questions.question: A light bulb also gives off heat. For a bulb, this heat is...
questions.memo: We do not use a bulb for heat, so the heat it gives off is wasted energy.

questions.question: True or false: 'wasted' energy is destroyed and gone forever.
questions.memo: False — wasted energy is not destroyed; it has spread out into the surroundings, usually as heat.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Wasted energy usually spreads to the surroundings as ___.'
questions.memo: Most wasted energy ends up as heat in the surroundings.

questions.question: A phone becomes slightly warm while it charges. This warmth is...
options: wasted energy spreading to the surroundings
a sign the phone is broken
questions.expected: wasted energy spreading to the surroundings
questions.memo: The warmth is energy wasted to the surroundings during charging.

questions.question: Why is no machine perfectly efficient?
options: Some energy is always wasted to the surroundings
Machines store all their energy forever
questions.expected: Some energy is always wasted to the surroundings
questions.memo: Every machine wastes some energy (usually as heat), so none is 100% efficient.

questions.question: An old bulb becomes very hot, while a new LED bulb stays cool, for the same light. Which one wastes less energy?
questions.memo: The LED gives the same light but produces far less waste heat, so it wastes less energy.

questions.question: For each device, sort the output as useful or wasted.

items.text: Picture and sound from a TV
Heat from the back of a TV

questions.expected: The output the device is meant to give is useful; the heat it also gives off is wasted.
questions.memo: Ask what the device is FOR: that output is useful; the extra heat is wasted.

questions.question: True or false: all the energy a device uses becomes useful energy.
questions.memo: False — some of the energy is always wasted, usually as heat to the surroundings.

questions.question: A car engine's useful output is movement. What is mostly wasted?
questions.memo: A lot of the fuel's energy is wasted as heat and sound rather than movement.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The energy that is used for the job we want is the ___ energy.'
questions.memo: The energy doing the wanted job is the useful energy.

questions.question: What is the USEFUL energy output of an electric heater?
questions.memo: A heater is used to give heat, so for a heater the heat is the useful output.

questions.question: For a hairdryer, which is useful and which is wasted?
options: Hot moving air is useful; the motor's sound is wasted
The sound is useful; the hot air is wasted
questions.expected: Hot moving air is useful; the motor's sound is wasted
questions.memo: A hairdryer is meant to blow hot air, so that is useful; the noise it makes is wasted energy.

questions.question: A loudspeaker's useful output is sound. What does it also waste?
questions.memo: Besides the useful sound, a loudspeaker wastes some energy as heat.

questions.question: Where does 'wasted' energy actually go?
options: It spreads out into the surroundings
It is stored in the device forever
questions.expected: It spreads out into the surroundings
questions.memo: Wasted energy spreads into the surroundings (usually as heat) — it is not destroyed.

questions.question: True or false: a more efficient device wastes less energy.
questions.memo: True — being more efficient means more of the energy does the useful job and less is wasted.

questions.question: Why are LED lights considered better than old-style bulbs?
options: They turn more of the energy into light and waste less as heat
They give no light at all
They waste more energy as heat
questions.expected: They turn more of the energy into light and waste less as heat
questions.memo: LEDs are more efficient — more of the energy becomes useful light and less is wasted as heat.

questions.question: A machine takes in 100 units of energy and gives out 70 units of useful energy. What happened to the other 30 units?
options: They were wasted to the surroundings, mostly as heat
questions.expected: They were wasted to the surroundings, mostly as heat
questions.memo: Energy is conserved: the 30 units are not destroyed but wasted to the surroundings, usually as heat.

NSSP.G7.EC.A6.title: The national electricity supply system
NSSP.G7.EC.A6.description: How energy is transferred through the national grid from power station to home, and ways to conserve electricity in the home.
NSSP.G7.EC.A6.recovery_strategy: Follow the path: power station → transformer (steps voltage up) → power lines → transformer (steps voltage down) → home. Saving electricity at home reduces what the station must generate.

questions.question: Where is most of a country's electricity generated?
questions.memo: Power stations generate the electricity that is then sent out across the country.

questions.question: The network of cables that carries electricity across the country is called the...
questions.memo: The national grid is the system of power lines that carries electricity around the country.

questions.question: A transformer near the power station changes the voltage so it can travel far. It...
questions.memo: A step-up transformer raises the voltage so electricity can be sent over long distances with less energy loss.

questions.question: Before electricity reaches homes, a transformer changes the voltage to make it safe to use. It...
questions.memo: A step-down transformer lowers the voltage to a safer level before it enters homes.

questions.question: True or false: electricity travels from the power station to people's homes.
questions.memo: True — electricity flows from the power station, through the grid, to homes.

questions.question: Put the journey of electricity in the correct order, from where it is made to a home.

items.text: Power lines carry it across the country

questions.memo: Power station → step-up transformer → power lines → step-down transformer → home.

questions.question: Which of these is a good way to save electricity at home?
options: Switch off lights when you leave a room
Leave every light on all day
Boil a full kettle for one cup
questions.expected: Switch off lights when you leave a room
questions.memo: Switching off lights you are not using saves electricity.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'When we save electricity at home, the power station has to generate ___.'
questions.memo: Using less electricity at home means the station generates less.

questions.question: Leaving a TV on standby all day...
questions.memo: A TV on standby still uses some electricity, so leaving it on all day wastes energy.

questions.question: Why is electricity sent at very high voltage over long distances?
options: Less energy is lost along the power lines
It is cheaper to make at the home
questions.expected: Less energy is lost along the power lines
questions.memo: High voltage means less energy is wasted as the electricity travels the long distance through the lines.

questions.question: True or false: electricity flows from homes back to the power station to be used there.
questions.memo: False — electricity flows from the power station out to homes, not the other way around.

questions.question: Which of these usually uses the MOST electricity in a home?
questions.memo: Heating water in a geyser uses a large amount of electricity compared with small devices.

questions.question: A family wants to lower their electricity bill. What is the best action?
options: Use energy-saving lights and switch off appliances not in use
Keep all the lights on for safety
questions.expected: Use energy-saving lights and switch off appliances not in use
questions.memo: Energy-saving habits like LED lights and switching off appliances cut the electricity used and the bill.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The network that carries electricity around the country is the national ___.'
questions.memo: The national grid carries electricity across the country.

questions.question: Which of these saves electricity?
options: Using LED bulbs instead of old bulbs
Leaving the oven door open while it heats
Running a half-empty load many times
Keeping the heater on with windows open
questions.expected: Using LED bulbs instead of old bulbs
questions.memo: LED bulbs use much less electricity for the same light, so they save energy.

questions.question: Why is it better to switch appliances off at the wall instead of leaving them on standby?
options: Standby uses no electricity, so it makes no difference
questions.memo: Devices on standby keep drawing a little electricity, so switching them off fully saves energy.

questions.question: Sort each action by whether it saves or wastes electricity.

items.text: Switching off lights you are not using
Boiling a full kettle for one cup

questions.expected: Switching off lights, using LEDs and insulating the geyser save; leaving the fridge open and over-boiling waste.
questions.memo: Actions that cut needless use save electricity; actions that let energy escape or use more than needed waste it.

questions.question: True or false: a transformer changes the voltage of electricity.
questions.memo: True — transformers step the voltage up or down as electricity moves through the grid.

questions.question: A power station burns coal to make electricity. How does saving electricity at home help?
options: The station burns less coal, which reduces pollution
It makes the station burn more coal
It has no effect on the station
questions.expected: The station burns less coal, which reduces pollution
questions.memo: Lower demand means the station generates less and burns less coal, cutting pollution.

questions.question: Put simply, why does switching off unused appliances across many homes help the whole country?
options: It lowers demand, so power stations generate less and waste less
It forces power stations to work harder
questions.expected: It lowers demand, so power stations generate less and waste less
questions.memo: When many homes use less, total demand drops, so power stations generate less and waste fewer resources.

NSSP.G7.PEB.A1.title: Relationship of the Sun to the Earth
NSSP.G7.PEB.A1.description: How the Sun's energy and the tilt of the Earth cause the seasons; the Sun as the source of energy for life; and stored solar energy in food and fuels.
NSSP.G7.PEB.A1.caps_topic: Relationship of the Sun to the Earth
NSSP.G7.PEB.A1.recovery_strategy: Seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct light and has summer; the one tilted away has winter — at the same time.

questions.question: What is the main source of energy for life on Earth?
questions.memo: The Sun provides the light and heat energy that supports almost all life on Earth.

questions.question: What causes the seasons on Earth?
options: The tilt of the Earth as it orbits the Sun
The Earth moving closer to and further from the Sun
questions.expected: The tilt of the Earth as it orbits the Sun
questions.memo: The Earth's tilt means each hemisphere leans toward or away from the Sun during the year, causing the seasons.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun gives the Earth both light and heat.
questions.memo: True — the Sun provides both light and heat energy to the Earth.

questions.question: When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it is...
questions.memo: Tilted toward the Sun, a hemisphere gets more direct sunlight, so it is summer there.

questions.question: When a hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, it is...
questions.memo: Tilted away from the Sun, a hemisphere gets less direct sunlight, so it is winter there.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the tilted Earth orbiting the Sun. Which hemisphere is having summer?
options: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun
The hemisphere tilted away from the Sun
questions.expected: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun
questions.memo: The hemisphere leaning toward the Sun receives more direct light and is having summer.

questions.question: It is summer in South Africa (the southern hemisphere). This means the southern hemisphere is...
questions.memo: In southern-hemisphere summer, that hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Seasons are caused by the ___ of the Earth, not by its distance from the Sun.'
questions.memo: The Earth's tilt causes the seasons.

questions.question: Some people think summer happens because the Earth is closer to the Sun. This idea is...
options: incorrect — seasons are caused by the Earth's tilt
questions.expected: incorrect — seasons are caused by the Earth's tilt
questions.memo: It is a common misconception. Seasons come from the tilt, not the small change in distance.

questions.question: Stored solar energy can be found in...
questions.memo: Food (from plants) and fuels (like coal) store energy that originally came from the Sun.

questions.question: True or false: plants use the Sun's energy to make their food.
questions.memo: True — plants capture the Sun's energy to make food, which begins almost every food chain.

questions.question: Coal is sometimes called 'stored solar energy'. Why?
options: It formed from ancient plants that captured sunlight long ago
It is made of trapped sunlight beams
It is dug up from the Sun
questions.expected: It formed from ancient plants that captured sunlight long ago
questions.memo: Coal formed from ancient plants that had captured the Sun's energy, so it stores old solar energy.

questions.question: A plant on a windowsill grows and leans toward the light. Why?
options: It needs sunlight to make food
It is trying to stay cool
questions.expected: It needs sunlight to make food
questions.memo: Plants grow toward light because they need the Sun's energy to make food.

questions.question: Why is the Sun important for almost all living things?
options: It provides the energy that plants use to make food, which feeds other living things
It provides gravity for the oceans
It gives off no energy at all
questions.expected: It provides the energy that plants use to make food, which feeds other living things
questions.memo: The Sun's energy is captured by plants and passes along food chains to almost all living things.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Energy from the Sun is captured by ___ to make food.'
questions.memo: Plants capture the Sun's energy to make food.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a way the Sun's energy is used on Earth?
questions.memo: The Sun warms the Earth, powers plants and runs solar panels, but it does not make materials magnetic.

questions.question: True or false: when it is summer in the southern hemisphere, it is winter in the northern hemisphere.
questions.memo: True — the hemispheres tilt opposite ways, so they have opposite seasons at the same time.

questions.question: A solar panel and a growing plant both rely on the same thing. What is it?
questions.memo: Both the solar panel and the plant use energy from the Sun.

questions.question: A hemisphere tilted away from the Sun receives sunlight at a low, slanted angle. This makes it...
questions.memo: Slanted, less direct sunlight spreads its energy out, so it is cooler — winter.

questions.question: Which is the BEST explanation of why we have seasons?
options: Earth's tilt means each hemisphere leans toward or away from the Sun during the year, changing how directly sunlight hits it
The Earth moves much closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun gets hotter in summer
The Moon changes the Earth's temperature
questions.expected: Earth's tilt means each hemisphere leans toward or away from the Sun during the year, changing how directly sunlight hits it
questions.memo: The tilt changes how directly sunlight strikes each hemisphere through the year, which gives us the seasons.

NSSP.G7.PEB.A2.title: Relationship of the Moon to the Earth
NSSP.G7.PEB.A2.description: The relative positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon; gravity between them; and how the Moon's gravity, with the Sun's, causes the tides.
NSSP.G7.PEB.A2.caps_topic: Relationship of the Moon to the Earth
NSSP.G7.PEB.A2.recovery_strategy: Tides are mainly caused by the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans (the Sun adds a smaller pull). The water bulges toward and away from the Moon, giving two high tides a day.

questions.question: The Moon moves around the...
questions.memo: The Moon orbits (moves around) the Earth.

questions.question: What is the main cause of ocean tides?
options: The Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans
questions.expected: The Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans
questions.memo: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, causing them to bulge and giving us the tides.

questions.question: True or false: gravity is a force that pulls objects toward each other.
questions.memo: True — gravity is an attracting force that pulls objects toward each other.

questions.question: Tides are when the level of the sea...
questions.memo: Tides are the regular rising and falling of the sea level.

questions.question: How many high tides does most of the coastline get in a day?
questions.memo: Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the Earth, its oceans and the Moon. Where is it high tide?
options: Where the water bulges toward and away from the Moon
Only on the side facing the Sun
