questions.expected: Where the water bulges toward and away from the Moon
questions.memo: The Moon's gravity makes the ocean bulge on the near and far sides, and those bulges are the high tides.

questions.question: At a beach, the sea is high in the morning and low in the afternoon. This is because of...
options: the tides, caused by the Moon
questions.expected: the tides, caused by the Moon
questions.memo: The changing sea level is the tide, mainly caused by the Moon's gravity.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Tides are mainly caused by the ___ gravity.'
questions.memo: The Moon's gravity is the main cause of the tides.

questions.question: What does gravity keep the Moon doing?
questions.memo: Gravity between the Earth and Moon keeps the Moon orbiting the Earth.

questions.question: Are ocean tides caused by the wind?
options: No — they are mainly caused by the Moon's gravity
Yes — wind is the main cause
Yes — only strong storms cause tides
questions.expected: No — they are mainly caused by the Moon's gravity
questions.memo: Wind can make waves, but the tides themselves are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun also affects the tides, but less than the Moon.
questions.memo: True — the Sun's gravity adds a smaller pull on the oceans than the Moon's.

questions.question: Why does the side of the Earth facing the Moon have a high tide?
options: The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean water toward it, making it bulge
The Moon pushes the water down
The Sun blocks the water there
The water freezes on that side
questions.expected: The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean water toward it, making it bulge
questions.memo: The Moon's gravity pulls the nearest ocean water toward it, creating a bulge — a high tide.

questions.question: Tides are at their highest when the Sun and Moon line up. Why?
options: The Sun and Moon pull together, adding their gravity
The Sun cancels out the Moon
questions.expected: The Sun and Moon pull together, adding their gravity
questions.memo: When the Sun and Moon line up, their gravitational pulls add together, making the highest tides.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The force that pulls the oceans to cause tides is ___.'
questions.memo: Gravity is the force (mainly from the Moon) that pulls the oceans to make tides.

questions.question: Which of these does the Moon NOT do?
questions.memo: The Moon does not make its own light — it reflects light from the Sun.

questions.question: Which statement about the relative positions is correct?
options: The Moon orbits the Earth, and the Earth orbits the Sun
The Moon orbits the Sun directly
questions.expected: The Moon orbits the Earth, and the Earth orbits the Sun
questions.memo: The Moon goes around the Earth, while the Earth goes around the Sun.

questions.question: True or false: the Moon's gravity is strong enough to affect the Earth's oceans.
questions.memo: True — even from far away, the Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans enough to cause tides.

questions.question: Why do we see different shapes (phases) of the Moon during a month?
options: We see different amounts of its sunlit side as it orbits the Earth
The Moon changes its own shape
Clouds cover parts of the Moon
The Earth's shadow always covers half the Moon
questions.expected: We see different amounts of its sunlit side as it orbits the Earth
questions.memo: As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half, which we call the phases.

questions.question: A rock pool at the shore is covered by the sea twice each day. Why?
options: There are two high tides each day from the Moon's pull
The pool moves up and down
The Sun pushes water into it
questions.expected: There are two high tides each day from the Moon's pull
questions.memo: Two high tides a day, caused by the Moon, cover the rock pool twice daily.

questions.question: Which statement BEST describes how tides happen?
options: The Moon's gravity pulls Earth's oceans into bulges, and as the Earth spins, each coast passes through high and low tides
The wind pushes all the water to one side once a day
The Sun heats the sea so it rises
The oceans randomly rise and fall
questions.expected: The Moon's gravity pulls Earth's oceans into bulges, and as the Earth spins, each coast passes through high and low tides
questions.memo: The Moon's gravity makes ocean bulges; the spinning Earth carries each coast through those bulges, giving high and low tides.

NSSP.G7.PEB.A3.title: Historical development of astronomy
NSSP.G7.PEB.A3.description: Early indigenous knowledge of the sky (using stars and seasons), and modern developments in astronomy that built on it.
NSSP.G7.PEB.A3.recovery_strategy: Indigenous communities used the stars and the Sun to track seasons, plant crops and navigate — careful observation that laid the groundwork for modern astronomy.

questions.question: Long ago, before clocks and calendars, people used the stars to...
options: tell the time of year and find their direction
questions.expected: tell the time of year and find their direction
questions.memo: People used the stars as a natural calendar and compass to track seasons and find direction.

questions.question: True or false: indigenous communities in South Africa observed the stars and the seasons.
questions.memo: True — indigenous communities watched the sky carefully and built up useful knowledge.

questions.question: Early farmers watched the sky mainly to know when to...
questions.memo: The appearance of certain stars told farmers when the season was right to plant.

questions.question: Which modern tool helps us see distant stars and planets more clearly?
questions.memo: A telescope makes faraway objects in space look closer and clearer.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Careful ___ of the sky over many years built up early astronomy knowledge.'
questions.memo: Early astronomy came from careful, patient observation of the sky.

questions.question: Sailors long ago used the stars to...
options: navigate and find their way at sea
questions.expected: navigate and find their way at sea
questions.memo: Before modern instruments, sailors used the stars to navigate across the oceans.

questions.question: Why was indigenous knowledge of the stars valuable?
options: It helped people farm, navigate and track the seasons
It was only used for decoration
It replaced the need for food
questions.expected: It helped people farm, navigate and track the seasons
questions.memo: Star knowledge had practical value — farming, navigation and knowing the seasons.

questions.question: Did people long ago know nothing useful about the stars?
options: No — they had detailed, useful knowledge of the sky
Yes — they knew nothing at all
Yes — the stars were a mystery to everyone
No — but their knowledge was useless
questions.expected: No — they had detailed, useful knowledge of the sky
questions.memo: It is a misconception that early people knew nothing. Their careful observations were detailed and useful.

questions.question: True or false: modern astronomy built on the observations made by earlier people.
questions.memo: True — today's astronomy grew from the careful observations of earlier people.

questions.question: The rising of certain stars at a particular time of year was used as a sign of...
questions.memo: Certain stars appearing in the sky marked the start of a season, such as the time to plant.

questions.question: Sort each item as early sky knowledge or a modern development in astronomy.

items.text: Watching the stars with the naked eye
Tracking the seasons by the stars

questions.expected: Naked-eye watching, tracking seasons and oral star stories are early; telescopes and space probes are modern.
questions.memo: Early knowledge came from naked-eye observation and oral tradition; modern astronomy uses instruments like telescopes and probes.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ makes faraway objects in space look closer and clearer.'
questions.memo: A telescope is used to see distant objects in space more clearly.

questions.question: A community plants its crops each year when a certain star first appears at dawn. They are using...
options: star knowledge to track the season
the star to water the crops
the star's heat to warm the soil
questions.expected: star knowledge to track the season
questions.memo: Using a star's appearance to time planting is practical, observation-based seasonal knowledge.

questions.question: How is modern astronomy different from early astronomy?
options: It uses instruments like telescopes and satellites, not just the naked eye
It no longer looks at the sky at all
questions.expected: It uses instruments like telescopes and satellites, not just the naked eye
questions.memo: Modern astronomy adds powerful instruments to the careful observation that early people began.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa has modern astronomy facilities, such as large telescopes.
questions.memo: True — South Africa hosts large modern telescopes used by astronomers.

questions.question: Which is an example of indigenous knowledge of the sky?
options: Using star patterns to mark the seasons
Taking photos with a space telescope
questions.expected: Using star patterns to mark the seasons
questions.memo: Reading star patterns to mark seasons is indigenous sky knowledge; the others are modern technology.

questions.question: Why should we respect early indigenous astronomy?
options: It was careful science that helped people survive and laid the groundwork for today's astronomy
It was only superstition with no value
It was exactly the same as modern astronomy
questions.expected: It was careful science that helped people survive and laid the groundwork for today's astronomy
questions.memo: Indigenous astronomy was careful, practical observation that helped communities and built a foundation for modern science.

questions.question: Before clocks and calendars, the sky was used as a...
questions.memo: People read the sky like a calendar (for seasons) and a compass (for direction).

questions.question: Which of these is a modern development in astronomy?
options: Watching stars with only the eyes
Passing down star stories by word of mouth
questions.memo: Space telescopes and probes are modern developments; the others are early, naked-eye methods.

questions.question: Which is the BEST summary of how astronomy developed?
options: Indigenous people built useful sky knowledge through careful observation, and modern astronomers extended it using telescopes and other instruments
Astronomy only began when telescopes were invented
Early people knew nothing, so modern astronomy started from scratch
Astronomy has never changed over time
questions.expected: Indigenous people built useful sky knowledge through careful observation, and modern astronomers extended it using telescopes and other instruments
questions.memo: Modern astronomy grew out of the careful observations of earlier people, then extended them with new instruments.

NSSP.G8.LL.A1.title: Photosynthesis & respiration
NSSP.G8.LL.A1.description: Photosynthesis: green plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food (glucose) and release oxygen. Respiration: living cells release energy from food using oxygen, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
NSSP.G8.LL.A1.recovery_strategy: Photosynthesis takes IN carbon dioxide + water (and light) and gives OUT glucose + oxygen. Respiration is the reverse: it uses glucose + oxygen and releases energy + carbon dioxide + water.

questions.question: What is photosynthesis?
options: The process by which green plants make their own food using sunlight
The melting of ice into water
questions.expected: The process by which green plants make their own food using sunlight
questions.memo: Photosynthesis is how green plants use sunlight to make their own food.

questions.question: Photosynthesis takes IN carbon dioxide and water, and gives OUT...
questions.memo: Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose (food) and release oxygen.

questions.question: Which gas do plants RELEASE during photosynthesis?
questions.memo: Plants give out oxygen during photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which gas do plants TAKE IN during photosynthesis?
questions.memo: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis.

questions.question: True or false: plants need sunlight to carry out photosynthesis.
questions.memo: True — sunlight provides the energy plants use to make food.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Photosynthesis happens in the green parts of a plant, using a green substance called ___.'
questions.memo: Chlorophyll is the green substance that traps light energy for photosynthesis.

questions.question: What does respiration release from food?
questions.memo: Respiration releases the energy stored in food so the body can use it.

questions.question: Respiration uses oxygen and food, and gives out...
questions.memo: Respiration uses glucose and oxygen, releasing energy plus carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: Sort each substance by whether it is TAKEN IN or GIVEN OUT during photosynthesis.
questions.expected: Taken in: carbon dioxide, water, light. Given out: glucose and oxygen.
questions.memo: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide, water and light, and gives out glucose and oxygen.

questions.question: True or false: respiration happens only in animals, not in plants.
questions.memo: False — both plants and animals carry out respiration to release energy from food.

questions.question: During photosynthesis, do plants take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide?
options: No — they take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
Yes — they take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide
No — they take in nothing at all
questions.expected: No — they take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
questions.memo: A common mix-up: in photosynthesis plants take IN carbon dioxide and give OUT oxygen.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Living cells release energy from food during ___.'
questions.memo: Respiration is the process that releases energy from food in living cells.

questions.question: Where in a plant does most photosynthesis happen?
questions.memo: Leaves contain the most chlorophyll, so most photosynthesis happens there.

questions.question: A healthy plant is kept in complete darkness for several days. What can it NOT do?
options: Take up water through its roots
questions.memo: Without light, the plant cannot photosynthesise, so it cannot make food.

questions.question: Why are plants important for animals?
options: They release the oxygen animals need to breathe
They remove all oxygen from the air
questions.expected: They release the oxygen animals need to breathe
questions.memo: Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis, which animals need for respiration.

questions.question: Which two things are needed for respiration?
questions.memo: Respiration uses oxygen and glucose (food) to release energy.

questions.question: True or false: photosynthesis stores energy in food, and respiration releases that energy.
questions.memo: True — photosynthesis stores the Sun's energy in food; respiration releases it for use.

questions.question: A sealed glass jar with a healthy plant and a small insect is left in the light. The insect stays alive because the plant...
options: releases oxygen that the insect needs
produces extra carbon dioxide for the insect
questions.expected: releases oxygen that the insect needs
questions.memo: In the light the plant photosynthesises and releases oxygen, which the insect uses to respire.

questions.question: How are photosynthesis and respiration opposite processes?
options: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen; respiration uses them up
They both only happen in animals
They are exactly the same process
questions.expected: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen; respiration uses them up
questions.memo: Photosynthesis builds glucose and releases oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy — opposite directions.

questions.question: Why is photosynthesis the starting point of most food chains?
options: It captures the Sun's energy as food that other living things then use
It removes all energy from the Sun
questions.expected: It captures the Sun's energy as food that other living things then use
questions.memo: Plants trap the Sun's energy as food; that energy then passes to the animals along the food chain.

NSSP.G8.LL.A2.title: Interactions & interdependence
NSSP.G8.LL.A2.description: Ecosystems and ecology: producers, consumers and decomposers; food chains and food webs; the flow of energy; balance in an ecosystem; adaptations; and conservation.
NSSP.G8.LL.A2.caps_topic: Interactions and interdependence within the environment
NSSP.G8.LL.A2.recovery_strategy: Energy flows one way along the arrows: from the producer (plant) to the animal that eats it, and on to the next. The arrow points to the eater. Producers make food; consumers eat; decomposers break down dead matter.

questions.question: What is a producer in an ecosystem?
options: A plant that makes its own food
An animal that eats other animals
A fungus that breaks down dead matter
questions.expected: A plant that makes its own food
questions.memo: Producers (mostly green plants) make their own food by photosynthesis.

questions.question: An animal that eats other living things is called a...
questions.memo: Consumers cannot make their own food, so they eat other living things.

questions.question: What do decomposers, such as fungi and many bacteria, do?
options: Break down dead plants and animals
questions.expected: Break down dead plants and animals
questions.memo: Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

questions.question: In the food chain grass → buck → lion, what is the lion?
options: A consumer that eats the buck
questions.expected: A consumer that eats the buck
questions.memo: The lion eats the buck, so it is a consumer further along the chain.

questions.question: True or false: a food chain shows what eats what in an ecosystem.
questions.memo: True — a food chain shows the feeding links from one living thing to the next.

questions.question: Put this food chain in the correct order, starting with the producer.
questions.memo: The chain runs producer first: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake.

questions.question: An animal that eats only plants is called a...
questions.memo: A herbivore eats only plants.

questions.question: An animal that eats only other animals is called a...
questions.memo: A carnivore eats only other animals.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Energy enters most food chains from the ___.'
questions.memo: Plants capture the Sun's energy, so the Sun is where the energy in a food chain begins.

questions.question: In a food chain, which way does energy flow?
options: From the plant to the animals that eat it
From the top predator back to the plant
It does not flow at all
questions.expected: From the plant to the animals that eat it
questions.memo: Energy flows one way, from the producer to each consumer that eats the one before it.

questions.question: In the food chain grass → mouse → owl, does energy flow from the owl back to the grass?
options: No — it flows from the grass to the mouse to the owl
Yes — energy flows from the owl to the grass
No — energy does not flow in food chains
questions.expected: No — it flows from the grass to the mouse to the owl
questions.memo: Energy flows in the direction of the arrows: grass → mouse → owl, never backwards.

questions.question: Sort each living thing by its role in the ecosystem.
questions.expected: Grass and tree make their own food (producers); lion and zebra eat others (consumers); the mushroom breaks down dead matter (decomposer).
questions.memo: Producers make food, consumers eat other living things, and decomposers break down dead matter.

questions.question: What is a food web?
options: A single food chain on its own
A spider's web that traps food
questions.memo: A food web shows how many food chains in an ecosystem connect to each other.

questions.question: True or false: if all the plants in an ecosystem died, the animals that eat them would have no food.
questions.memo: True — producers are the base of the food chain, so losing them affects everything above.

questions.question: What does it mean for an ecosystem to be 'balanced'?
options: The numbers of predators and prey stay roughly steady over time
Every animal is exactly the same size
questions.expected: The numbers of predators and prey stay roughly steady over time
questions.memo: In a balanced ecosystem, populations stay fairly stable because the feeding links keep them in check.

questions.question: In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, what is likely if all the frogs are removed?
options: Snakes have less food and grasshoppers may increase
questions.expected: Snakes have less food and grasshoppers may increase
questions.memo: Removing frogs leaves snakes with less food, and the grasshoppers the frogs ate are likely to increase — the balance shifts.

questions.question: A polar bear's thick fur and fat layer are an example of...
options: an adaptation to its cold environment
questions.expected: an adaptation to its cold environment
questions.memo: Features that help an organism survive in its environment, like thick fur in the cold, are adaptations.

questions.question: Why do we conserve ecosystems?
options: To protect the variety of living things and keep ecosystems healthy
To use up all the resources quickly
questions.expected: To protect the variety of living things and keep ecosystems healthy
questions.memo: Conservation protects biodiversity and keeps ecosystems working well for the future.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'An animal that eats both plants and animals is an ___.'
questions.memo: An omnivore eats both plants and animals.

questions.question: A new predator is brought into an area and eats most of the small birds. What is the BEST prediction?
options: The insects the birds used to eat may increase, upsetting the balance
Nothing in the ecosystem will change
The plants will all immediately die
The new predator will become a producer
questions.expected: The insects the birds used to eat may increase, upsetting the balance
questions.memo: Removing the small birds releases the insects they ate, so insect numbers can rise and the ecosystem's balance is disturbed.

NSSP.G8.LL.A3.title: Micro-organisms
NSSP.G8.LL.A3.description: The main types of micro-organisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists); harmful micro-organisms that cause disease and decay; and useful micro-organisms in food, medicine and decomposition.
NSSP.G8.LL.A3.recovery_strategy: Micro-organisms can be harmful (cause disease or spoil food) OR useful (make bread, yoghurt and medicine, and break down dead matter). Judge each by what it does, not assume all are bad.

questions.question: What are micro-organisms?
options: Living things too small to see without a microscope
Large animals that live in water
questions.expected: Living things too small to see without a microscope
questions.memo: Micro-organisms are living things so small you need a microscope to see them.

questions.question: Which of these is a micro-organism?
questions.memo: Bacteria are micro-organisms; the others are large or non-living.

questions.question: True or false: some micro-organisms are useful to humans.
questions.memo: True — many micro-organisms are useful, for example in making food and medicine.

questions.question: Yeast, a type of fungus, is used to...
questions.memo: Yeast produces gas as it feeds, which makes bread dough rise.

questions.question: Which type of micro-organism causes illnesses like the common cold and flu?
questions.memo: Viruses cause many illnesses, including colds and flu.

questions.question: Sort each micro-organism by whether it is harmful or useful in the example given.
questions.expected: Food-poisoning bacteria and the flu virus are harmful; bread yeast, yoghurt bacteria and decomposing bacteria are useful.
questions.memo: Judge each by what it does: causing illness or spoiling food is harmful; making food or recycling dead matter is useful.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Bacteria that turn milk into yoghurt are ___ micro-organisms.'
questions.memo: Yoghurt-making bacteria are useful micro-organisms.

questions.question: Which is a harmful effect of some micro-organisms?
questions.memo: Harmful micro-organisms can cause disease and make food go bad.

questions.question: Are all bacteria harmful?
options: No — many bacteria are useful or harmless
No — there is no such thing as bacteria
questions.expected: No — many bacteria are useful or harmless
questions.memo: It is a common misconception that all bacteria are harmful. Many are useful, such as those that make yoghurt or recycle nutrients.

questions.question: Bread dough rises when yeast is added because the yeast...
questions.memo: Yeast feeds on sugars and gives off gas, which makes the dough rise.

questions.question: Why are decomposer micro-organisms useful in nature?
options: They break down dead matter and recycle nutrients into the soil
questions.expected: They break down dead matter and recycle nutrients into the soil
questions.memo: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead plants and animals back into the soil for new growth.

questions.question: True or false: yeasts and moulds are types of fungi, and some are micro-organisms.
questions.memo: True — yeasts and moulds are fungi, and many are tiny micro-organisms.

questions.question: Medicines that are made using micro-organisms to fight bacterial infections are called...
questions.memo: Antibiotics, often made with the help of micro-organisms, fight bacterial infections.

questions.question: Food left in a warm, damp place spoils quickly. Why?
options: Micro-organisms grow and multiply fast in warm, damp conditions
Food makes its own micro-organisms from nothing
Damp air has no effect on food
questions.expected: Micro-organisms grow and multiply fast in warm, damp conditions
questions.memo: Warmth and moisture help micro-organisms grow quickly, so the food spoils faster.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ causes diseases such as flu and measles.'
questions.memo: Viruses cause diseases like flu and measles.

questions.question: Why does keeping food in a fridge slow down spoiling?
options: The cold slows the growth of micro-organisms
The cold makes food rot faster
questions.expected: The cold slows the growth of micro-organisms
questions.memo: Cold temperatures slow micro-organisms down, so food stays fresh longer.

questions.question: Which correctly pairs a micro-organism with a USEFUL job?
questions.memo: Yeast is used to make bread — a useful job. The other pairings are wrong.

questions.question: True or false: washing your hands helps stop harmful micro-organisms from spreading.
questions.memo: True — washing hands removes harmful micro-organisms and helps stop disease spreading.

questions.question: Cheese and yoghurt are made with the help of...
questions.memo: Useful micro-organisms help turn milk into cheese and yoghurt.

questions.question: Why are micro-organisms sometimes described as both 'friend and foe'?
options: Some cause disease and decay, while others make food, medicine and recycle nutrients
They are always harmful in every way
They are always useful in every way
They have no effect on people at all
questions.expected: Some cause disease and decay, while others make food, medicine and recycle nutrients
questions.memo: Micro-organisms are a mixed group: some harm us, while many others are very useful.

NSSP.G8.MM.A1.title: Atoms
NSSP.G8.MM.A1.description: Atoms as the building blocks of matter; the sub-atomic particles (protons, neutrons and electrons); pure substances; elements and compounds; and mixtures of elements and compounds.
NSSP.G8.MM.A1.recovery_strategy: An element is made of only one kind of atom (oxygen, gold). A compound is two or more different atoms chemically joined (water = hydrogen + oxygen). A mixture is not chemically joined and can be separated.

questions.question: What are atoms?
options: The tiny building blocks that make up all matter
questions.expected: The tiny building blocks that make up all matter
questions.memo: Atoms are the tiny building blocks that make up all matter.

questions.question: Which three particles make up an atom?
questions.memo: Atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.question: What charge does a proton have?
questions.memo: Protons have a positive charge.

questions.question: What charge does an electron have?
questions.memo: Electrons have a negative charge.

questions.question: What charge does a neutron have?
questions.memo: Neutrons are neutral — they have no charge.

questions.question: Look at the model of an atom. Which particles are found in the central nucleus?
questions.memo: The nucleus at the centre holds the protons and neutrons; electrons move around the outside.

questions.question: True or false: an element is made of only one kind of atom.
questions.memo: True — an element contains only one kind of atom.

questions.question: Water (H2O) is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined together. Water is a...
questions.memo: Different atoms chemically joined make a compound, so water is a compound.

questions.question: Oxygen gas is made of only oxygen atoms. Oxygen is an...
questions.memo: Made of only one kind of atom, oxygen is an element.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Two or more different atoms chemically joined make a ___.'
questions.memo: Different atoms chemically joined make a compound.

questions.question: Sort each substance as an element or a compound.
questions.expected: Oxygen, gold and iron are elements; water and carbon dioxide are compounds.
questions.memo: One kind of atom = element (oxygen, gold, iron); different atoms joined = compound (water, carbon dioxide).

questions.question: Is water an element?
options: No — it is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen
Yes — water is a single atom
questions.expected: No — it is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen
questions.memo: Water is made of two different atoms joined, so it is a compound, not an element.

questions.question: True or false: a compound can be broken down into the elements it is made from.
questions.memo: True — a compound can be broken down (chemically) into its elements.

questions.question: A pure substance is...
options: made of only one kind of particle
always a mixture of many things
questions.expected: made of only one kind of particle
questions.memo: A pure substance contains only one kind of particle throughout.

questions.question: How is a mixture different from a compound?
options: In a mixture the substances are not chemically joined and can be separated
A mixture is always a single element
A mixture cannot ever be separated
A mixture is made of one kind of atom
questions.expected: In a mixture the substances are not chemically joined and can be separated
questions.memo: In a mixture the substances are simply mixed (not chemically joined), so they can be separated; in a compound they are chemically joined.

questions.question: Air is made of several gases that are mixed but not chemically joined. Air is a...
questions.memo: The gases in air are not chemically joined, so air is a mixture.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The centre of an atom is called the ___.'
questions.memo: The centre of an atom is the nucleus, which holds protons and neutrons.

questions.question: Which particle moves around the outside of the atom?
questions.memo: Electrons move around the outside of the atom, around the nucleus.

questions.question: Why is gold called an element?
options: It is made of only one kind of atom
It is a mixture of many metals
It is made of hydrogen and oxygen
questions.expected: It is made of only one kind of atom
questions.memo: Gold contains only gold atoms, so it is an element.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide is written as CO2. What does this tell you about it?
options: It is a compound of carbon and oxygen atoms joined together
It is a mixture that can be separated by hand
It is made of only carbon atoms
questions.expected: It is a compound of carbon and oxygen atoms joined together
questions.memo: CO2 shows carbon and oxygen atoms chemically joined, so carbon dioxide is a compound.

NSSP.G8.MM.A2.title: Particle model of matter
NSSP.G8.MM.A2.description: The particle model: all matter is made of tiny moving particles. It explains the solid, liquid and gas states, changes of state, density (mass and volume), expansion and contraction, and pressure.
NSSP.G8.MM.A2.recovery_strategy: Solid = particles packed tightly in a fixed shape; liquid = particles close but able to slide (takes the container's shape); gas = particles far apart and moving fast (fills the container). Heating gives particles more energy and spreads them out.

questions.question: What does the particle model of matter say?
options: All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving
All matter is solid and still
Matter is made of one giant block
questions.expected: All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving
questions.memo: The particle model says all matter is made of tiny, constantly moving particles.

questions.question: In a SOLID, the particles are...
options: packed closely in a fixed arrangement
spread out to fill any container
questions.expected: packed closely in a fixed arrangement
questions.memo: Solid particles are packed tightly in fixed positions and only vibrate in place.

questions.question: In a GAS, the particles are...
options: packed tightly in a fixed shape
questions.memo: Gas particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

questions.question: In a LIQUID, the particles are...
options: close together but able to slide past each other
fixed in place and unable to move
questions.expected: close together but able to slide past each other
questions.memo: Liquid particles are close together but can slide, so a liquid takes the shape of its container.

questions.question: True or false: gas particles are packed tightly together and cannot move.
questions.memo: False — gas particles are far apart and move freely and quickly.

questions.question: Sort each example into its state of matter.
questions.expected: Ice and a brick are solids; water and juice are liquids; water vapour is a gas.
questions.memo: Fixed shape = solid; flows and takes the container's shape = liquid; fills the whole space = gas.

questions.question: When a solid is heated until it melts, it becomes a...
questions.memo: Melting changes a solid into a liquid.

questions.question: When a liquid is heated until it boils, it becomes a...
questions.memo: Boiling changes a liquid into a gas.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Heating gives particles more energy, so they move ___ and spread out.'
questions.memo: Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster and spread apart.

questions.question: Why does a gas fill its whole container?
options: Its particles are far apart and move freely in all directions
It is pulled to the bottom only
questions.expected: Its particles are far apart and move freely in all directions
questions.memo: Gas particles spread out and move in all directions, so a gas fills any container it is in.

questions.question: Density is a measure of...
options: how much mass is packed into a certain volume
questions.expected: how much mass is packed into a certain volume
questions.memo: Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume.

questions.question: A small stone sinks in water. This is because the stone is...
questions.memo: Objects that are more dense than water sink in it.

questions.question: True or false: most materials expand when heated and contract when cooled.
questions.memo: True — heating usually makes materials expand; cooling makes them contract.

questions.question: A metal lid is stuck on a glass jar. Running the metal lid under hot water helps loosen it. Why?
options: The metal expands a little when heated, loosening the lid
The hot water makes the glass bigger than the metal
The water glues the lid on
questions.expected: The metal expands a little when heated, loosening the lid
questions.memo: Heat makes the metal lid expand slightly, so it grips the jar less tightly.

questions.question: What causes the pressure of a gas inside a container?
options: Gas particles hitting the walls of the container
The container shrinking on its own
questions.expected: Gas particles hitting the walls of the container
questions.memo: Pressure comes from the many gas particles bumping into the container walls.

questions.question: Pumping more air into a tyre increases the pressure inside. Why?
options: More particles hit the walls more often
questions.expected: More particles hit the walls more often
questions.memo: More air means more particles, so there are more collisions with the walls — higher pressure.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Particles in a ___ are packed tightly and only vibrate in place.'
questions.memo: In a solid, the particles are held in fixed positions and only vibrate.

questions.question: Why can liquids be poured but solids cannot?
options: Liquid particles can slide past each other, but solid particles are held in fixed positions
questions.expected: Liquid particles can slide past each other, but solid particles are held in fixed positions
questions.memo: Liquid particles can move past each other, so a liquid flows; solid particles are fixed, so a solid keeps its shape.

questions.question: True or false: when water freezes into ice, it changes state from liquid to solid.
questions.memo: True — freezing changes liquid water into solid ice.

questions.question: A balloon left in the hot sun slowly expands. Using the particle model, why does this happen?
options: The air particles gain energy, move faster and push the balloon outward
The air particles freeze and shrink
The particles stop moving in the heat
questions.expected: The air particles gain energy, move faster and push the balloon outward
questions.memo: Heat gives the air particles more energy; they move faster and hit the balloon harder and more often, pushing it outward.

NSSP.G8.MM.A3.title: Chemical reactions
NSSP.G8.MM.A3.description: Chemical reactions: reactants change into new products with different properties; signs that a reaction has happened; and how a chemical change differs from a physical change.
NSSP.G8.MM.A3.recovery_strategy: A chemical reaction makes a NEW substance (e.g. burning, rusting). A physical change (melting, dissolving) makes no new substance and can usually be reversed. Ask: is a new substance formed?

questions.question: In a chemical reaction, the starting substances are called the...
questions.memo: The substances you start with in a reaction are the reactants.

questions.question: The new substances formed in a chemical reaction are called the...
questions.memo: The new substances made in a reaction are the products.

questions.question: A chemical reaction always forms...
questions.memo: A chemical reaction always produces at least one new substance.

questions.question: True or false: melting ice is a chemical reaction.
questions.memo: False — melting makes no new substance (it is still water), so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which of these is a sign that a chemical reaction has happened?
options: A new colour, a gas, or heat and light is produced
The substance is poured into another cup
questions.expected: A new colour, a gas, or heat and light is produced
questions.memo: Signs of a chemical reaction include a colour change, bubbles of gas, or heat and light being given off.

questions.question: Burning wood is a...
questions.memo: Burning makes new substances (ash, gases), so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: Dissolving sugar in water is a...
options: way of making a new substance
questions.memo: The sugar is still sugar (you could get it back by evaporating), so dissolving is a physical change.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a reaction, reactants change into ___.'
questions.memo: Reactants change into products during a reaction.

questions.question: Sort each change as a chemical change or a physical change.
questions.expected: Burning paper and rusting iron are chemical changes; melting ice, dissolving salt and boiling water are physical changes.
questions.memo: If a new substance forms (burning, rusting) it is chemical; if not (melting, dissolving, boiling) it is physical.

questions.question: Is melting a chemical reaction?
options: No — no new substance forms, so it is a physical change
Yes — melting makes a new substance
No — melting does not change anything
questions.expected: No — no new substance forms, so it is a physical change
questions.memo: Melting changes the state but makes no new substance, so it is a physical change, not a chemical reaction.

questions.question: True or false: a chemical change is usually hard to reverse.
questions.memo: True — chemical changes make new substances and are usually difficult to reverse (you cannot un-burn wood).

questions.question: Iron left outside in damp air slowly turns to rust. This is a...
questions.memo: Rust is a new substance, so rusting is a chemical reaction.

questions.question: A physical change...
options: does not make a new substance and can often be reversed
questions.expected: does not make a new substance and can often be reversed
questions.memo: A physical change makes no new substance and can usually be reversed, like melting and freezing.

questions.question: Why is baking a cake a chemical change?
options: New substances form and it cannot be turned back into the raw ingredients
You can easily separate the eggs and flour again
questions.expected: New substances form and it cannot be turned back into the raw ingredients
questions.memo: Baking creates new substances; you cannot get the raw eggs, flour and sugar back, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Burning is a ___ change because new substances are formed.'
questions.memo: Burning forms new substances, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: Two liquids are mixed; the mixture bubbles, gives off gas and becomes warm. This suggests...
questions.memo: Bubbling gas and heat being given off are signs that a chemical reaction is taking place.

questions.question: Which pair are BOTH physical changes?
options: Baking a cake and burning paper
questions.memo: Melting and dissolving both make no new substance, so both are physical changes.

questions.question: True or false: in a chemical reaction, the products have different properties from the reactants.
questions.memo: True — the new products have different properties from the starting reactants.

questions.question: Which is the best evidence that a chemical reaction has happened?
options: A new substance with new properties has formed
The substance was moved to a new container
The substance got slightly colder while staying the same
questions.expected: A new substance with new properties has formed
questions.memo: The clearest evidence of a chemical reaction is the formation of a new substance with new properties.

questions.question: A clean iron nail is left in damp air for weeks and becomes coated with orange-brown rust. Why is this a chemical change and not a physical one?
options: Rust is a new substance with different properties from the iron
The rust can easily be turned back into iron by hand
questions.expected: Rust is a new substance with different properties from the iron
questions.memo: Rust is a brand-new substance with different properties from iron, so rusting is a chemical change.

NSSP.G8.EC.A1.title: Static electricity
NSSP.G8.EC.A1.description: How rubbing (friction) moves tiny charges to build up static electricity; positive and negative charges; and how like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
NSSP.G8.EC.A1.recovery_strategy: Like charges repel (push apart); unlike charges attract (pull together). Two negatives or two positives push apart; a positive and a negative pull together.

questions.question: Static electricity can build up when two materials are...
questions.memo: Rubbing (friction) moves tiny charges between materials, building up static electricity.

questions.question: A balloon rubbed on a jersey can stick to a wall because it has become...
questions.memo: Rubbing gives the balloon a static charge, which lets it cling to the wall.

questions.question: Two NEGATIVE charges placed near each other will...
questions.memo: Like charges repel, so two negatives push apart.

questions.question: A positive charge and a negative charge placed near each other will...
questions.memo: Unlike charges attract, so a positive and a negative pull together.

questions.question: True or false: rubbing certain materials together can give them a static charge.
questions.memo: True — friction can move charges and leave the materials charged.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Like charges ___ each other.'
questions.memo: Like charges repel (push apart).

questions.question: Unlike charges...
options: have no effect on each other
questions.memo: Unlike (opposite) charges attract each other.

questions.question: After rubbing a balloon on your hair, your hairs stand up and spread apart. Why?
options: The hairs gain the same charge and repel each other
The hairs lose all their charge
questions.expected: The hairs gain the same charge and repel each other
questions.memo: The hairs all gain the same charge, and like charges repel, so the hairs push apart.

questions.question: Do two positive charges attract each other?
questions.memo: Two positive charges are alike, and like charges repel, so they push apart.

questions.question: Sort each pair of charges by whether they attract or repel.

items.text: A positive and a negative charge
A negative and a positive charge

questions.expected: Like charges (two negatives, two positives) repel; unlike charges (positive with negative) attract.
questions.memo: Same charges repel; opposite charges attract.

questions.question: Lightning is a large natural example of...
options: a chemical reaction in the soil
questions.memo: Lightning is a huge discharge of static electricity built up in storm clouds.

questions.question: True or false: unlike charges repel each other.
questions.memo: False — unlike (opposite) charges attract; it is LIKE charges that repel.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A positive and a negative charge ___ each other.'
questions.memo: Opposite charges attract each other.

questions.question: Which action would build up a static charge?
options: Rubbing a plastic comb on a wool jersey
Leaving a comb on a table
Putting a comb in the fridge
questions.expected: Rubbing a plastic comb on a wool jersey
questions.memo: Rubbing the comb on wool transfers charge by friction, building up static electricity.

questions.question: A plastic comb is rubbed on a cloth and then held near tiny pieces of paper, which jump up to it. Why?
options: The charged comb attracts the paper
The paper is blown by the wind
questions.expected: The charged comb attracts the paper
questions.memo: The comb's static charge attracts the small pieces of paper, lifting them up.

questions.question: Charges that are the SAME (both positive or both negative)...
questions.memo: Same (like) charges push apart — they repel.

questions.question: Why does a charged balloon stick to a wall?
options: It attracts opposite charges in the wall and is pulled against it
It becomes magnetic and sticks to metal
It is blown there by the wind
questions.expected: It attracts opposite charges in the wall and is pulled against it
questions.memo: The charged balloon attracts opposite charges in the wall, so it is pulled toward and held against it.

questions.question: True or false: static electricity is caused by electric charges building up on a surface.
questions.memo: True — static electricity is a build-up of electric charge on a surface.

questions.question: Which two objects would attract each other?
options: A positively charged object and a negatively charged object
Two objects with the same charge
questions.expected: A positively charged object and a negatively charged object
questions.memo: Opposite charges attract, so a positive and a negative object pull together.

questions.question: After walking across a carpet, you feel a small shock when you touch a metal door handle. Why?
options: Static charge built up on you and discharges to the metal
The handle is plugged into the mains
questions.expected: Static charge built up on you and discharges to the metal
questions.memo: Walking on the carpet charges you up; touching the metal lets the static charge jump across as a small shock.

NSSP.G8.EC.A2.title: Energy transfer in electrical systems
NSSP.G8.EC.A2.description: Electric circuits and current; the components of a circuit (cell, wires, switch, bulb) and their job; and the effects of an electric current (heating, lighting and magnetic effects).
NSSP.G8.EC.A2.recovery_strategy: Current only flows in a complete (closed) loop from the cell, through the components, and back. If there is a break (open switch, loose wire), no current flows and the bulb stays off.

questions.question: What is an electric circuit?
options: A complete path that lets an electric current flow
questions.expected: A complete path that lets an electric current flow
questions.memo: A circuit is a complete path around which an electric current can flow.

questions.question: Which component is the source of energy in a simple circuit?
questions.memo: The cell (or battery) provides the energy that drives the current.

questions.question: What is the job of a switch in a circuit?
options: To open or close the circuit, turning the current on or off
questions.expected: To open or close the circuit, turning the current on or off
questions.memo: A switch opens or closes the circuit to turn the current off or on.

questions.question: True or false: an electric current needs a complete loop to flow.
questions.memo: True — current only flows when the circuit forms a complete (closed) loop.

questions.question: Look at the simple circuit diagram. For the bulb to light, the circuit must be...
questions.memo: The bulb only lights when the loop is complete so current can flow all the way round.

questions.question: If the switch in a simple circuit is left OPEN, what happens to the bulb?
options: It stays off because no current can flow
questions.expected: It stays off because no current can flow
questions.memo: An open switch breaks the loop, so no current flows and the bulb stays off.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Current only flows when the circuit is a complete ___.'
questions.memo: Current needs a complete loop to flow.

questions.question: What is the job of the wires in a circuit?
options: To carry the current between the components
questions.expected: To carry the current between the components
questions.memo: Wires connect the components and carry the current around the circuit.

questions.question: A glowing light bulb shows which effect of an electric current?
questions.memo: Current heats the bulb's thin wire until it glows — the heating and lighting effect.

questions.question: True or false: an electric current can produce a magnetic effect.
questions.memo: True — a current flowing in a wire produces a magnetic effect (used in electromagnets).

questions.question: A torch does not switch on. Which is a likely reason?
options: There is a break in the circuit, such as a flat cell or loose wire
The torch has too complete a circuit
The bulb is working too well
questions.expected: There is a break in the circuit, such as a flat cell or loose wire
questions.memo: If the loop is broken (flat cell, loose wire, open switch), no current flows and the torch stays off.

questions.question: Which list gives the basic components of a simple circuit?
questions.memo: A simple circuit usually has a cell, connecting wires, a switch and a bulb.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The ___ provides the energy that pushes the current around the circuit.'
questions.memo: The cell (battery) provides the energy for the current.

questions.question: Does a current flow in an incomplete (open) circuit?
options: No — the loop is broken, so no current flows
Yes — but only half of it
questions.expected: No — the loop is broken, so no current flows
questions.memo: An open circuit has a gap, so the current cannot flow and devices stay off.

questions.question: An electric heater works by which effect of the current?
questions.memo: A heater uses the heating effect of the current to warm a coil of wire.

questions.question: True or false: closing a switch completes the circuit and lets the current flow.
questions.memo: True — closing the switch completes the loop so current can flow.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the effects of an electric current?
questions.memo: Current can heat, light and produce a magnetic effect, but it does not turn into a solid object.

questions.question: A loose wire in a circuit stops the bulb from lighting. Why?
options: It breaks the loop, so the current cannot flow
It makes the current flow backwards
questions.expected: It breaks the loop, so the current cannot flow
questions.memo: A loose wire creates a gap in the loop, so the current stops and the bulb goes off.

questions.question: Why is a metal wire used to connect the components in a circuit?
options: Metal makes light on its own
questions.memo: Metals are good conductors, so they carry the current between components.

questions.question: In a circuit with a cell, switch and bulb, the bulb is off even though the cell is full and the bulb works. What should you check FIRST?
options: Whether the switch is open or a wire is loose, breaking the loop
Whether the bulb is too new
Whether the cell is too strong
Whether the wires are too short to carry current
questions.expected: Whether the switch is open or a wire is loose, breaking the loop
questions.memo: If the parts work, the most likely problem is a break in the loop — an open switch or a loose connection.

NSSP.G8.EC.A3.title: Series & parallel circuits
NSSP.G8.EC.A3.description: Series circuits (one single loop) and parallel circuits (more than one path); how each behaves when a bulb is removed; and different output devices.
NSSP.G8.EC.A3.recovery_strategy: Series = one single loop, so removing one bulb breaks the whole circuit and all go off. Parallel = separate paths, so removing one bulb leaves the others on.

questions.question: A series circuit has...
options: one single loop for the current
many separate paths for the current
questions.expected: one single loop for the current
questions.memo: In a series circuit there is just one path, so all the current follows the same single loop.

questions.question: A parallel circuit has...
options: more than one path for the current
questions.expected: more than one path for the current
questions.memo: A parallel circuit splits into more than one path for the current.

questions.question: In a SERIES circuit with two bulbs, what happens to the second bulb if the first bulb is removed?
options: It goes off, because the single loop is broken
It stays on and gets brighter
questions.expected: It goes off, because the single loop is broken
questions.memo: Removing one bulb breaks the single series loop, so the other bulb goes off too.

questions.question: In a PARALLEL circuit with two bulbs on separate paths, what happens to the second bulb if the first bulb is removed?
options: It stays on, because it has its own path
questions.expected: It stays on, because it has its own path
questions.memo: Each bulb in parallel has its own path, so removing one leaves the other still lit.

questions.question: True or false: in a series circuit the current has only one path to follow.
questions.memo: True — a series circuit has a single path for the current.

questions.question: Look at the two circuit diagrams. Which one is the PARALLEL circuit?
options: The one where the bulbs are on separate branches
The one where the bulbs are in a single loop
questions.expected: The one where the bulbs are on separate branches
questions.memo: A parallel circuit has the bulbs on separate branches, each with its own path back to the cell.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ circuit has only one loop, so a break anywhere stops all the current.'
questions.memo: A series circuit has one loop, so any break stops the whole circuit.

questions.question: Why are the lights in a house usually wired in parallel rather than in series?
options: So one light can be switched off or fail without the others going off
So that all lights must be on at once
So they can only work outdoors
questions.expected: So one light can be switched off or fail without the others going off
questions.memo: Parallel wiring means each light is on its own path, so one can go off without affecting the rest.

questions.question: True or false: removing one bulb in a parallel circuit switches off all the other bulbs.
questions.memo: False — in parallel each bulb has its own path, so the others stay on.

questions.question: Sort each statement under the circuit it describes.

items.text: Removing one bulb switches all off
Removing one bulb leaves others on

questions.expected: Single loop and all-go-off describe a series circuit; multiple paths and others-stay-on describe a parallel circuit.
questions.memo: Series = one loop, all depend on each other. Parallel = separate paths, independent of each other.

questions.question: In a string of old decoration lights wired in series, one bulb breaks and they ALL go out. Why?
options: The broken bulb breaks the single loop, so no current flows
The other bulbs ran out of energy
The broken bulb stole the others' light
questions.expected: The broken bulb breaks the single loop, so no current flows
questions.memo: In series there is one loop; a broken bulb makes a gap, so the current stops and every bulb goes out.

questions.question: Which is an example of an output device in a circuit?
options: A buzzer that makes a sound
questions.expected: A buzzer that makes a sound
questions.memo: Output devices, such as bulbs and buzzers, turn electrical energy into light or sound.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a ___ circuit, each device has its own separate path to the cell.'
questions.memo: In a parallel circuit each device sits on its own separate path.

questions.question: Two bulbs are connected one after the other in a single loop. This is a...
questions.memo: Components connected one after another in a single loop form a series circuit.

questions.question: True or false: a buzzer and a bulb are both output devices.
questions.memo: True — both turn electrical energy into a useful output (sound or light).

questions.question: A car's headlights stay on even when a tail light fails. This tells you the lights are wired in...
questions.memo: Because one light can fail without the others going off, they must be on separate parallel paths.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of a parallel circuit over a series circuit?
options: Each device can work on its own, even if another fails
It can never be switched off
questions.expected: Each device can work on its own, even if another fails
questions.memo: A key advantage of parallel is that devices are independent — one failing does not switch off the rest.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a series circuit, the components are connected one ___ the other.'
questions.memo: Series components are joined one after the other in a single loop.

questions.question: True or false: in a series circuit, all the components share a single path.
questions.memo: True — in series, all components are on the same single path.

questions.question: You want to build a set of lights where each one can be switched on and off without affecting the others. Which circuit should you use, and why?
options: Parallel, because each light is on its own path
Series, because there is only one loop
Series, because a break stops all of them
Either one works exactly the same
questions.expected: Parallel, because each light is on its own path
questions.memo: Parallel gives each light its own path, so they can be controlled independently — one off does not affect the others.

NSSP.G8.EC.A4.title: Visible light
NSSP.G8.EC.A4.description: Light travels in straight lines; the spectrum of visible colours; opaque, transparent and translucent materials; and the absorption, reflection and refraction of light.
NSSP.G8.EC.A4.recovery_strategy: Reflection = light bounces OFF a surface (a mirror). Refraction = light BENDS as it passes from one material into another (a straw looking bent in water). Reflect = bounce; refract = bend.

questions.question: How does light travel?
questions.memo: Light travels in straight lines (we can show this with shadows and narrow beams).

questions.question: What is reflection of light?
options: Light bending as it enters water
Light being soaked up by a black object
Light being made by the Sun
questions.memo: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface, like a mirror.

questions.question: What is refraction of light?
options: Light bending as it passes from one material into another
Light being absorbed by a surface
Light travelling in a straight line
questions.expected: Light bending as it passes from one material into another
questions.memo: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water.

questions.question: Light bouncing off a flat mirror is an example of...
questions.memo: Light bouncing off a mirror is reflection.

questions.question: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface. This is caused by...
questions.memo: Light bends (refracts) as it passes between the water and the air, making the straw look bent.

questions.question: True or false: white light can be split into a spectrum of colours.
questions.memo: True — white light is made of many colours, which can be split into a spectrum (like a rainbow).

questions.question: A material you cannot see through at all is described as...
questions.memo: Opaque materials block light, so you cannot see through them.

questions.question: A material you can see through clearly, like clear glass, is described as...
questions.memo: Transparent materials let light pass through, so you can see through them clearly.

questions.question: Sort each material by how it lets light through.
questions.expected: Clear glass and clear water are transparent; a wooden door, metal sheet and brick wall are opaque.
questions.memo: If light passes through and you can see clearly, it is transparent; if light is blocked, it is opaque.

questions.question: Why does a black object look black?
options: It absorbs most of the light that falls on it
It makes its own black light
It bends the light into the ground
questions.expected: It absorbs most of the light that falls on it
questions.memo: A black object absorbs most light and reflects very little, so it looks black.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Light bouncing off a surface is called ___.'
questions.memo: Light bouncing off a surface is reflection.

questions.question: Is light bouncing off a mirror reflection or refraction?
options: Absorption — the light is soaked up
Neither — light cannot hit a mirror
questions.memo: Light bouncing off a mirror is reflection (reflect = bounce). Refraction is bending as light passes through.

questions.question: A frosted glass window lets some light through but you cannot see a clear image. It is...
questions.memo: Translucent materials let some light through but scatter it, so you cannot see a clear image.

questions.question: How do we see a tree that does not make its own light?
options: Light reflects off the tree and enters our eyes
The tree sends light out of itself
We make light with our eyes
We do not need light to see
questions.expected: Light reflects off the tree and enters our eyes
questions.memo: We see most objects because light bounces off them and travels into our eyes.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A rainbow forms when light is split into the ___ of colours.'
questions.memo: A rainbow shows the spectrum — the band of colours that make up white light.

questions.question: True or false: a shadow forms because light travels in straight lines and is blocked by an object.
questions.memo: True — because light travels in straight lines, an object blocks it and casts a shadow.

questions.question: Which surface reflects light the best?
questions.memo: Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light well; dark, rough surfaces absorb most of it.

questions.question: Light passes from air into a glass block and changes direction slightly. This bending is called...
questions.memo: Light bending as it moves from one material into another is refraction.

questions.question: True or false: reflection means light bounces off, while refraction means light bends as it passes through.
questions.memo: True — reflect = bounce off; refract = bend through. That is the key difference.

questions.question: On a hot day a wet road can look like it has a shiny pool of water far ahead, which vanishes as you get closer. This 'mirage' is caused by...
options: light refracting (bending) as it passes through air of different temperatures
the road making its own light
questions.expected: light refracting (bending) as it passes through air of different temperatures
questions.memo: Light bends (refracts) through layers of hot and cooler air, creating the watery-looking mirage.

NSSP.G8.PEB.A1.title: The Solar System
NSSP.G8.PEB.A1.description: The Sun at the centre; the planets and other objects (moons, asteroids, comets) that orbit it; the order of the planets; and Earth's position in the Solar System.
NSSP.G8.PEB.A1.recovery_strategy: The Sun is a star at the centre; the planets orbit it. Planets do not make their own light — they reflect the Sun's. The order from the Sun starts Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars …

questions.question: What is at the centre of our Solar System?
questions.memo: The Sun sits at the centre of the Solar System, with the planets orbiting it.

questions.question: The Sun is a...
questions.memo: The Sun is a star — a huge ball of hot gas that gives off its own light.

questions.question: The paths the planets follow around the Sun are called...
questions.memo: Planets move around the Sun along paths called orbits.

questions.question: True or false: Earth is one of the planets in the Solar System.
questions.memo: True — Earth is the third planet from the Sun.

questions.question: Which position from the Sun is Earth?
questions.memo: Earth is the third planet from the Sun (after Mercury and Venus).

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the Solar System. Which object is the Sun?
options: The third object from the centre
The smallest object on the edge
questions.memo: The Sun is the bright star at the centre, with the planets orbiting around it.

questions.question: Put the first four planets in order, starting from the one nearest the Sun.
questions.memo: From the Sun outward, the first four planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.

questions.question: Besides planets, what else orbits the Sun?
questions.memo: The Solar System also has moons, asteroids and comets orbiting the Sun.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Planets do not make their own light; they ___ the Sun's light.'
questions.memo: Planets shine because they reflect sunlight, not because they make their own light.

questions.question: Does the Sun orbit the Earth?
options: No — the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun
Yes — the Sun goes around the Earth
Yes — they orbit each other equally
questions.expected: No — the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun
questions.memo: The Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun, not the other way round.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun is a planet.
questions.memo: False — the Sun is a star, not a planet.

questions.question: A moon is an object that orbits a...
questions.memo: A moon orbits a planet (for example, our Moon orbits Earth).

questions.question: Why can we see planets like Venus shining in the night sky?
options: They reflect light from the Sun
They make their own light like stars
They glow because they are hot inside
questions.expected: They reflect light from the Sun
questions.memo: Planets do not make their own light — we see them because they reflect sunlight.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The ___ is a star at the centre of our Solar System.'
questions.memo: The Sun is the star at the centre of the Solar System.

questions.question: Which is the largest object in the Solar System?
questions.memo: The Sun is by far the largest object in the Solar System.

questions.question: Why is the Sun so important to the Solar System?
options: Its gravity holds the planets in orbit and it provides light and heat
questions.expected: Its gravity holds the planets in orbit and it provides light and heat
questions.memo: The Sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit, and its light and heat make life on Earth possible.

questions.question: True or false: all the planets orbit the Sun.
questions.memo: True — every planet in the Solar System orbits the Sun.

questions.question: Which list shows the first four planets in the correct order from the Sun?
questions.memo: From the Sun outward: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.

questions.question: True or false: the Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
questions.memo: True — Earth is the third planet, after Mercury and Venus.

questions.question: Why do the planets stay moving around the Sun instead of flying off into space?
options: The Sun's gravity keeps them in their orbits
There is nothing in space to push them
They are tied to the Sun by ropes
They are too heavy to move
questions.expected: The Sun's gravity keeps them in their orbits
questions.memo: The Sun's strong gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them moving in their orbits.

NSSP.G8.PEB.A2.title: Beyond the Solar System
NSSP.G8.PEB.A2.description: The Milky Way galaxy and the stars in it; our nearest star; and how huge space distances are measured in light-years, light-hours and light-minutes.
NSSP.G8.PEB.A2.recovery_strategy: A light-year is a DISTANCE — how far light travels in one year. The Sun is our nearest star; the Milky Way is the galaxy that holds it and billions of others.

questions.question: Our Solar System is part of a galaxy called the...
questions.memo: Our galaxy is called the Milky Way.

questions.question: What is a galaxy?
options: A huge group of stars, gas and dust
questions.expected: A huge group of stars, gas and dust
questions.memo: A galaxy is an enormous group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.

questions.question: Our nearest star is the...
questions.memo: The Sun is the star closest to Earth — our nearest star.

questions.question: True or false: there are billions of stars in the Milky Way.
questions.memo: True — the Milky Way contains billions of stars.

questions.question: A light-year is a measure of...
questions.memo: A light-year measures distance — how far light travels in one year.

questions.question: Is a light-year a measure of time?
options: No — it is a distance: how far light travels in a year
Yes — it is how long a year of light lasts
Yes — it measures how old a star is
questions.expected: No — it is a distance: how far light travels in a year
questions.memo: Despite the word 'year', a light-year is a distance, not a time.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ is the distance that light travels in one year.'
questions.memo: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year.

questions.question: How fast does light travel?
options: Very fast — about 300 000 km every second
The same speed as a car
questions.expected: Very fast — about 300 000 km every second
questions.memo: Light is extremely fast, travelling about 300 000 km every second.

questions.question: Stars look like tiny points of light in the night sky because...
options: they are switched on at night
questions.memo: Stars are huge, but they look tiny because they are so far from Earth.

questions.question: Which is bigger?
options: A galaxy is much bigger than a single solar system
A solar system is bigger than a galaxy
They are exactly the same size
A planet is bigger than a galaxy
questions.expected: A galaxy is much bigger than a single solar system
questions.memo: A galaxy contains billions of stars and solar systems, so it is far bigger than one solar system.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun is just one of the many billions of stars in the Milky Way.
questions.memo: True — the Sun is one ordinary star among billions in the Milky Way.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Our galaxy is called the ___ Way.'
questions.memo: Our galaxy is the Milky Way.

questions.question: Why do we measure space distances in light-years instead of kilometres?
options: The distances are so huge that kilometres would be impractically large numbers
Kilometres do not exist in space
questions.expected: The distances are so huge that kilometres would be impractically large numbers
questions.memo: Space distances are so vast that light-years are a more practical unit than enormous numbers of kilometres.

questions.question: Light-hours and light-minutes also measure...
questions.memo: Like light-years, light-hours and light-minutes measure distance (how far light travels in that time).

questions.question: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. We can therefore say the Sun is about...
questions.memo: Since light takes 8 minutes to reach us, the Sun is about 8 light-minutes away.

questions.question: Beyond the Milky Way, there are...
questions.memo: The Universe contains many billions of other galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun is the closest star to Earth.
questions.memo: True — the Sun is our nearest star by far.

questions.question: A star is 4 light-years away. What does this mean?
options: Its light takes 4 years to reach us
questions.expected: Its light takes 4 years to reach us
questions.memo: A distance of 4 light-years means the star's light takes 4 years to travel to Earth.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The huge distances to the stars are measured in ___.'
questions.memo: Distances to the stars are measured in light-years.

questions.question: When you look at a star that is 100 light-years away, what are you actually seeing?
options: Light that left the star 100 years ago
The star exactly as it is right now
Light made by your own eyes
questions.expected: Light that left the star 100 years ago
questions.memo: Its light took 100 years to reach you, so you see the star as it was 100 years ago.

NSSP.G8.PEB.A3.title: Looking into space
NSSP.G8.PEB.A3.description: Early ways of viewing space; how telescopes let us see further and more clearly; and modern space exploration with satellites, probes and space telescopes.
NSSP.G8.PEB.A3.recovery_strategy: A telescope gathers light to make faraway objects in space look closer and clearer (a microscope is for tiny near objects). Bigger and better telescopes let us see fainter, more distant objects.

questions.question: What is a telescope used for?
options: To see faraway objects in space more clearly
To see tiny things up close
questions.expected: To see faraway objects in space more clearly
questions.memo: A telescope makes distant objects in space look closer and clearer.

questions.question: Long ago, before telescopes, people studied space using...
questions.memo: Before telescopes, people observed space with the naked eye.

questions.question: How does a telescope work?
options: It gathers light to make distant objects look closer and clearer
It makes its own light to shine on stars
It pushes objects closer to Earth
questions.expected: It gathers light to make distant objects look closer and clearer
questions.memo: A telescope collects light from distant objects, making them appear bigger, brighter and clearer.

questions.question: True or false: bigger telescopes can usually see fainter, more distant objects.
questions.memo: True — larger telescopes gather more light, so they can see fainter and more distant objects.

questions.question: Does a telescope make tiny nearby things look bigger, like a microscope?
options: No — a telescope is for faraway objects; a microscope is for tiny near ones
Yes — they do exactly the same job
Yes — a telescope is just a strong microscope
No — a telescope is for hearing distant sounds
questions.expected: No — a telescope is for faraway objects; a microscope is for tiny near ones
questions.memo: A telescope is for distant objects in space; a microscope is for tiny things close up — different jobs.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ gathers light to see faraway objects in space.'
questions.memo: A telescope gathers light to view distant objects in space.

questions.question: A modern way to explore space without people leaving Earth is to use a...
questions.memo: Space telescopes and probes let us explore space without sending people.

questions.question: Sort each method by whether it is an EARLY way or a MODERN way of studying space.

items.text: Studying the sky with only the eyes
Sending a space probe to a planet
Watching star patterns to track the seasons

questions.expected: Naked-eye observation and tracking seasons by the stars are early ways; modern telescopes, probes and satellites are modern ways.
questions.memo: Early ways used the eyes alone; modern ways use instruments like telescopes, probes and satellites.

questions.question: Satellites and space probes help us to...
options: explore and gather information about space
questions.expected: explore and gather information about space
questions.memo: Satellites and probes gather data and images that help us learn about space.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa has large modern telescopes used by astronomers.
questions.memo: True — South Africa hosts large modern telescopes used for astronomy.

questions.question: To study a very distant galaxy, an astronomer would use...
questions.memo: A powerful telescope gathers enough light to study faint, distant galaxies.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A space ___ is a telescope placed above the Earth, out in space.'
questions.memo: A space telescope is a telescope launched above the Earth into space.

questions.question: Why can a telescope in space often see more clearly than one on the ground?
options: It is above the Earth's atmosphere, which blurs the view
It is closer to the stars by walking distance
It uses no light at all
The ground telescope is always switched off
questions.expected: It is above the Earth's atmosphere, which blurs the view
questions.memo: The atmosphere blurs and dims starlight; a space telescope is above it, giving a clearer view.

questions.question: A microscope is used for...
questions.memo: A microscope magnifies tiny objects up close — the opposite job to a telescope.

questions.question: How have telescopes changed our understanding of space?
options: They let us see far more, and fainter, objects than the eye alone
They stopped people studying the sky
They only show objects on Earth
questions.expected: They let us see far more, and fainter, objects than the eye alone
