questions.memo: Telescopes reveal far more detail and many faint, distant objects the naked eye cannot see.

questions.question: True or false: space probes can travel to other planets to gather information.
questions.memo: True — space probes travel to other planets and send back data and images.

questions.question: A view through a ground telescope shimmers and blurs on a windy night. This is partly because of...
options: the telescope making its own light
questions.memo: Moving air in the atmosphere bends the light, making the view shimmer and blur.

questions.question: Which of these is a modern space tool?
questions.memo: A space telescope is a modern instrument; the others are older or simple methods.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Bigger telescopes gather more ___, so they can see fainter objects.'
questions.memo: Larger telescopes collect more light, letting them see fainter, more distant objects.

questions.question: Why is it worth the huge effort of putting a telescope in space?
options: Above the atmosphere it gives a much clearer, steadier view of distant objects
It is cheaper than a ground telescope
It brings the stars closer to Earth
questions.expected: Above the atmosphere it gives a much clearer, steadier view of distant objects
questions.memo: A space telescope escapes the blurring atmosphere, giving sharp, steady views worth the effort and cost.

NSSP.G9.LL.A1.title: Cells as the basic units of life
NSSP.G9.LL.A1.description: The cell as the basic unit of life; the main parts of a cell; the differences between plant and animal cells; and how cells are organised into tissues, organs and systems.
NSSP.G9.LL.A1.caps_topic: Cells as the basic units of life
NSSP.G9.LL.A1.recovery_strategy: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. ONLY plant cells also have a cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts. Organisation goes: cells → tissues → organs → systems.

questions.question: What is the basic unit of life?
questions.memo: The cell is the basic building block of all living things.

questions.question: Which parts are found in BOTH plant and animal cells?
questions.memo: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.

questions.question: Which part is found ONLY in plant cells, not in animal cells?
questions.memo: A cell wall is found only in plant cells; both cell types have the others.

questions.question: Chloroplasts, where photosynthesis happens, are found in...
questions.memo: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells, where photosynthesis takes place.

questions.question: True or false: the nucleus controls the activities of the cell.
questions.memo: True — the nucleus is the control centre of the cell.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the cell. Which structure is the thin outer boundary that controls what enters and leaves?
questions.memo: The cell membrane is the outer boundary that controls what enters and leaves the cell.

questions.question: Put these levels of organisation in order, from smallest to largest.
questions.memo: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs make systems.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The jelly-like substance that fills a cell is the ___.'
questions.memo: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance that fills the cell.

questions.question: Do animal cells have a cell wall?
options: No — only plant cells have a cell wall
Yes — all cells have a cell wall
Yes — only animal cells have a cell wall
No — no cells have a cell wall
questions.expected: No — only plant cells have a cell wall
questions.memo: Animal cells have no cell wall; the cell wall is a plant-cell feature.

questions.question: A group of similar cells working together forms a...
questions.memo: Similar cells working together make up a tissue.

questions.question: Several different tissues working together form an...
questions.memo: Different tissues working together make up an organ, such as the heart.

questions.question: Sort each cell part by whether it is found in plant cells ONLY, or in BOTH plant and animal cells.
questions.expected: Plant cells only: cell wall, chloroplast, large vacuole. Both: nucleus and cell membrane.
questions.memo: Cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole are plant-only; the nucleus and cell membrane are in both.

questions.question: True or false: the cell wall gives a plant cell support and a fixed shape.
questions.memo: True — the strong cell wall supports the plant cell and keeps its shape.

questions.question: Which part controls what enters and leaves the cell?
questions.memo: The cell membrane controls what passes in and out of the cell.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Cells → tissues → organs → ___.'
questions.memo: Organs working together form systems, the largest level here.

questions.question: A scientist views a cell that has a cell wall and chloroplasts. What kind of cell is it?
options: A cell from no living thing
questions.memo: A cell wall and chloroplasts are plant-cell features, so it is a plant cell.

questions.question: Why is the cell called the 'basic unit of life'?
options: All living things are made of one or more cells
Cells are the largest things in the body
Only plants are made of cells
questions.expected: All living things are made of one or more cells
questions.memo: Every living thing is built from cells, so the cell is the basic unit of life.

questions.question: True or false: a large vacuole that stores water and keeps the cell firm is mainly found in plant cells.
questions.memo: True — plant cells usually have one large vacuole that stores water and helps keep the cell firm.

questions.question: The heart is an example of a...
questions.memo: The heart is made of several tissues working together, so it is an organ.

questions.question: A learner finds a cell with no cell wall and no chloroplasts, but it does have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. What is it?
questions.memo: No cell wall and no chloroplasts, but the basic parts present — this is an animal cell.

NSSP.G9.LL.A2.title: Systems in the human body
NSSP.G9.LL.A2.description: The main systems of the human body (such as the circulatory, respiratory, digestive, skeletal, muscular and nervous systems) and the basic job of each.
NSSP.G9.LL.A2.recovery_strategy: Match each system to one key job: circulatory = transports blood; respiratory = takes in oxygen; digestive = breaks down food; skeletal = supports the body; nervous = sends messages.

questions.question: What is the main job of the circulatory system?
options: To transport blood around the body
questions.expected: To transport blood around the body
questions.memo: The circulatory system transports blood, carrying oxygen and nutrients around the body.

questions.question: What is the main job of the respiratory system?
options: To take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide
questions.expected: To take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide
questions.memo: The respiratory system brings in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

questions.question: What is the main job of the digestive system?
options: To break down food so the body can use it
questions.expected: To break down food so the body can use it
questions.memo: The digestive system breaks food into small pieces the body can absorb.

questions.question: Which body system supports the body and protects organs?
questions.memo: The skeletal system (bones) supports the body and protects organs like the brain and heart.

questions.question: True or false: the nervous system carries messages around the body.
questions.memo: True — the nervous system sends and receives messages, controlling and coordinating the body.

questions.question: Sort each body system with its main job.
questions.expected: Circulatory → transports blood; respiratory → takes in oxygen; digestive → breaks down food.
questions.memo: Match each system to its one key job: circulatory transports, respiratory takes in oxygen, digestive breaks down food.

questions.question: The heart is the main organ of which system?
questions.memo: The heart pumps blood, so it is the main organ of the circulatory system.

questions.question: The lungs are the main organs of which system?
questions.memo: The lungs take in oxygen, so they belong to the respiratory system.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The ___ system uses muscles to move the body.'
questions.memo: The muscular system uses muscles to move the body.

questions.question: Does the respiratory system pump blood around the body?
options: No — that is the job of the circulatory system
Yes — the lungs pump the blood
No — blood is not pumped at all
questions.expected: No — that is the job of the circulatory system
questions.memo: Pumping blood is the circulatory system's job; the respiratory system handles breathing.

questions.question: True or false: the body's systems work together to keep us alive.
questions.memo: True — the systems depend on each other; for example, the circulatory and respiratory systems work together.

questions.question: Which system would you depend on most to run fast in a race?
options: The muscular and skeletal systems (working with the circulatory and respiratory systems)
Only the nervous system on its own
questions.expected: The muscular and skeletal systems (working with the circulatory and respiratory systems)
questions.memo: Running uses muscles and bones to move, supported by the heart and lungs delivering oxygen — several systems together.

questions.question: Which system sends fast electrical messages to control the body?
questions.memo: The nervous system carries fast messages that control and coordinate the body.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The skeletal system is made up of ___.'
questions.memo: The skeletal system is made of bones, which support and protect the body.

questions.question: Which two systems work together to supply the body with oxygen?
questions.memo: The lungs take in oxygen and the blood carries it around, so the respiratory and circulatory systems work together.

questions.question: True or false: each body system does a completely separate job and never affects the others.
questions.memo: False — the systems are interdependent and work together, not in isolation.

questions.question: Which system removes waste carbon dioxide from the body when you breathe out?
questions.memo: The respiratory system removes carbon dioxide when you breathe out.

questions.question: The stomach and intestines are organs of which system?
questions.memo: The stomach and intestines digest food, so they are part of the digestive system.

questions.question: Why does the body need many different systems instead of just one?
options: Each system does a special job, and together they keep the whole body working
The body has systems only for decoration
Systems do not actually do anything
questions.expected: Each system does a special job, and together they keep the whole body working
questions.memo: Different systems handle different needs, and together they keep the whole body alive and healthy.

questions.question: If the circulatory system stopped working, why would the other systems quickly fail too?
options: Blood would no longer deliver oxygen and nutrients to the rest of the body
The body would have too much energy
questions.expected: Blood would no longer deliver oxygen and nutrients to the rest of the body
questions.memo: The circulatory system delivers oxygen and nutrients everywhere, so if it stops, the other systems are quickly starved and fail.

NSSP.G9.LL.A3.title: Human reproduction
NSSP.G9.LL.A3.description: The purpose of reproduction and the changes of puberty; the male and female reproductive organs; and the stages of reproduction (from fertilisation to birth).
NSSP.G9.LL.A3.recovery_strategy: The order is: fertilisation (sperm meets egg) → the fertilised egg develops in the uterus → the baby grows → birth. Puberty is the time the body matures and becomes able to reproduce.

questions.question: What is the purpose of reproduction?
options: To produce new individuals and continue the species
questions.expected: To produce new individuals and continue the species
questions.memo: Reproduction produces offspring so the species continues.

questions.question: Puberty is the time when...
options: the body matures and becomes able to reproduce
a person becomes a baby again
questions.expected: the body matures and becomes able to reproduce
questions.memo: Puberty is when the body changes and becomes able to reproduce.

questions.question: Human fertilisation is the joining of a sperm cell and...
questions.memo: Fertilisation joins a sperm cell with an egg cell.

questions.question: In which organ does a baby develop?
questions.memo: A baby develops in the uterus (womb).

questions.question: True or false: the male reproductive cells are called sperm.
questions.memo: True — sperm are the male reproductive cells.

questions.question: Put the stages of human reproduction in the correct order.

items.text: The fertilised egg develops in the uterus

questions.memo: The order is fertilisation → development in the uterus → growth → birth.

questions.question: The female reproductive cell is called the...
questions.memo: The egg (ovum) is the female reproductive cell.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Fertilisation happens when a sperm joins with an ___.'
questions.memo: Fertilisation is a sperm joining with an egg.

questions.question: Which comes FIRST in human reproduction?
questions.memo: Fertilisation comes first, before the egg develops and the baby grows.

questions.question: True or false: puberty usually happens during the teenage years.
questions.memo: True — puberty usually takes place during the teenage years.

questions.question: Why does the body change during puberty?
options: So that the body becomes able to reproduce
So the body stops needing food
questions.expected: So that the body becomes able to reproduce
questions.memo: Puberty prepares the body to be able to reproduce.

questions.question: Where does fertilisation usually take place in the female body?
questions.memo: Fertilisation usually happens in the fallopian tube, after which the fertilised egg moves to the uterus.

questions.question: After fertilisation, the fertilised egg moves to the uterus and...
options: develops into a baby over time
questions.expected: develops into a baby over time
questions.memo: The fertilised egg attaches in the uterus and develops into a baby over the following months.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The final stage, when the baby is born, is called ___.'
questions.memo: Birth is the final stage, when the baby is born.

questions.question: True or false: reproduction is needed for a species to continue from one generation to the next.
questions.memo: True — without reproduction, a species could not continue.

questions.question: Which organ produces sperm in the male reproductive system?
questions.memo: The testes produce sperm in the male reproductive system.

questions.question: Which organ releases egg cells in the female reproductive system?
questions.memo: The ovaries produce and release egg cells.

questions.question: Does birth come before or after fertilisation?
options: After — fertilisation happens first, birth happens last
questions.expected: After — fertilisation happens first, birth happens last
questions.memo: Fertilisation is the first stage and birth is the last, so birth comes after.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A fertilised egg develops into a baby inside the ___.'
questions.memo: The fertilised egg develops into a baby inside the uterus.

questions.question: Why must fertilisation happen before a baby can develop?
options: A new individual only begins once a sperm and egg join
Babies form from eggs alone without sperm
questions.expected: A new individual only begins once a sperm and egg join
questions.memo: Development of a new individual only starts after a sperm fertilises an egg.

NSSP.G9.LL.A4.title: Circulatory & respiratory systems
NSSP.G9.LL.A4.description: Breathing and gaseous exchange in the lungs; the heart and blood vessels that circulate blood; and how the circulatory and respiratory systems work together to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
NSSP.G9.LL.A4.recovery_strategy: We breathe IN oxygen and breathe OUT carbon dioxide. The lungs do gaseous exchange; the heart pumps blood to carry the oxygen around the body and bring carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

questions.question: Which gas do we breathe IN that the body needs?
questions.memo: We breathe in oxygen, which the body needs for respiration.

questions.question: Which waste gas do we breathe OUT?
questions.memo: We breathe out carbon dioxide, a waste gas from respiration.

questions.question: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.memo: The heart is the pump that pushes blood around the body.

questions.question: Where in the body does gaseous exchange (swapping oxygen for carbon dioxide) take place?
questions.memo: Gaseous exchange happens in the lungs, where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.

questions.question: True or false: the blood carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.
questions.memo: True — blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and delivers it around the body.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the heart and lungs. Which organ takes in air for gaseous exchange?
questions.memo: The lungs take in air, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.

questions.question: Does the body breathe in carbon dioxide and breathe out oxygen?
options: No — we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide
Yes — we breathe in carbon dioxide and out oxygen
questions.expected: No — we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide
questions.memo: It is the other way round: in comes oxygen, out goes carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Blood vessels called ___ carry blood around the body.'
questions.memo: Blood is carried in vessels — arteries, veins and capillaries.

questions.question: How do the circulatory and respiratory systems work together?
options: The lungs add oxygen to the blood, and the heart pumps that blood around the body
The heart breathes and the lungs pump
questions.expected: The lungs add oxygen to the blood, and the heart pumps that blood around the body
questions.memo: The respiratory system loads oxygen into the blood; the circulatory system carries it everywhere.

questions.question: True or false: when you exercise, you breathe faster because your body needs more oxygen.
questions.memo: True — exercise increases the body's need for oxygen, so breathing speeds up.

questions.question: What does the blood carry AWAY from the body's cells to be breathed out?
questions.memo: Blood carries waste carbon dioxide from the cells back to the lungs to be breathed out.

questions.question: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
options: To pump oxygen-rich blood to the muscles more quickly
questions.expected: To pump oxygen-rich blood to the muscles more quickly
questions.memo: Running muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to deliver blood quickly.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Oxygen passes from the lungs into the ___, which carries it around the body.'
questions.memo: Oxygen passes into the blood, which delivers it to the body's cells.

questions.question: Which part of the body protects the heart and lungs?
questions.memo: The rib cage surrounds and protects the heart and lungs.

questions.question: True or false: the lungs are part of the respiratory system and the heart is part of the circulatory system.
questions.memo: True — the lungs belong to the respiratory system and the heart to the circulatory system.

questions.question: Why do the body's cells need a constant supply of oxygen?
options: To release energy from food during respiration
questions.expected: To release energy from food during respiration
questions.memo: Cells use oxygen to release energy from food (respiration), so they need a steady supply.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The ___ pumps blood, while the lungs handle breathing.'
questions.memo: The heart pumps blood; the lungs do the breathing.

questions.question: When you breathe out, where has the carbon dioxide come from?
options: From the body's cells, carried to the lungs by the blood
From food in the stomach directly
questions.expected: From the body's cells, carried to the lungs by the blood
questions.memo: Cells produce carbon dioxide during respiration; the blood carries it to the lungs to be breathed out.

questions.question: True or false: the circulatory system delivers both oxygen and nutrients to the body's cells.
questions.memo: True — the blood carries oxygen from the lungs and nutrients from digestion to the cells.

questions.question: A person holds their breath. Why do they soon feel the urge to breathe again?
options: Carbon dioxide builds up and oxygen runs low, so the body forces a breath
questions.expected: Carbon dioxide builds up and oxygen runs low, so the body forces a breath
questions.memo: Holding your breath lets carbon dioxide build up and oxygen drop, so the body strongly signals you to breathe.

NSSP.G9.LL.A5.title: Digestive system
NSSP.G9.LL.A5.description: What makes a healthy, balanced diet; the parts of the alimentary canal; and how food is digested and absorbed as it passes through the gut.
NSSP.G9.LL.A5.recovery_strategy: Food travels: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine. Digestion breaks food into small pieces the body can absorb. A balanced diet has the right mix of food groups.

questions.question: What does the digestive system do?
options: Breaks food down into small pieces the body can absorb
questions.expected: Breaks food down into small pieces the body can absorb
questions.memo: The digestive system breaks food into small pieces the body can absorb and use.

questions.question: Where does digestion begin?
questions.memo: Digestion begins in the mouth, where food is chewed and mixed with saliva.

questions.question: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
questions.memo: The oesophagus carries swallowed food from the mouth down to the stomach.

questions.question: Where are most digested nutrients absorbed into the blood?
questions.memo: Most digested nutrients are absorbed into the blood through the wall of the small intestine.

questions.question: True or false: a balanced diet contains the right mix of different food groups.
questions.memo: True — a balanced diet has the right mix of food groups in healthy amounts.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the digestive system. Which organ is the stomach?
options: The muscular bag where food is churned after the oesophagus
The long tube just after the mouth
questions.expected: The muscular bag where food is churned after the oesophagus
questions.memo: The stomach is the muscular bag, after the oesophagus, where food is churned and broken down further.

questions.question: Put the path of food through the digestive system in the correct order.
questions.memo: Food travels: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Chewing food in the mouth mixes it with ___, which begins digestion.'
questions.memo: Saliva in the mouth helps begin breaking down the food.

questions.question: Does food travel from the stomach back up to the mouth as part of normal digestion?
options: No — food moves on from the stomach to the intestines
Yes — it goes back to the mouth
Yes — it cycles round many times
No — food never leaves the mouth
questions.expected: No — food moves on from the stomach to the intestines
questions.memo: Food moves forward through the gut — from the stomach onward to the intestines, not back to the mouth.

questions.question: What is the main job of the large intestine?
options: To absorb water and form waste
questions.expected: To absorb water and form waste
questions.memo: The large intestine absorbs water from the remaining material and forms solid waste.

questions.question: True or false: digestion breaks large pieces of food into smaller pieces the body can absorb.
questions.memo: True — digestion breaks food down small enough to be absorbed into the blood.

questions.question: Which food group is the body's main source of energy?
questions.memo: Carbohydrates (like bread, rice and maize) are the body's main energy source.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Food is pushed from the mouth to the stomach through the ___.'
questions.memo: The oesophagus carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

questions.question: Why is eating fruit and vegetables, which contain fibre, good for digestion?
options: Fibre helps food move through the gut and keeps it healthy
Fibre is the body's main energy source
questions.expected: Fibre helps food move through the gut and keeps it healthy
questions.memo: Fibre helps keep food moving smoothly through the digestive system.

questions.question: Which food group is important for growth and repair of the body?
questions.memo: Proteins (like meat, beans and eggs) are needed for growth and repairing the body.

questions.question: True or false: eating only one type of food gives the body a balanced diet.
questions.memo: False — a balanced diet needs a variety of food groups, not just one type.

questions.question: After the small intestine, the leftover material passes into the...
questions.memo: After the small intestine, the remaining material moves into the large intestine.

questions.question: Why must food be digested before the body can use it?
options: Large food pieces must be broken down small enough to be absorbed into the blood
Food is already small enough to use whole
The body uses food without changing it
questions.expected: Large food pieces must be broken down small enough to be absorbed into the blood
questions.memo: Food must be broken into small molecules so it can be absorbed into the blood and used by cells.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Most nutrients are absorbed into the blood through the wall of the ___ intestine.'
questions.memo: Most nutrients are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine.

questions.question: A learner eats a meal of only sweets and fizzy drinks. Why is this an unhealthy, unbalanced diet?
options: It is high in sugar but lacks proteins, fibre, vitamins and minerals the body needs
questions.expected: It is high in sugar but lacks proteins, fibre, vitamins and minerals the body needs
questions.memo: Sweets and fizzy drinks are mostly sugar; a balanced diet also needs protein, fibre, vitamins and minerals.

NSSP.G9.MM.A1.title: Compounds
NSSP.G9.MM.A1.description: How the Periodic Table organises elements; how compounds form when elements combine; and how compounds are named (for example, the rule for names ending in -ide and -ate).
NSSP.G9.MM.A1.recovery_strategy: When two elements join, the name usually ends in -ide (sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride). When oxygen is part of a group with another element, the name often ends in -ate (e.g. carbonate, sulfate).

questions.question: How does a compound form?
options: When two or more different elements join chemically
When one element is cut in half
questions.expected: When two or more different elements join chemically
questions.memo: A compound forms when different elements join chemically in fixed proportions.

questions.question: When sodium reacts with chlorine, the compound formed is called...
questions.memo: Two elements joining gives an -ide name, so sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride.

questions.question: A compound made of just two elements usually has a name ending in...
questions.memo: Compounds of two elements usually end in -ide (e.g. oxide, chloride, sulfide).

questions.question: Which compound name tells you that oxygen is part of a group within it?
questions.memo: Names ending in -ate (like carbonate) usually contain oxygen joined with another element in a group.

questions.question: True or false: the Periodic Table organises all the known elements.
questions.memo: True — the Periodic Table is an organised table of all the known elements.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'When two elements combine, the compound name usually ends in ___.'
questions.memo: Two-element compounds usually end in -ide.

questions.question: Water is a compound made of which two elements?
questions.memo: Water (H2O) is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.question: A compound of magnesium and oxygen is called...
questions.memo: Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide (an -ide name for two elements).

questions.question: Iron joins with sulfur to form...
questions.memo: Iron + sulfur → iron sulfide (two elements give an -ide name).

questions.question: Which of these is a compound?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide is a compound of carbon and oxygen; the others are single elements.

questions.question: Sort each substance as an element or a compound.
questions.expected: Oxygen and iron are elements; sodium chloride, water and carbon dioxide are compounds.
questions.memo: One kind of atom = element; different elements chemically joined = compound.

questions.question: True or false: a compound can have very different properties from the elements it is made of.
questions.memo: True — a compound's properties can be completely different from those of its elements.

questions.question: Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet sodium chloride is...
options: ordinary table salt, which is safe to eat
questions.expected: ordinary table salt, which is safe to eat
questions.memo: Joined as a compound, sodium and chlorine make table salt, which is safe to eat — very different from the elements.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A compound containing an oxygen group, like calcium carbonate, ends in ___.'
questions.memo: Names ending in -ate (e.g. carbonate, sulfate) usually contain an oxygen group.

questions.question: Which two elements make up magnesium oxide?
questions.memo: Magnesium oxide is made of magnesium and oxygen.

questions.question: Why does a particular compound always have the same name and formula?
options: Its elements always join in the same fixed proportions
Its name is chosen at random
Compounds change formula all the time
Elements never join in fixed amounts
questions.expected: Its elements always join in the same fixed proportions
questions.memo: A compound's elements combine in fixed proportions, so it has a fixed formula and name.

questions.question: Calcium reacts with oxygen to form...
questions.memo: Calcium + oxygen → calcium oxide.

questions.question: True or false: the properties of a compound are simply the average of the properties of its elements.
questions.memo: False — a compound usually has its own new properties, not just an average of its elements.

questions.question: NaCl is the chemical formula for...
questions.memo: NaCl stands for sodium chloride (Na = sodium, Cl = chlorine).

questions.question: Why is sodium chloride safe to eat, even though sodium and chlorine on their own are dangerous?
options: Joining chemically forms a new compound with completely different properties
The danger is just hidden inside
Chlorine gas is safe to breathe
questions.expected: Joining chemically forms a new compound with completely different properties
questions.memo: When elements bond into a compound, the result can be totally different and safe — like table salt.

NSSP.G9.MM.A2.title: Chemical reactions & equations
NSSP.G9.MM.A2.description: Representing reactions with word and symbol equations; the idea that atoms are not created or destroyed; and balancing simple chemical equations.
NSSP.G9.MM.A2.recovery_strategy: In any reaction, atoms are only rearranged — none are made or lost. A balanced equation must have the same number of each kind of atom on both sides (reactants = products).

questions.question: In a word equation, the substances on the LEFT of the arrow are the...
questions.memo: The reactants (starting substances) are written on the left of the arrow.

questions.question: In a word equation, the substances on the RIGHT of the arrow are the...
questions.memo: The products (substances made) are written on the right of the arrow.

questions.question: What does the arrow in a chemical equation mean?
questions.memo: The arrow means the reactants react to form the products.

questions.question: True or false: in a chemical reaction, atoms are only rearranged — none are made or destroyed.
questions.memo: True — atoms are conserved; they are only rearranged into new substances.

questions.question: What must be true for a chemical equation to be 'balanced'?
options: The same number of each kind of atom on both sides
More atoms on the product side
More atoms on the reactant side
Only the names need to match
questions.expected: The same number of each kind of atom on both sides
questions.memo: A balanced equation has equal numbers of each kind of atom on the reactant and product sides.

questions.question: Complete the word equation: 'magnesium + oxygen → ___.'
questions.memo: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

questions.question: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
options: Because atoms are never created or destroyed in a reaction
Because products weigh less than reactants
questions.expected: Because atoms are never created or destroyed in a reaction
questions.memo: Balancing reflects the law that atoms are conserved — the same atoms appear on both sides.

questions.question: In the reaction 'hydrogen + oxygen → water', which are the reactants?
questions.memo: Hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants; water is the product.

questions.question: True or false: a symbol equation uses chemical symbols and formulae instead of words.
questions.memo: True — symbol equations use formulae like H2O instead of words like 'water'.

questions.question: In the equation 'carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide', what is the product?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide is the product; carbon and oxygen are the reactants.

questions.question: If a reaction starts with 10 atoms in total, how many atoms are there after the reaction?
options: 10 — atoms are not created or destroyed
questions.expected: 10 — atoms are not created or destroyed
questions.memo: Atoms are conserved, so the same number remains — just rearranged.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a balanced equation, the reactants and products have the same number of each kind of ___.'
questions.memo: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

questions.question: Complete the word equation: 'iron + sulfur → ___.'
questions.memo: Iron reacts with sulfur to form iron sulfide.

questions.question: Can a balanced equation have more atoms of an element on the product side than on the reactant side?
options: No — the number of each atom must be equal on both sides
Yes — products always have more atoms
No — products always have fewer atoms
questions.expected: No — the number of each atom must be equal on both sides
questions.memo: A balanced equation must have equal numbers of each atom on both sides — none are gained or lost.

questions.question: True or false: word equations and symbol equations can both describe the same reaction.
questions.memo: True — the same reaction can be shown in words or in chemical symbols.

questions.question: In 'zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen', which is a product?
questions.memo: Zinc chloride and hydrogen are the products; zinc and hydrochloric acid are the reactants.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Atoms are only ___ in a reaction, never made or destroyed.'
questions.memo: In a reaction, atoms are simply rearranged into new combinations.

questions.question: Why does the total mass usually stay the same during a chemical reaction in a closed container?
options: The same atoms are present before and after, just rearranged
Some atoms vanish to balance it
questions.expected: The same atoms are present before and after, just rearranged
questions.memo: Because atoms are conserved, the total mass stays the same in a closed container.

questions.question: True or false: in the equation 'reactants → products', the products are the new substances formed.
questions.memo: True — the products on the right are the new substances formed in the reaction.

questions.question: When magnesium burns in oxygen, the magnesium oxide formed weighs MORE than the magnesium alone. Why does this not break the rule that atoms are conserved?
options: Oxygen atoms from the air have joined the magnesium, so their mass is added too
The rule only applies to gases
questions.expected: Oxygen atoms from the air have joined the magnesium, so their mass is added too
questions.memo: The extra mass comes from oxygen atoms joining the magnesium — no atoms are created, they are just added from the air.

NSSP.G9.MM.A3.title: Reactions of metals with oxygen
NSSP.G9.MM.A3.description: The general reaction of a metal with oxygen to form a metal oxide; examples (iron, magnesium); the formation of rust; and ways to prevent rusting.
NSSP.G9.MM.A3.recovery_strategy: metal + oxygen → metal oxide. Rusting is iron reacting with oxygen AND water, so keeping iron dry or coated (paint, oil, galvanising) prevents rust.

questions.question: When a metal reacts with oxygen, it forms a...
questions.memo: The general reaction is metal + oxygen → metal oxide.

questions.question: Complete the word equation: 'magnesium + oxygen → ___.'
questions.memo: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

questions.question: When iron reacts slowly with oxygen and water, the orange-brown substance formed is called...
questions.memo: Iron reacting with oxygen and water forms rust, which is a form of iron oxide.

questions.question: Which TWO things are needed for iron to rust?
questions.memo: Rusting needs both oxygen and water; keeping either away prevents rust.

questions.question: True or false: magnesium burns with a bright white flame when it reacts with oxygen.
questions.memo: True — magnesium burns with a bright white flame, forming white magnesium oxide.

questions.question: Which is a good way to PREVENT iron from rusting?
options: Painting or oiling it to keep out oxygen and water
questions.expected: Painting or oiling it to keep out oxygen and water
questions.memo: A coating like paint or oil keeps oxygen and water away, preventing rust.

questions.question: Does iron rust faster when it is kept completely dry?
options: No — rusting needs water, so dry iron rusts much more slowly
questions.expected: No — rusting needs water, so dry iron rusts much more slowly
questions.memo: Without water, iron rusts very slowly, so keeping it dry helps prevent rust.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The general reaction is metal + oxygen → metal ___.'
questions.memo: metal + oxygen → metal oxide.

questions.question: When iron reacts with oxygen, the product is called...
questions.memo: Iron + oxygen → iron oxide (rust is a form of iron oxide).

questions.question: Galvanising covers iron with a layer of zinc. How does this help?
options: The zinc layer keeps oxygen and water away from the iron
The zinc makes the iron rust faster
The zinc adds water to the iron
questions.expected: The zinc layer keeps oxygen and water away from the iron
questions.memo: Galvanising coats the iron in zinc, blocking the oxygen and water that cause rust.

questions.question: True or false: a metal oxide forms when a metal combines with oxygen.
questions.memo: True — metal + oxygen gives a metal oxide.

questions.question: Sort each item by whether it speeds up rusting or helps prevent it.
questions.expected: Damp air and water speed up rusting; paint, oil and galvanising prevent it.
questions.memo: Anything that brings oxygen and water to the iron speeds rust; anything that keeps them away prevents it.

questions.question: Why does a metal oxide form when steel wool is burned in air?
options: The iron in the steel reacts with oxygen in the air
The steel turns into pure carbon
The steel reacts with nitrogen only
questions.expected: The iron in the steel reacts with oxygen in the air
questions.memo: Burning steel wool lets the iron react with oxygen, forming iron oxide.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and ___.'
questions.memo: Rusting needs both oxygen and water.

questions.question: True or false: keeping a steel tool oiled helps stop it from rusting.
questions.memo: True — a layer of oil keeps oxygen and water off the steel, preventing rust.

questions.question: Which colour is the magnesium oxide formed when magnesium burns?
questions.memo: Burning magnesium forms a white powder, magnesium oxide.

questions.question: An iron gate near the sea rusts faster than one inland. Why?
options: Salty, damp sea air speeds up rusting
The gate is colder by the sea
questions.expected: Salty, damp sea air speeds up rusting
questions.memo: Damp, salty sea air provides plenty of water (and salt speeds the process), so rusting is faster.

questions.question: Which word equation is correct?
questions.memo: Iron reacting with oxygen gives iron oxide.

questions.question: True or false: rusting is a chemical change because a new substance (iron oxide) is formed.
questions.memo: True — rust is a new substance, so rusting is a chemical change.

questions.question: Two identical nails are left out: one is painted and one is bare, both in damp air. After weeks, why has only the bare nail rusted?
options: The paint kept oxygen and water away from the painted nail
The painted nail was made of plastic
The bare nail was kept dry
questions.expected: The paint kept oxygen and water away from the painted nail
questions.memo: The paint formed a barrier against oxygen and water, so the painted nail did not rust while the bare one did.

NSSP.G9.MM.A4.title: Reactions of non-metals with oxygen
NSSP.G9.MM.A4.description: The general reaction of a non-metal with oxygen to form a non-metal oxide; examples (carbon, sulfur); and how many non-metal oxides dissolve in water to form acids.
NSSP.G9.MM.A4.recovery_strategy: non-metal + oxygen → non-metal oxide. Non-metal oxides (like carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide) usually dissolve in water to form ACIDS, while metal oxides tend to be basic.

questions.question: When a non-metal reacts with oxygen, it forms a...
questions.memo: The general reaction is non-metal + oxygen → non-metal oxide.

questions.question: Complete the word equation: 'carbon + oxygen → ___.'
questions.memo: Carbon burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide.

questions.question: When sulfur burns in oxygen, it forms...
questions.memo: Sulfur + oxygen → sulfur dioxide.

questions.question: When non-metal oxides dissolve in water, they usually form...
questions.memo: Non-metal oxides like carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide dissolve to form acids.

questions.question: True or false: carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form a weak acid.
questions.memo: True — carbon dioxide dissolves to form a weak acid (this is why rain is slightly acidic).

questions.question: Does carbon dioxide dissolve in water to form a base?
options: No — it forms a weak acid
Yes — it forms a strong base
Yes — it forms a neutral solution only
No — it does not dissolve at all
questions.expected: No — it forms a weak acid
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide is a non-metal oxide, so it dissolves to form an acid, not a base.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-metal oxide?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide is the oxide of a non-metal (carbon); the others are metal oxides.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'non-metal + oxygen → non-metal ___.'
questions.memo: non-metal + oxygen → non-metal oxide.

questions.question: Burning sulfur gives off a choking gas, sulfur dioxide. When it dissolves in water, it...
questions.memo: Sulfur dioxide is a non-metal oxide, so it dissolves to form an acid.

questions.question: Sort each oxide by what it forms in water.
questions.expected: Non-metal oxides (carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide) form acids; metal oxides (magnesium oxide, calcium oxide) tend to be basic.
questions.memo: Non-metal oxides → acids; metal oxides → basic.

questions.question: True or false: metal oxides tend to be basic.
questions.memo: True — metal oxides tend to be basic, the opposite of acidic non-metal oxides.

questions.question: Why is 'acid rain' linked to burning coal and fuels?
options: Sulfur dioxide from burning fuels dissolves in rain to make acid
Burning fuels make the rain basic
Fuels add metals to the rain
Rain has no link to burning fuels
questions.expected: Sulfur dioxide from burning fuels dissolves in rain to make acid
questions.memo: Burning fuels releases sulfur dioxide, a non-metal oxide that dissolves in rain to form acid rain.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide is the oxide of which element?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide is the oxide formed when carbon reacts with oxygen.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Non-metal oxides usually dissolve in water to form ___.'
questions.memo: Non-metal oxides dissolve in water to form acids.

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide is formed when...
questions.memo: Sulfur dioxide forms when sulfur burns in oxygen.

questions.question: A non-metal burns in oxygen and its oxide is dissolved in water. The solution turns blue litmus red. What does this show?
options: The non-metal oxide formed an acid
The non-metal oxide formed a base
questions.expected: The non-metal oxide formed an acid
questions.memo: Turning blue litmus red shows the solution is acidic, as expected from a non-metal oxide.

questions.question: True or false: all oxides dissolve in water to form bases.
questions.memo: False — non-metal oxides form acids, while metal oxides tend to be basic.

questions.question: Which pair are BOTH non-metal oxides?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are both non-metal oxides; the others are metal oxides.

questions.question: How do metal oxides and non-metal oxides behave differently in water?
options: Metal oxides tend to be basic; non-metal oxides tend to form acids
questions.expected: Metal oxides tend to be basic; non-metal oxides tend to form acids
questions.memo: Metal oxides tend to be basic; non-metal oxides tend to form acids — a key difference.

questions.question: Why is normal rain naturally slightly acidic, even without pollution?
options: Carbon dioxide in the air dissolves into the rain, forming a weak acid
Rain is made of pure acid
Rain absorbs bases from the air
questions.expected: Carbon dioxide in the air dissolves into the rain, forming a weak acid
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide naturally in the air dissolves into rain to form a weak acid, so rain is slightly acidic.

NSSP.G9.MM.A5.title: Acids, bases & the pH value
NSSP.G9.MM.A5.description: The pH scale as a measure of how acidic or basic a substance is; pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic; and reading the pH of common substances.
NSSP.G9.MM.A5.recovery_strategy: On the pH scale: below 7 = acidic, exactly 7 = neutral, above 7 = basic. The LOWER the pH, the stronger the acid; the HIGHER the pH, the stronger the base.

questions.question: What does the pH scale measure?
options: How acidic or basic a substance is
questions.expected: How acidic or basic a substance is
questions.memo: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a substance is.

questions.question: A substance with a pH below 7 is...
questions.memo: A pH below 7 means the substance is acidic.

questions.question: A substance with a pH of exactly 7 is...
questions.memo: A pH of exactly 7 is neutral (like pure water).

questions.question: A substance with a pH above 7 is...
questions.memo: A pH above 7 means the substance is basic (alkaline).

questions.question: True or false: pure water has a pH of 7.
questions.memo: True — pure water is neutral, with a pH of 7.

questions.question: The table shows the pH of three substances. Which is the MOST acidic?
questions.memo: The lower the pH, the more acidic. Lemon juice (pH 2) is the most acidic.

questions.question: Which has the LOWER pH, a strong acid or a weak acid?
options: Acids do not have a pH
questions.memo: The stronger the acid, the lower its pH.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A pH below 7 is ___.'
questions.memo: A pH below 7 is acidic.

questions.question: Lemon juice has a pH of 2. It is...
questions.memo: A pH of 2 is well below 7, so lemon juice is acidic.

questions.question: Soap has a pH of about 9. It is...
questions.memo: A pH of 9 is above 7, so soap is basic.

questions.question: Sort each substance by its pH range.
questions.expected: Lemon juice and vinegar are acidic; pure water is neutral; soap and bleach are basic.
questions.memo: Below 7 = acidic, exactly 7 = neutral, above 7 = basic.

questions.question: True or false: the higher the pH, the stronger the base.
questions.memo: True — a higher pH means a stronger base.

questions.question: The table shows the pH of three substances. Which is the strongest BASE?
questions.memo: The higher the pH, the stronger the base. Oven cleaner (pH 13) is the strongest base.

questions.question: Does a high pH mean a strong acid?
options: No — a high pH means a strong base
Yes — a high pH means a strong acid
No — a high pH means neutral
questions.expected: No — a high pH means a strong base
questions.memo: A common mix-up: a HIGH pH means a strong BASE; a LOW pH means a strong acid.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A pH of exactly 7 is ___.'
questions.memo: A pH of 7 is neutral.

questions.question: Which pH value is the MOST basic?
questions.memo: The higher the pH, the more basic; pH 13 is the most basic here.

questions.question: A substance turns universal indicator red and has a pH of about 1. It is...
questions.memo: Red on universal indicator with a pH of 1 shows a strong acid.

questions.question: True or false: the lower the pH, the stronger the acid.
questions.memo: True — a lower pH means a stronger acid.

questions.question: Which of these is acidic?
questions.memo: Stomach acid has a pH of 2, well below 7, so it is acidic.

questions.question: Two acids are tested: one has a pH of 1 and the other a pH of 5. Which is the stronger acid, and why?
options: The pH 1 acid, because the lower the pH the stronger the acid
The pH 5 acid, because a higher pH means a stronger acid
questions.expected: The pH 1 acid, because the lower the pH the stronger the acid
questions.memo: A lower pH means a stronger acid, so pH 1 is stronger than pH 5.

NSSP.G9.MM.A6.title: Reactions of acids with bases
NSSP.G9.MM.A6.description: Neutralisation, where an acid and a base react to form a salt and water; the general reactions of an acid with a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide and a metal carbonate; and everyday applications.
NSSP.G9.MM.A6.recovery_strategy: Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. With a metal carbonate you also get carbon dioxide gas (acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide).

questions.question: When an acid reacts with a base, the reaction is called...
questions.memo: An acid reacting with a base is called neutralisation.

questions.question: Complete the general equation: 'acid + base → ___.'
questions.memo: Neutralisation gives a salt and water: acid + base → salt + water.

questions.question: True or false: neutralisation produces a salt and water.
questions.memo: True — acid + base → salt + water.

questions.question: Complete the equation: 'acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + ___.'
questions.memo: With a metal carbonate you also get carbon dioxide gas.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Acid + base → salt + ___.'
questions.memo: Neutralisation forms a salt and water.

questions.question: When an acid is added to a carbonate, bubbles of gas form. Which gas is it?
questions.memo: Acid reacting with a carbonate releases carbon dioxide gas (the fizzing).

questions.question: Indigestion is caused by too much stomach acid. An antacid tablet helps because it...
options: is a base that neutralises the excess acid
adds more acid to the stomach
removes all water from the stomach
questions.expected: is a base that neutralises the excess acid
questions.memo: An antacid is a base that neutralises the extra stomach acid, easing indigestion.

questions.question: Complete the equation: 'acid + metal oxide → ___.'
questions.memo: A metal oxide is a base, so acid + metal oxide → salt + water.

questions.question: Complete the equation: 'acid + metal hydroxide → ___.'
questions.memo: A metal hydroxide is a base, so acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water.

questions.question: True or false: adding a base to an acid raises the pH toward 7.
questions.memo: True — neutralising an acid with a base moves the pH up toward neutral (7).

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + ___.'
questions.memo: Acid + metal carbonate also gives off carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Why does adding lime (a base) to acidic soil help farmers?
options: It neutralises the acid, making the soil less acidic for crops
It makes the soil more acidic
It turns the soil into rock
questions.expected: It neutralises the acid, making the soil less acidic for crops
questions.memo: Lime is a base that neutralises excess soil acid, helping crops grow.

questions.question: Sort each product by when it is formed.
questions.expected: Salt and water are always made in neutralisation; carbon dioxide is the extra product only when a carbonate reacts.
questions.memo: acid + base → salt + water (always); acid + carbonate also gives carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide. What are the products?
questions.memo: Acid + base → salt + water, so this gives sodium chloride (a salt) and water.

questions.question: True or false: a salt is formed when an acid is neutralised by a base.
questions.memo: True — neutralisation always produces a salt (and water).

questions.question: A bee sting is acidic. Why might dabbing it with a mild base help?
options: The base neutralises the acid of the sting
The base makes the sting hotter
questions.expected: The base neutralises the acid of the sting
questions.memo: A mild base can neutralise the acidic sting, easing it.

questions.question: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, which gas turns limewater milky?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky — the test that confirms it.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'An acid and a base react to form a salt and ___.'
questions.memo: Acid + base → salt + water.

questions.question: Why is neutralisation useful in everyday life?
options: It cancels harmful acids or bases — for example antacids and treating acidic soil
It always makes things more dangerous
questions.expected: It cancels harmful acids or bases — for example antacids and treating acidic soil
questions.memo: Neutralisation is used to control acids and bases — antacids, soil treatment, treating stings and more.

questions.question: Vinegar (an acid) is poured onto bicarbonate of soda (a carbonate) and it fizzes strongly. What is the gas, and why does it fizz?
options: Carbon dioxide, released because the acid reacts with the carbonate
Hydrogen, because acid reacts with a metal
Oxygen, given off by the vinegar
questions.expected: Carbon dioxide, released because the acid reacts with the carbonate
questions.memo: Acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide; the carbon dioxide is the fizzing gas.

NSSP.G9.MM.A7.title: Reactions of acids with metals
NSSP.G9.MM.A7.description: The general reaction of an acid with a metal to form a salt and hydrogen gas; recognising the bubbles of hydrogen; and the 'pop' test for hydrogen.
NSSP.G9.MM.A7.recovery_strategy: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas. The bubbles are hydrogen, which gives a squeaky 'pop' with a lit splint.

questions.question: Complete the general equation: 'acid + metal → ___.'
questions.memo: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas.

questions.question: Which gas is given off when an acid reacts with a metal?
questions.memo: Acid reacting with a metal gives off hydrogen gas.

questions.question: True or false: bubbles of gas form when a reactive metal is added to an acid.
questions.memo: True — the bubbles are hydrogen gas being released.

questions.question: What is the test for hydrogen gas?
options: A lit splint makes a squeaky 'pop'
questions.expected: A lit splint makes a squeaky 'pop'
questions.memo: Hydrogen gives a squeaky 'pop' with a lit splint — the standard test.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Acid + metal → salt + ___ gas.'
questions.memo: Acid + metal gives a salt and hydrogen gas.

questions.question: Does an acid reacting with a metal give off oxygen?
options: Yes — it gives off carbon dioxide
No — no gas is given off
questions.memo: Acid + metal releases hydrogen, not oxygen.

questions.question: Zinc is added to hydrochloric acid and bubbles form. The bubbles are...
questions.memo: The bubbles when a metal reacts with acid are hydrogen gas.

questions.question: Complete the equation: 'zinc + hydrochloric acid → ___ + hydrogen.'
questions.memo: Zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen.

questions.question: True or false: a squeaky 'pop' when a lit splint is held to a gas confirms the gas is hydrogen.
questions.memo: True — the squeaky pop test confirms hydrogen.

questions.question: Complete the equation: 'magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + ___.'
questions.memo: Magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen.

questions.question: Why do bubbles form faster when a more reactive metal is added to acid?
options: A more reactive metal reacts faster with the acid
questions.expected: A more reactive metal reacts faster with the acid
questions.memo: A more reactive metal reacts faster, releasing hydrogen more quickly.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The squeaky pop test shows the gas is ___.'
questions.memo: The squeaky pop test identifies hydrogen.

questions.question: A piece of gold is dropped into acid and no bubbles form. What does this suggest?
options: Gold is unreactive, so it does not react with the acid
The acid is too strong to react
questions.expected: Gold is unreactive, so it does not react with the acid
questions.memo: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not react with the acid and no hydrogen is released.

questions.question: In 'magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen', which product is the salt?
questions.memo: Magnesium chloride is the salt; hydrogen is the gas given off.

questions.question: True or false: hydrogen gas is lighter than air.
questions.memo: True — hydrogen is the lightest gas, lighter than air.

questions.question: When iron filings are added to an acid and bubbles rise, those bubbles are...
questions.memo: Iron reacting with acid releases hydrogen gas.

questions.question: Hydrogen is lighter than air. How could you collect it from an acid–metal reaction?
options: In an upside-down test tube held above the reaction
By pouring it into the sink
questions.expected: In an upside-down test tube held above the reaction
questions.memo: Because hydrogen rises, it can be collected in an upturned test tube held above the reaction.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Acid + metal makes a salt and hydrogen ___.'
questions.memo: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas.

questions.question: Which word equation is correct?
questions.memo: The correct general reaction is acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.

questions.question: A learner adds a metal to acid, collects the gas, and holds a lit splint to it: it goes 'pop'. What gas is it, and what does the result confirm?
options: Hydrogen — confirming the reaction acid + metal → salt + hydrogen
Oxygen — confirming acid + metal → salt + oxygen
Carbon dioxide — confirming a carbonate reaction
questions.expected: Hydrogen — confirming the reaction acid + metal → salt + hydrogen
questions.memo: The squeaky pop shows hydrogen, which confirms acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.

NSSP.G9.EC.A1.title: Forces
NSSP.G9.EC.A1.description: What a force is and what it can do (change an object's speed, direction or shape); contact forces (such as friction and applied force); and non-contact (field) forces (such as gravity and magnetism).
NSSP.G9.EC.A1.recovery_strategy: A contact force needs the objects to touch (friction, a push). A non-contact (field) force acts at a distance without touching (gravity, magnetism). Ask: do the objects have to touch?

questions.question: What is a force?
questions.memo: A force is simply a push or a pull acting on an object.

questions.question: A force can change an object's...
questions.memo: Forces can change how fast something moves, the direction it moves, or its shape.

questions.question: Friction is an example of a...
questions.memo: Friction acts where surfaces touch, so it is a contact force.

questions.question: Gravity is an example of a...
questions.memo: Gravity acts at a distance without touching, so it is a non-contact force.

questions.question: True or false: a force can make a still object start moving.
questions.memo: True — a force can start a still object moving.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A force that acts without the objects touching is a ___ force.'
questions.memo: A force that acts at a distance is a non-contact force.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-contact force?
questions.memo: Magnetism acts at a distance, so it is a non-contact force.

questions.question: Sort each force as a contact force or a non-contact force.
questions.expected: Friction, a push and air resistance are contact forces; gravity and magnetism are non-contact forces.
questions.memo: If the objects must touch, it is a contact force; if it acts at a distance, it is non-contact.

questions.question: Is gravity a contact force?
options: No — it acts at a distance, so it is non-contact
Yes — it needs surfaces to touch
Yes — it is the same as friction
No — gravity is not a force
questions.expected: No — it acts at a distance, so it is non-contact
questions.memo: Gravity pulls objects without touching them, so it is a non-contact force.

questions.question: True or false: friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces.
questions.memo: True — friction acts against the motion of surfaces sliding over each other.

questions.question: When you stretch a spring, the force changes its...
questions.memo: Stretching changes the spring's shape — one of the effects of a force.

questions.question: A ball rolling across grass gradually slows down because of...
questions.memo: Friction between the ball and the grass opposes its motion, slowing it down.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Gravity pulls objects toward the ___.'
questions.memo: On Earth, gravity pulls objects toward the Earth (downward).

questions.question: Which pair are BOTH contact forces?
questions.memo: Friction and a push both need contact, so both are contact forces.

questions.question: How can you tell that a force is non-contact?
options: The objects do not need to touch for it to act
It needs surfaces to rub together
questions.expected: The objects do not need to touch for it to act
questions.memo: A non-contact force acts across a gap, without the objects touching.

questions.question: A magnet attracts a paperclip across a small gap. This shows...
questions.memo: The magnet pulls the paperclip without touching it, showing a non-contact (magnetic) force.

questions.question: True or false: force is measured in newtons.
questions.memo: True — force is measured in newtons (N).

questions.question: Kicking a moving ball sideways changes its...
questions.memo: A kick can change both how fast the ball moves and the direction it moves in.

questions.question: Why is gravity called a field force?
options: It acts over a distance without the objects touching
It only works in fields and farms
It is the same as friction
questions.expected: It acts over a distance without the objects touching
questions.memo: A field (non-contact) force like gravity acts across a distance, with no contact needed.

questions.question: A ball dropped from a height speeds up as it falls. Which force causes this, and is it a contact or non-contact force?
questions.memo: Gravity pulls the ball down and speeds it up; it acts without contact, so it is a non-contact force.

NSSP.G9.EC.A2.title: Electric cells as energy systems
NSSP.G9.EC.A2.description: How an electric cell (battery) stores chemical energy and changes it into electrical energy to drive a current; and the idea of cells joined together.
