questions.question: What kind of energy does an electric cell store?
questions.memo: A cell stores chemical energy, ready to be changed into electrical energy.

questions.question: A cell changes its stored chemical energy into...
questions.memo: A cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy to drive a current.

questions.question: True or false: a cell provides the energy that drives the current in a circuit.
questions.memo: True — the cell supplies the energy that pushes the current around the circuit.

questions.question: When the chemicals in a cell are used up, the cell...
questions.memo: Once its chemicals are used up, the cell goes flat and can no longer drive a current.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A cell changes ___ energy into electrical energy.'
questions.memo: A cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy.

questions.question: Does a cell make energy out of nothing?
options: No — it changes stored chemical energy into electrical energy
Yes — it makes energy from the air
questions.expected: No — it changes stored chemical energy into electrical energy
questions.memo: A cell transfers energy from one form to another; it does not create energy from nothing.

questions.question: A battery is...
options: two or more cells joined together
questions.expected: two or more cells joined together
questions.memo: A battery is made of two or more cells joined together.

questions.question: A torch stops working even though the bulb is fine. What is the likely cause?
options: The cell is flat (its chemicals are used up)
The torch has too much energy
questions.expected: The cell is flat (its chemicals are used up)
questions.memo: If the bulb is fine, a flat cell is the likely reason — its stored energy has run out.

questions.question: True or false: joining more cells in series gives more energy to the circuit.
questions.memo: True — more cells in series provide more energy, for example making a bulb brighter.

questions.question: Which describes the energy change in a working cell?
questions.memo: A cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'When its chemicals are used up, a cell goes ___.'
questions.memo: A cell goes flat once its chemical energy is used up.

questions.question: Why does a rechargeable cell work again after being charged?
options: Charging puts chemical energy back into the cell
questions.expected: Charging puts chemical energy back into the cell
questions.memo: Charging restores the chemical energy, so the cell can supply electrical energy again.

questions.question: Replacing one cell in a torch with two cells in series makes the bulb...
options: brighter, because there is more energy
dimmer, because there is less energy
questions.expected: brighter, because there is more energy
questions.memo: More cells in series give more energy, so the bulb shines brighter.

questions.question: True or false: a cell creates electrical energy out of nothing.
questions.memo: False — a cell changes stored chemical energy into electrical energy; it does not create energy.

questions.question: Which of these stores energy to power a phone?
questions.memo: The cell (battery) stores the energy that powers the phone.

questions.question: How is an electric cell different from a power station?
options: A cell stores a small amount of chemical energy; a power station generates far more
A cell is bigger than a power station
A power station stores chemical energy in a cell
questions.expected: A cell stores a small amount of chemical energy; a power station generates far more
questions.memo: A cell holds a small store of energy; a power station generates electricity on a huge scale.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'An electric ___ changes chemical energy into electrical energy.'
questions.memo: An electric cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy.

questions.question: A flat battery has...
questions.memo: A flat battery has used up the chemical energy it stored.

questions.question: True or false: a cell transfers energy from one form to another rather than making energy.
questions.memo: True — a cell transfers chemical energy into electrical energy, in line with conservation of energy.

questions.question: Why does a cell eventually stop working, even when the rest of the circuit is fine?
options: Its stored chemical energy runs out
It makes too much new energy
questions.expected: Its stored chemical energy runs out
questions.memo: A cell only holds a fixed store of chemical energy; once that is used up, it stops driving the current.

NSSP.G9.EC.A3.title: Resistance
NSSP.G9.EC.A3.description: Resistance as the opposing of current flow; how resistors are used; and the factors that affect the resistance of a wire (length, thickness and material).
NSSP.G9.EC.A3.recovery_strategy: Resistance opposes the current. A LONGER wire has more resistance; a THICKER wire has LESS resistance. More resistance means less current flows.

questions.question: What is resistance in a circuit?
options: The opposing of the flow of current
The energy stored in a cell
The length of a wire only
questions.expected: The opposing of the flow of current
questions.memo: Resistance is how much a component opposes (slows) the flow of current.

questions.question: More resistance in a circuit means...
questions.memo: Higher resistance opposes the current more, so less current flows.

questions.question: A LONGER wire has...
options: the same as a short wire
questions.memo: A longer wire has more resistance than a short one of the same kind.

questions.question: A THICKER wire has...
questions.memo: A thicker wire has less resistance, so more current can flow.

questions.question: True or false: a resistor is a component that adds resistance to a circuit.
questions.memo: True — a resistor is used to add resistance and control the current.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Resistance ___ the flow of current.'
questions.memo: Resistance opposes (slows down) the flow of current.

questions.question: Does a thicker wire have MORE resistance than a thin one?
options: No — a thicker wire has less resistance
Yes — a thicker wire has more resistance
No — thicker wires carry no current
questions.expected: No — a thicker wire has less resistance
questions.memo: A thicker wire actually has LESS resistance, letting more current through.

questions.question: Which factors affect the resistance of a wire?
options: Its length, thickness and the material it is made of
questions.expected: Its length, thickness and the material it is made of
questions.memo: Resistance depends on the wire's length, thickness and material.

questions.question: Replacing a thin wire in a circuit with a thicker one (same length and material) makes the current...
questions.memo: A thicker wire has less resistance, so more current flows.

questions.question: Sort each wire by whether it has more or less resistance.
questions.expected: Long and thin wires have more resistance; thick and short wires have less.
questions.memo: Longer and thinner → more resistance; shorter and thicker → less resistance.

questions.question: True or false: a higher resistance lets more current flow.
questions.memo: False — higher resistance means LESS current flows.

questions.question: What is a resistor used for in a circuit?
options: To control the size of the current
To make light on its own
questions.expected: To control the size of the current
questions.memo: A resistor controls (limits) how much current flows in a circuit.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A longer wire has ___ resistance than a short one of the same kind.'
questions.memo: A longer wire has more resistance.

questions.question: Why does a long, thin wire have a high resistance?
options: Both its length and its thinness add resistance
questions.expected: Both its length and its thinness add resistance
questions.memo: Length increases resistance and thinness increases resistance, so a long thin wire has high resistance.

questions.question: Adding resistance can be used to dim a light. Why does this work?
options: More resistance reduces the current, so the bulb is dimmer
More resistance adds energy to the bulb
Resistance has no effect on brightness
More resistance makes the bulb brighter
questions.expected: More resistance reduces the current, so the bulb is dimmer
questions.memo: Higher resistance lowers the current, which makes the bulb shine less brightly.

questions.question: Which wire has the LEAST resistance?
questions.memo: Short and thick both reduce resistance, so a short thick wire has the least.

questions.question: True or false: the material a wire is made of affects its resistance.
questions.memo: True — different materials have different resistances, even at the same length and thickness.

questions.question: Increasing the resistance in a circuit makes a bulb...
questions.memo: More resistance lowers the current, so the bulb becomes dimmer.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'More resistance means ___ current.'
questions.memo: More resistance means less current flows.

questions.question: Two wires are made of the same metal: one is long and thin, the other short and thick. Which one carries more current, and why?
options: The short thick wire, because it has the lowest resistance
The long thin wire, because it has the lowest resistance
They carry exactly the same current
questions.expected: The short thick wire, because it has the lowest resistance
questions.memo: Short and thick both lower resistance, so that wire has the least resistance and carries the most current.

NSSP.G9.EC.A4.title: Series & parallel circuits
NSSP.G9.EC.A4.description: Comparing series and parallel circuits more closely; how adding components changes the current; and where each type of circuit is used.
NSSP.G9.EC.A4.recovery_strategy: Series = one path; adding more bulbs in series shares the energy, so each is dimmer, and a break stops them all. Parallel = separate paths, so each bulb is independent and stays at full brightness.

questions.question: A series circuit has...
options: one single path for the current
questions.expected: one single path for the current
questions.memo: In a series circuit there is one single path for the current.

questions.question: A parallel circuit has...
options: more than one path for the current
questions.expected: more than one path for the current
questions.memo: A parallel circuit has more than one path for the current.

questions.question: Adding more bulbs in SERIES makes each bulb...
questions.memo: More bulbs in series share the cell's energy, so each one is dimmer.

questions.question: In a PARALLEL circuit, removing one bulb...
options: leaves the others on at full brightness
makes the others brighter and then off
questions.expected: leaves the others on at full brightness
questions.memo: Each bulb in parallel has its own path, so removing one leaves the others on at full brightness.

questions.question: True or false: in a series circuit, a break anywhere stops all the current.
questions.memo: True — a series circuit is one loop, so any break stops the whole current.

questions.question: Look at the two circuit diagrams. Which one is the PARALLEL circuit?
options: The one with the bulbs on separate branches
The one with all bulbs in a single loop
questions.expected: The one with the bulbs on separate branches
questions.memo: A parallel circuit has the bulbs on separate branches, each with its own path to the cell.

questions.question: Why do bulbs in a series circuit get dimmer as you add more of them?
options: They share the energy from the cell
Each one makes its own energy
The cell grows weaker by itself
questions.expected: They share the energy from the cell
questions.memo: In series the bulbs share the cell's energy, so each gets less and shines dimmer.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a ___ circuit, each bulb has its own path and stays at full brightness.'
questions.memo: In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own path and stays at full brightness.

questions.question: A string of lights wired in series goes completely dark when one bulb is removed. Why?
options: The single loop is broken, so no current flows
The other bulbs ran out of energy
The cell switched off by itself
questions.expected: The single loop is broken, so no current flows
questions.memo: Series is one loop; removing a bulb breaks it, so the current stops and all the lights go out.

questions.question: Which type of circuit keeps each device working independently of the others?
questions.memo: Parallel circuits give each device its own path, so they work independently.

questions.question: True or false: adding more bulbs in series makes them brighter.
questions.memo: False — adding more bulbs in series makes each one dimmer, because they share the energy.

questions.question: Sort each description under the circuit it matches.

items.text: Bulbs get dimmer as you add more
One bulb off, others stay on

questions.expected: Single path and dimming describe a series circuit; separate paths and independent bulbs describe a parallel circuit.
questions.memo: Series shares one path (and the energy); parallel gives each device its own independent path.

questions.question: Why are home lights wired in parallel?
options: So each light works independently and one failing does not switch off the rest
So all lights must be on together
So the lights use no electricity
So a single broken bulb switches off the whole house
questions.expected: So each light works independently and one failing does not switch off the rest
questions.memo: Parallel wiring lets each light be controlled on its own and keeps the rest on if one fails.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a series circuit there is only one ___ for the current.'
questions.memo: A series circuit has a single path for the current.

questions.question: In a parallel circuit, the current...
options: flows in one single loop only
questions.memo: In parallel, the current splits to flow through each separate branch.

questions.question: Two bulbs are in parallel. One bulb is removed. The other bulb...
questions.memo: The remaining bulb has its own path, so it stays lit when the other is removed.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of wiring house lights in series?
options: If one bulb fails, all the lights go off
Each light can be switched on its own
The lights are always too bright
questions.expected: If one bulb fails, all the lights go off
questions.memo: In series, one failed bulb breaks the loop and switches off all the lights — a clear disadvantage.

questions.question: True or false: each bulb in a parallel circuit gets the full voltage of the cell.
questions.memo: True — each branch in parallel receives the full cell voltage, so the bulbs stay at full brightness.

questions.question: Why does adding another bulb in parallel barely dim the existing bulbs?
options: Each bulb has its own separate path to the cell
Each bulb makes its own energy
Adding bulbs always brightens the others
questions.expected: Each bulb has its own separate path to the cell
questions.memo: Because each parallel bulb has its own path to the cell, adding more does not make the others share and dim much.

questions.question: A set of decorative lights keeps shining even when one bulb is taken out. Is it series or parallel, and why?
options: Parallel, because each bulb has its own path
Series, because there is one single loop
Series, because removing one stops the rest
It could be either — there is no difference
questions.expected: Parallel, because each bulb has its own path
questions.memo: Since one bulb can be removed without the others going off, the lights must be wired in parallel.

NSSP.G9.EC.A5.title: Safety with electricity
NSSP.G9.EC.A5.description: Why electricity can be dangerous; safe practices in the home; and the role of safety features such as insulation, fuses and not mixing electricity with water.
NSSP.G9.EC.A5.recovery_strategy: Keep electricity away from water, never touch sockets or appliances with wet hands, do not overload plugs, and use insulated wires. If unsure, treat electricity as dangerous.

questions.question: Electricity and water together are...
questions.memo: Water conducts electricity, so the two together are dangerous.

questions.question: You should never touch a plug or switch with...
questions.memo: Wet hands conduct electricity, so never touch plugs or switches with them.

questions.question: True or false: overloading a plug with many appliances can be dangerous.
questions.memo: True — overloading a plug can overheat the wiring and start a fire.

questions.question: Why is the plastic insulation around wires important?
options: It stops you touching the live metal and getting a shock
It carries the current instead of the metal
questions.expected: It stops you touching the live metal and getting a shock
questions.memo: The insulation covers the live metal, protecting you from electric shocks.

questions.question: What does a fuse do?
options: Breaks the circuit if too much current flows
Adds more current to the circuit
questions.expected: Breaks the circuit if too much current flows
questions.memo: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit if the current gets dangerously high, protecting the appliance and people.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Never use electrical appliances near ___.'
questions.memo: Keep electrical appliances away from water to avoid shocks.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to use a hairdryer near a full bath?
options: Water conducts electricity and could cause a fatal shock
The hairdryer would get too cold
The water would put out the hairdryer's light
It is not dangerous at all
questions.expected: Water conducts electricity and could cause a fatal shock
questions.memo: If the hairdryer touches the water, electricity can flow through the water and the person, causing a deadly shock.

questions.question: Sort each action as safe or unsafe around electricity.

items.text: Using dry hands to plug in
Poking a metal fork into a socket
Switching off before fixing an appliance
Overloading one plug with many appliances

questions.expected: Dry hands and switching off first are safe; poking sockets, frayed wires and overloading are unsafe.
questions.memo: Safe practices keep you away from live current and water; unsafe ones risk shock or fire.

questions.question: True or false: it is safe to use an appliance with a damaged, frayed cord.
questions.memo: False — a frayed cord can expose live metal, risking shock or fire.

questions.question: Before fixing or cleaning an electrical appliance, you should first...
options: switch it off and unplug it
questions.expected: switch it off and unplug it
questions.memo: Always switch off and unplug an appliance before working on it, so there is no live current.

questions.question: A child reaches toward a wall socket with a metal object. This is...
options: a good way to test the socket
questions.memo: Pushing metal into a socket can cause a severe electric shock — it is very dangerous.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A ___ melts and breaks the circuit if the current becomes too high.'
questions.memo: A fuse protects a circuit by melting and breaking it if the current is too high.

questions.question: Why are electrical wires covered in plastic rather than left as bare metal?
options: Plastic is an insulator that protects you from the current
questions.expected: Plastic is an insulator that protects you from the current
questions.memo: The plastic is an insulator, keeping the live current safely away from your hands.

questions.question: True or false: electricity can flow through a person and cause a serious shock.
questions.memo: True — the human body can conduct electricity, so a shock can be serious or fatal.

questions.question: Which of these is a SAFE practice?
options: Keeping electrical appliances away from water
questions.expected: Keeping electrical appliances away from water
questions.memo: Keeping appliances away from water is a safe practice; the others are dangerous.

questions.question: Plugging many high-power appliances into one socket can...
options: overheat the wiring and start a fire
make the appliances run for free
questions.expected: overheat the wiring and start a fire
questions.memo: Overloading a socket draws too much current, which can overheat the wires and cause a fire.

questions.question: Which of these is UNSAFE?
options: Using a charger with bare wires showing
Switching off at the wall before unplugging
questions.expected: Using a charger with bare wires showing
questions.memo: Bare wires expose live metal, which is dangerous; the others are safe practices.

questions.question: True or false: if you are unsure whether something electrical is safe, you should treat it as dangerous.
questions.memo: True — when in doubt, treat electricity as dangerous and stay safe.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Wet hands and electricity are a ___ combination.'
questions.memo: Wet hands conduct electricity, making them a dangerous combination with electrical devices.

questions.question: Why should you never pull a plug out of a socket by the cord?
options: It can damage the wires, exposing live metal and risking a shock or fire
It makes the appliance run faster
questions.expected: It can damage the wires, exposing live metal and risking a shock or fire
questions.memo: Yanking the cord can pull the wires loose or bare the live metal, creating a shock or fire risk.

NSSP.G9.EC.A6.title: Energy & the national electricity grid
NSSP.G9.EC.A6.description: How electricity is generated (often by burning coal to drive turbines); nuclear power in South Africa; and how the national grid carries electricity to homes and industry.
NSSP.G9.EC.A6.caps_topic: Energy and the national electricity grid
NSSP.G9.EC.A6.recovery_strategy: Most South African electricity is generated by burning coal to make steam that spins turbines; some comes from nuclear and renewables. The national grid then carries it to homes and industry.

questions.question: Most of South Africa's electricity is generated by...
questions.memo: Most South African electricity comes from burning coal in power stations.

questions.question: In a coal power station, burning coal is used to heat water and make...
questions.memo: Burning coal heats water into steam.

questions.question: In a power station, the steam is used to spin...
questions.memo: The steam spins turbines connected to generators, which produce the electricity.

questions.question: Koeberg, near Cape Town, is a...
questions.memo: Koeberg is South Africa's nuclear power station.

questions.question: True or false: the national grid carries electricity to homes and industry.
questions.memo: True — the national grid is the network that carries electricity to homes and industry.

questions.question: Put the steps of generating electricity from coal in the correct order.

items.text: The grid carries it to homes

questions.memo: Burn coal → heat water to steam → steam spins the turbine → generator makes electricity → grid carries it to homes.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Most South African electricity comes from burning ___.'
questions.memo: Most South African electricity is generated by burning coal.

questions.question: Why is generating electricity by burning coal a problem?
options: It releases pollution and uses a non-renewable resource
It produces too little energy to use
questions.expected: It releases pollution and uses a non-renewable resource
questions.memo: Burning coal pollutes the air and uses up coal, which is non-renewable.

questions.question: Nuclear power stations use which fuel?
questions.memo: Nuclear power stations use uranium as their fuel.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa uses some nuclear and renewable energy as well as coal.
questions.memo: True — although coal dominates, South Africa also uses nuclear and growing amounts of renewable energy.

questions.question: During a power cut, what is happening?
options: No electricity is reaching homes from the grid
Homes are making too much electricity
The grid is generating extra power
questions.expected: No electricity is reaching homes from the grid
questions.memo: A power cut means electricity from the grid is not reaching the homes.

questions.question: Why is electricity sent across the grid at very high voltage?
options: Less energy is lost over long distances
It is cheaper to make at home
questions.expected: Less energy is lost over long distances
questions.memo: High voltage reduces the energy lost as electricity travels the long distances of the grid.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'In a power station, steam spins ___ to generate electricity.'
questions.memo: Steam spins turbines, which drive generators to make electricity.

questions.question: Which is a renewable source that South Africa also uses for electricity?
questions.memo: Wind and solar are renewable sources that South Africa is increasingly using.

questions.question: How does reducing electricity use at home help, given how most power is generated?
options: Power stations burn less coal, cutting pollution
It makes the grid generate more
It has no effect on the power stations
questions.expected: Power stations burn less coal, cutting pollution
questions.memo: Lower demand means less coal is burned, reducing pollution.

questions.question: The national grid is...
options: the network of power lines across the country
questions.expected: the network of power lines across the country
questions.memo: The national grid is the country-wide network of power lines that distributes electricity.

questions.question: True or false: nuclear power stations produce electricity without burning coal.
questions.memo: True — nuclear stations use uranium, not coal, to produce the heat that makes steam.

questions.question: Why might South Africa want more renewable energy in its grid?
options: To reduce pollution and its reliance on coal
To make electricity run out faster
questions.expected: To reduce pollution and its reliance on coal
questions.memo: More renewables cut pollution and reduce dependence on coal, which is non-renewable.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Koeberg is a ___ power station.'
questions.memo: Koeberg is a nuclear power station.

questions.question: Trace the energy in a coal power station: 'coal → ? → electricity'. What is the missing middle step?
options: Burning coal heats water to steam, which spins turbines that generate electricity
Coal is turned straight into electricity with no steam
Coal is sent directly down the wires
questions.expected: Burning coal heats water to steam, which spins turbines that generate electricity
questions.memo: The chemical energy in coal becomes heat, then steam, then movement of turbines, then electrical energy.

NSSP.G9.EC.A7.title: Cost of electrical power
NSSP.G9.EC.A7.description: How the electricity we use is measured and paid for; why appliances that use a lot of power cost more to run; and simple ways to reduce the cost.
NSSP.G9.EC.A7.recovery_strategy: The more power an appliance uses and the longer it runs, the more it costs. High-power appliances like geysers and heaters cost the most; switching them off when not needed saves money.

questions.question: An appliance that uses more power and runs for longer will cost...
questions.memo: More power used over more time means more energy used, so it costs more.

questions.question: Which household appliance usually costs the MOST to run?
questions.memo: Heating water uses a lot of power, so a geyser is one of the most expensive appliances to run.

questions.question: True or false: switching off appliances when they are not needed saves money.
questions.memo: True — switching off unused appliances reduces energy use and the electricity bill.

questions.question: A small phone charger uses...
options: very little power, so it costs little to run
the most power in the house
questions.expected: very little power, so it costs little to run
questions.memo: A phone charger draws very little power, so it is cheap to run.

questions.question: The table shows the power of three appliances. Which costs the MOST to run for one hour?
questions.memo: For the same time, the highest-power appliance costs the most — the geyser at 3000 W.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The more ___ an appliance uses, the more it costs to run.'
questions.memo: The more power (and the longer the time), the more it costs.

questions.question: Why does a heater left on all day cost a lot?
options: It uses a lot of power for a long time
It only costs money when off
questions.expected: It uses a lot of power for a long time
questions.memo: High power over a long time means a large amount of energy used, so a high cost.

questions.question: How is the electricity a home uses measured for billing?
questions.memo: Electricity is billed in units of energy called kilowatt-hours.

questions.question: A family wants to lower their electricity bill. The best action is to...
options: switch off high-power appliances when they are not in use
leave the geyser on all the time
questions.expected: switch off high-power appliances when they are not in use
questions.memo: Cutting the use of high-power appliances saves the most energy and money.

questions.question: The table shows two appliances and how long each runs. Which uses MORE energy in total?
questions.memo: Energy = power × time. For the same 3 hours, the much higher-power heater uses far more energy.

questions.question: True or false: two appliances of the same power cost different amounts if one runs for longer.
questions.memo: True — running for longer uses more energy, so it costs more.

questions.question: Which action would save the most money on electricity?
options: Using the geyser less and insulating it
Boiling a full kettle for one cup
Running the heater with windows open
questions.expected: Using the geyser less and insulating it
questions.memo: The geyser is a big energy user, so using it less and insulating it saves the most.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'An appliance that runs ___ uses more energy and costs more.'
questions.memo: The longer an appliance runs, the more energy it uses and the more it costs.

questions.question: Why do LED bulbs cost less to run than old-style bulbs?
options: They use less power for the same amount of light
They use more power for less light
questions.expected: They use less power for the same amount of light
questions.memo: LEDs are efficient — less power for the same light means a lower running cost.

questions.question: Leaving a heater on overnight costs much more than leaving a lamp on, because the heater...
questions.memo: The heater is a high-power appliance, so over the same time it uses far more energy than a lamp.

questions.question: Which costs more to run: a geyser or a clock?
questions.memo: The geyser uses a lot of power; the clock uses almost none, so the geyser costs far more.

questions.question: True or false: a higher-power appliance used for the same time uses more energy.
questions.memo: True — energy = power × time, so more power for the same time means more energy.

questions.question: How can a household cut its electricity cost the most?
options: Reduce the use of high-power appliances like geysers and heaters
questions.expected: Reduce the use of high-power appliances like geysers and heaters
questions.memo: Cutting back on the biggest energy users saves the most money.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Electrical energy used is often measured in ___-hours.'
questions.memo: Electrical energy is measured in kilowatt-hours.

questions.question: Appliance A uses 2000 W for 1 hour; appliance B uses 100 W for 1 hour. Which costs more to run, and why?
options: A, because it uses far more power for the same time
B, because lower power costs more
questions.expected: A, because it uses far more power for the same time
questions.memo: For the same time, the higher-power appliance (A, 2000 W) uses much more energy and costs more.

NSSP.G9.PEB.A1.title: The Earth as a system
NSSP.G9.PEB.A1.description: The Earth as a set of interacting spheres — the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere — and how matter and energy move between them.
NSSP.G9.PEB.A1.recovery_strategy: Lithosphere = land/rock, hydrosphere = water, atmosphere = air, biosphere = living things. These spheres interact and exchange matter and energy.

questions.question: What are the four main spheres of the Earth system?
questions.memo: The Earth system is made of the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere.

questions.question: The lithosphere is the Earth's...
questions.memo: The lithosphere is the solid land and rock of the Earth.

questions.question: The hydrosphere is all the Earth's...
questions.memo: The hydrosphere is all the water on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes and ice.

questions.question: The atmosphere is the Earth's...
questions.memo: The atmosphere is the layer of air (gases) around the Earth.

questions.question: The biosphere is...
options: all the living things on Earth
questions.expected: all the living things on Earth
questions.memo: The biosphere is made up of all the living things on Earth.

questions.question: True or false: the Earth's spheres interact with one another.
questions.memo: True — the spheres interact and exchange matter and energy.

questions.question: Sort each example into the correct sphere of the Earth.
questions.expected: Mountain → lithosphere; ocean → hydrosphere; air → atmosphere; forest → biosphere.
questions.memo: Rock/land = lithosphere; water = hydrosphere; air = atmosphere; living things = biosphere.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'All the living things on Earth make up the ___.'
questions.memo: All living things make up the biosphere.

questions.question: Is the biosphere all the rock of the Earth?
options: No — it is all the living things
Yes — it is all the rock
Yes — it is all the water
No — it is all the air
questions.expected: No — it is all the living things
questions.memo: The biosphere is all the living things; rock is the lithosphere.

questions.question: Rain falling from clouds onto the soil is an example of...
options: the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere interacting
questions.expected: the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere interacting
questions.memo: Rain links the air (atmosphere), the water (hydrosphere) and the land it lands on (lithosphere).

questions.question: True or false: matter and energy move between the Earth's spheres.
questions.memo: True — matter and energy are constantly exchanged between the spheres.

questions.question: A plant growing in soil, using water and air, involves which spheres?
questions.memo: The plant (biosphere) uses soil (lithosphere), water (hydrosphere) and air (atmosphere).

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The solid land of the Earth is the ___.'
questions.memo: The solid land is the lithosphere.

questions.question: Fish live mostly in which sphere?
questions.memo: Fish live in water, which is the hydrosphere.

questions.question: Why is the Earth described as a 'system'?
options: Its parts interact and affect each other
It is made of only one thing
questions.expected: Its parts interact and affect each other
questions.memo: The Earth is a system because its spheres interact and influence one another.

questions.question: A volcano erupts, sending rock and gases into the air. Which spheres are linked here?
questions.memo: Molten rock from the land (lithosphere) and gases entering the air (atmosphere) are linked by the eruption.

questions.question: True or false: the atmosphere is one of the spheres of the Earth system.
questions.memo: True — the atmosphere (the air) is one of the four spheres.

questions.question: Clouds and the air around us are part of the...
questions.memo: The air and the clouds in it are part of the atmosphere.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'All the water on Earth makes up the ___.'
questions.memo: All the Earth's water makes up the hydrosphere.

questions.question: A tree takes water from the soil and gases from the air, and is then eaten by an animal. How many of the Earth's spheres interact in this example?
options: All four — lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere
questions.expected: All four — lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere
questions.memo: Soil (lithosphere), water (hydrosphere), air (atmosphere) and living things (biosphere) all interact here.

NSSP.G9.PEB.A2.title: Lithosphere & the rock cycle
NSSP.G9.PEB.A2.description: The lithosphere as the solid outer layer of the Earth; the three rock types (igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic); and how the rock cycle changes one type into another.
NSSP.G9.PEB.A2.recovery_strategy: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens; sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment are pressed together; metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock.

questions.question: What is the lithosphere?
options: The solid outer layer of the Earth
questions.expected: The solid outer layer of the Earth
questions.memo: The lithosphere is the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth.

questions.question: What are the three main types of rock?
questions.memo: The three main rock types are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.

questions.question: Igneous rock forms when...
options: layers of mud are pressed together
heat and pressure change a rock
questions.memo: Igneous rock forms when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens.

questions.question: Sedimentary rock forms when...
options: layers of sediment are pressed together
heat and pressure change a rock
questions.expected: layers of sediment are pressed together
questions.memo: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment build up and are pressed together.

questions.question: Metamorphic rock forms when...
options: heat and pressure change an existing rock
molten rock cools at the surface
questions.expected: heat and pressure change an existing rock
questions.memo: Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock into a new one.

questions.question: Look at the rock cycle diagram. Which process forms IGNEOUS rock?
options: Cooling and hardening of molten rock
Heat and pressure on an existing rock
questions.expected: Cooling and hardening of molten rock
questions.memo: On the rock cycle, igneous rock forms where molten rock cools and hardens.

questions.question: True or false: the rock cycle changes one type of rock into another over time.
questions.memo: True — over long periods, rocks can change from one type to another through the rock cycle.

questions.question: Match each rock type to how it forms.

items.text: Layers of sediment are pressed together
Heat and pressure change an existing rock

questions.expected: Cooling molten rock → igneous; pressed sediment → sedimentary; heat and pressure → metamorphic.
questions.memo: Igneous = cooled magma; sedimentary = pressed layers; metamorphic = changed by heat and pressure.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Igneous rock forms when molten rock ___.'
questions.memo: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens.

questions.question: Does igneous rock form from layers of mud pressed together?
options: No — that is sedimentary rock; igneous forms from cooling molten rock
Yes — that is exactly how igneous rock forms
Yes — all rock forms that way
No — igneous rock forms from living things
questions.expected: No — that is sedimentary rock; igneous forms from cooling molten rock
questions.memo: Pressed layers form sedimentary rock; igneous rock forms from cooling molten rock.

questions.question: Put these rock-cycle stages in a sensible order, starting with molten rock.

items.text: Molten rock cools into igneous rock
The rock is worn down into sediment
Sediment is pressed into sedimentary rock
Heat and pressure change it into metamorphic rock

questions.memo: Molten rock → igneous rock → worn into sediment → sedimentary rock → heat and pressure → metamorphic rock.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms from cooling lava?
questions.memo: Lava that cools and hardens forms igneous rock.

questions.question: True or false: sedimentary rocks often form in visible layers.
questions.memo: True — sedimentary rocks usually show layers, because they form from layers of sediment.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Heat and pressure change rock into ___ rock.'
questions.memo: Heat and pressure form metamorphic rock.

questions.question: The lithosphere includes...
options: the rocks and soil of the Earth's surface
questions.expected: the rocks and soil of the Earth's surface
questions.memo: The lithosphere is the solid surface — the rocks and soil.

questions.question: A rock is buried deep underground, heated and squeezed until it becomes a new kind of rock. This is...
questions.memo: Heat and pressure on an existing rock form metamorphic rock.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms when sand and mud settle and are compacted over time?
questions.memo: Settled, compacted sediment forms sedimentary rock.

questions.question: True or false: rocks can change from one type to another in the rock cycle.
questions.memo: True — the rock cycle turns one rock type into another over time.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Rock formed from cooled molten rock is ___ rock.'
questions.memo: Cooled molten rock forms igneous rock.

questions.question: A rock is made of visible layers and contains the shells of sea creatures. Which type is it, and how did it form?
options: Sedimentary, from layers of sediment and remains pressed together
Molten, because it is still hot
questions.expected: Sedimentary, from layers of sediment and remains pressed together
questions.memo: Layers and shells point to sedimentary rock, formed from compacted sediment and the remains of living things.

NSSP.G9.PEB.A3.title: Mining of mineral resources
NSSP.G9.PEB.A3.description: Why we mine; how ores are extracted and refined to get useful metals; and the importance and impact of mining in South Africa.
NSSP.G9.PEB.A3.recovery_strategy: An ore is a rock that contains enough of a useful mineral or metal to be worth mining. The metal must be extracted from the ore and then refined (purified) before use.

questions.question: What is an ore?
options: A rock containing enough useful metal or mineral to be worth mining
A pure block of metal ready to use
questions.expected: A rock containing enough useful metal or mineral to be worth mining
questions.memo: An ore is a rock with enough useful metal or mineral in it to make mining worthwhile.

questions.question: Why do we mine?
options: To get useful minerals and metals out of the Earth
questions.expected: To get useful minerals and metals out of the Earth
questions.memo: Mining gets useful minerals and metals out of the ground.

questions.question: After the ore is mined, the metal in it must be...
questions.memo: The metal is first extracted from the ore, then refined to make it pure.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa is rich in mineral resources such as gold and platinum.
questions.memo: True — South Africa is well known for gold, platinum and other mineral resources.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A rock with enough useful metal to be worth mining is called an ___.'
questions.memo: Such a rock is called an ore.

questions.question: Is an ore a pure, ready-to-use metal?
options: No — the metal must first be extracted from the ore
Yes — an ore is pure metal
No — an ore contains no metal
questions.expected: No — the metal must first be extracted from the ore
questions.memo: An ore is rock mixed with the metal; the metal has to be extracted and refined first.

questions.question: Put the steps of getting a usable metal in the correct order.

items.text: Extract the metal from the ore

questions.memo: Find the ore → mine it → extract the metal → refine it into a pure, usable metal.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'refine' a metal?
options: To make it pure by removing impurities
To dig it out of the ground
questions.expected: To make it pure by removing impurities
questions.memo: Refining removes impurities to give a purer metal.

questions.question: Why is gold mining important to South Africa?
options: It provides jobs, materials and income for the country
It has no effect on the country
questions.expected: It provides jobs, materials and income for the country
questions.memo: Mining provides jobs, valuable materials and income, which matter to the economy.

questions.question: Which of these is a mineral resource mined in South Africa?
questions.memo: Gold (along with platinum, coal and diamonds) is mined in South Africa.

questions.question: True or false: mining can have negative effects on the environment.
questions.memo: True — mining can damage land, produce waste and cause pollution.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Getting the metal out of its ore is called ___.'
questions.memo: Getting the metal out of the ore is called extraction.

questions.question: Why must ore be processed before the metal is useful?
options: The metal is mixed with other rock and must be separated and purified
questions.expected: The metal is mixed with other rock and must be separated and purified
questions.memo: In an ore, the metal is combined with rock, so it must be separated out and refined.

questions.question: A deep hole or tunnel dug to reach minerals underground is called a...
questions.memo: A mine is dug to reach and remove minerals from underground.

questions.question: A mine brings benefits like jobs and materials, but it also causes...
questions.memo: Alongside its benefits, mining can damage the environment and cause pollution.

questions.question: True or false: refining removes impurities to give a purer metal.
questions.memo: True — refining purifies the metal by removing impurities.

questions.question: Which step comes FIRST?
questions.memo: You must first find and mine the ore before extracting and refining the metal.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'South Africa is well known for mining ___.'
questions.memo: South Africa is famous for mining gold (among other minerals).

questions.question: Why is mining important to South Africa's economy?
options: It provides jobs, materials and export income
questions.expected: It provides jobs, materials and export income
questions.memo: Mining supports the economy through jobs, useful materials and income from exports.

questions.question: Iron ore is dug up, the iron is separated from the rock, and then the iron is purified. In simple terms, what are the two main steps AFTER mining?
options: Extracting the metal from the ore, then refining it
Refining the ore, then burying it
Selling the rock, then mining again
Melting the soil, then cooling it
questions.expected: Extracting the metal from the ore, then refining it
questions.memo: After mining, the metal is extracted from the ore and then refined (purified) for use.

NSSP.G9.PEB.A4.title: Atmosphere
NSSP.G9.PEB.A4.description: The layers of the atmosphere (such as the troposphere and stratosphere); the gases that make up the air; and the greenhouse effect and its link to climate.
NSSP.G9.PEB.A4.recovery_strategy: Greenhouse gases trap some of the Sun's heat in the atmosphere, keeping the Earth warm. Too much greenhouse gas traps too much heat, warming the planet further. The troposphere is the lowest layer, where weather happens.

questions.question: What is the atmosphere?
options: The layer of gases (air) around the Earth
The solid rock of the Earth
questions.expected: The layer of gases (air) around the Earth
questions.memo: The atmosphere is the layer of gases (air) that surrounds the Earth.

questions.question: In which layer of the atmosphere does our weather happen?
questions.memo: Weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere.

questions.question: Which gas makes up most of the air?
questions.memo: Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths of the air; oxygen is most of the rest.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Greenhouse gases trapping some of the Sun's heat in the atmosphere
The Earth cooling down at night
questions.expected: Greenhouse gases trapping some of the Sun's heat in the atmosphere
questions.memo: The greenhouse effect is greenhouse gases trapping some of the Sun's heat, keeping the Earth warm.

questions.question: True or false: the atmosphere is made mostly of gases.
questions.memo: True — the atmosphere is made of gases (air).

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the atmosphere's layers. Which is the LOWEST layer?
questions.memo: The troposphere is the lowest layer, closest to the ground, where weather occurs.

questions.question: Do greenhouse gases cool the Earth down?
options: No — they trap heat and keep the Earth warm
Yes — they make the Earth colder
Yes — they block all the Sun's heat
No — they have no effect on temperature
questions.expected: No — they trap heat and keep the Earth warm
questions.memo: Greenhouse gases trap heat and warm the Earth; they do not cool it.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'The lowest layer of the atmosphere is the ___.'
questions.memo: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere.

questions.question: The layer just above the troposphere, containing the ozone layer, is the...
questions.memo: The stratosphere sits above the troposphere and contains the ozone layer.

questions.question: Put the atmosphere's layers in order, from the ground upward.
questions.memo: From the ground up: troposphere → stratosphere → mesosphere → thermosphere.

questions.question: True or false: without any greenhouse effect, the Earth would be much colder.
questions.memo: True — some greenhouse effect is needed to keep the Earth warm enough for life.

questions.question: Too much greenhouse gas in the atmosphere causes...
options: the Earth to warm further (global warming)
questions.expected: the Earth to warm further (global warming)
questions.memo: Extra greenhouse gas traps too much heat, warming the planet — global warming.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Greenhouse gases ___ heat in the atmosphere.'
questions.memo: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

questions.question: Why is some greenhouse effect important for life on Earth?
options: It keeps the Earth warm enough for living things
It makes the Earth too hot for life
questions.expected: It keeps the Earth warm enough for living things
questions.memo: Without any greenhouse effect, the Earth would be too cold; it keeps temperatures suitable for life.

questions.question: Burning a lot of fossil fuels adds greenhouse gases to the air, which...
options: trap more heat and warm the planet
questions.expected: trap more heat and warm the planet
questions.memo: Extra greenhouse gases from burning fuels trap more heat, warming the planet.

questions.question: Clouds, rain and wind all occur in which layer?
questions.memo: Weather — clouds, rain and wind — happens in the troposphere.

questions.question: True or false: the atmosphere helps protect life on Earth.
questions.memo: True — the atmosphere provides air to breathe, keeps the Earth warm and shields it from some of the Sun's harmful rays.

questions.question: Which of these is a greenhouse gas?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Weather happens in the ___ layer of the atmosphere.'
questions.memo: Weather happens in the troposphere.

questions.question: Why are scientists concerned about rising carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere?
options: More carbon dioxide traps more heat, warming the Earth and changing the climate
More carbon dioxide cools the Earth too much
Carbon dioxide removes all the oxygen
Carbon dioxide has no effect on climate
questions.expected: More carbon dioxide traps more heat, warming the Earth and changing the climate
questions.memo: Rising carbon dioxide strengthens the greenhouse effect, warming the planet and disrupting the climate.

NSSP.G9.PEB.A5.title: Birth, life & death of stars
NSSP.G9.PEB.A5.description: How a star is born from a cloud of gas and dust; the long stable life of a star like the Sun; and what happens when a star runs out of fuel and dies.
NSSP.G9.PEB.A5.caps_topic: Birth, life and death of stars
NSSP.G9.PEB.A5.recovery_strategy: A star is born when a cloud of gas and dust pulls together and heats up; it lives for a long, stable time while it has fuel; when the fuel runs out, it dies. Order: gas cloud → star shines → fuel runs out → star dies.

questions.question: A star is born from...
options: a cloud of gas and dust
questions.expected: a cloud of gas and dust
questions.memo: A star is born when a cloud of gas and dust pulls together and heats up.

questions.question: A star like the Sun spends most of its life...
options: shining steadily while it has fuel
questions.expected: shining steadily while it has fuel
questions.memo: For most of its life a star shines steadily, while it still has fuel.

questions.question: A star dies when...
questions.memo: A star dies once it has used up the fuel that lets it shine.

questions.question: True or false: stars do not last forever.
questions.memo: True — stars are born, live for a long time, and eventually die.

questions.question: Put the stages of a star's life in order.

items.text: A cloud of gas and dust
The star runs out of fuel

questions.memo: Gas cloud → star forms and shines → fuel runs out → star dies.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A star is born when a cloud of gas and ___ pulls together.'
questions.memo: A star forms from a cloud of gas and dust pulling together.

questions.question: Does a star die before it is born from a gas cloud?
options: No — it is born from the cloud first, then dies much later
Yes — birth and death happen together
questions.expected: No — it is born from the cloud first, then dies much later
questions.memo: A star is born from the gas cloud, shines for a long time, and dies only much later.

questions.question: What pulls the gas and dust together to form a star?
questions.memo: Gravity pulls the cloud of gas and dust together until it heats up and a star forms.

questions.question: Our Sun is currently...
options: in the long, stable part of its life
questions.expected: in the long, stable part of its life
questions.memo: The Sun is a middle-aged star, in the long stable phase of shining steadily.

questions.question: True or false: a star shines because of energy released in its core.
questions.memo: True — a star shines using the energy released in its hot core.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'A star dies when it runs out of ___.'
questions.memo: A star dies when its fuel runs out.

questions.question: What is the FIRST stage of a star's life?
options: A cloud of gas and dust coming together
The star running out of fuel
questions.expected: A cloud of gas and dust coming together
questions.memo: The first stage is a cloud of gas and dust pulling together under gravity.

questions.question: Why does a star eventually die?
options: It uses up the fuel that lets it shine
It is hit by the Sun
questions.expected: It uses up the fuel that lets it shine
questions.memo: Once a star has used up its fuel, it can no longer shine, so it dies.

questions.question: A star has used up all its fuel and stops shining. It is...
options: at the end of its life (dying)
in the middle of its life
becoming a gas cloud again for the first time
questions.expected: at the end of its life (dying)
questions.memo: Running out of fuel and no longer shining marks the end of a star's life.

questions.question: True or false: the Sun is a star that will eventually run out of fuel.
questions.memo: True — like all stars, the Sun will one day run out of fuel (in billions of years).

questions.question: Which comes FIRST in a star's life?
options: Forming from a gas and dust cloud
questions.expected: Forming from a gas and dust cloud
questions.memo: A star first forms from a gas and dust cloud, before it shines and later dies.

questions.question: Fill in the gap: 'Gravity pulls a cloud of gas and dust together to form a ___.'
questions.memo: Gravity pulls the cloud together to form a star.

questions.question: How is a star's life cycle similar to that of a living thing?
options: It has a birth, a long life, and a death
It can reproduce by laying eggs
questions.expected: It has a birth, a long life, and a death
questions.memo: Like living things, a star is 'born', 'lives' for a long time, and eventually 'dies'.

questions.question: Most of a star's life is spent...
questions.memo: A star spends most of its life in the stable phase of shining steadily.

questions.question: Which correctly puts a star's life in order, with the right idea?
options: Gas cloud → star shines for a long time → fuel runs out → star dies
Star dies → gas cloud → star shines → fuel runs out
Star shines → gas cloud → star dies → fuel runs out
Fuel runs out → star dies → gas cloud → star shines
questions.expected: Gas cloud → star shines for a long time → fuel runs out → star dies
questions.memo: The correct order is: gas cloud → star forms and shines → fuel runs out → star dies.
